artistBio: Lenore Tawney (1907–2007) began weaving in her forties and became a leader of the fiber art movement. She lived simply and drew on Zen and Christian mysticism. In 1963 she showed in the landmark exhibition Woven Forms in New York.

title: Fabric Works
medium: Sewn fabric from her own clothing and household linens
about: Late in her life, Bourgeois cut up her own clothes, towels and linens and sewed them into books, heads and figures. The fabric holds memories of her life. Sewing for her was about repair, holding together what was broken. Her famous spider sculptures honor her mother, a patient weaver and mender.
artistBio: Louise Bourgeois (1911–2010) grew up in France, where her family ran a workshop restoring old tapestries. She moved to New York in 1938. She became one of the most important artists of the 20th century, working in many materials, and returned to fabric in her final decades.

title: The Vanity of Small Differences
medium: Wool, cotton, acrylic, polyester and silk tapestry
about: Six large tapestries that follow the life of Tim Rakewell from a working-class childhood to wealth and an early death. They are inspired by Hogarth's 18th-century series A Rake's Progress. Perry looks at how taste in furniture, clothes and food marks social class in Britain. They are funny and sharp.
artistBio: Grayson Perry was born in 1960 in Essex and is a potter, printmaker and broadcaster. He won the Turner Prize in 2003. He designed the tapestries on a computer, and they were woven by machine. They have toured widely in the UK and abroad.

title: The Key in the Hand
c: Chiharu Shiota Key in the Hand
about: A room filled with a dense web of red yarn, hanging from the ceiling with tens of thousands of old keys tied into it, over two wooden boats. Keys hold memories of the people who used them and the places they protected. The red threads connect them like blood or fate. It filled Japan's pavilion at the Venice Biennale.
artistBio: Chiharu Shiota was born in Osaka in 1972 and lives in Berlin. She is known for huge installations of thread, often red or black, wrapped around objects like beds, dresses and pianos. Her work is about memory, loss and the connections between people.

title: Soundsuits
medium: Found materials, sequins, buttons, twigs, hair, knitting
about: Full-body suits covered in buttons, twigs, sequins, beads or dyed hair. They make sound when worn. Cave made the first one from twigs after the 1992 beating of Rodney King, thinking about how it feels to be seen only as a threat. A Soundsuit hides race, gender and class, so you see only wonder.
artistBio: Nick Cave was born in 1959 in Missouri and trained as a dancer and sculptor. He teaches at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. He has made more than 500 Soundsuits, often worn in joyful public performances.

title: Nelson's Ship in a Bottle
medium: Glass, resin and printed cotton (Dutch wax) sails
c: Nelson's Ship in a Bottle Shonibare
about: A model of Admiral Nelson's flagship inside a giant glass bottle, with sails made of brightly patterned "African" wax-print fabric. That fabric was first produced by Dutch companies imitating Indonesian batik and was later embraced in West Africa. Shonibare uses it to show how tangled the histories of empire, trade and identity are.
artistBio: Yinka Shonibare was born in London in 1962, grew up in Lagos and returned to London. Wax-print fabric is his signature material. The ship stood on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square and is now at the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich.

title: Blanket Stories
about: Tall columns of folded wool blankets, each donated by someone along with its story: a wedding gift, a baby's blanket, a blanket from a hard winter. In Seneca culture and many others, blankets are given to honor people at important moments. The stacks become monuments of shared memory, built by a community.
artistBio: Marie Watt was born in 1967 and is a citizen of the Seneca Nation. She lives in Portland, Oregon. She often makes her work through sewing circles, where people gather to stitch and talk together, so making art becomes a social act.

title: Knotted Hemp Sculptures
about: Large, rich-colored figures knotted from hemp rope. They look like goddesses, plants or forest beings, at once human and botanical. Mukherjee drew on Indian temple sculpture and on the natural world. The slow knotting gives the forms a strong, living presence.
artistBio: Mrinalini Mukherjee (1949–2015) was born in Mumbai and studied in Baroda. Her parents were both artists. She worked mainly in fiber, later in ceramics and bronze. A major retrospective of her work, Phenomenal Nature, was shown at the Met Breuer in New York in 2019.

title: Bottari
about: Bundles made by tying up old clothes in brightly colored Korean bedcovers, the kind given to newlyweds. A bottari is what people carry when they move, migrate or flee. In one famous work, she rode a truck piled with bottari through the places she had lived. The bundles hold a whole life, ready to leave.
artistBio: Kimsooja was born in Daegu, South Korea, in 1957. She started sewing as art after sewing a bedcover with her mother. She works with fabric, video and performance, and often thinks of herself as a needle moving through the world.

title: Seoul Home / L.A. Home
about: A full-size copy of his childhood home in Seoul, sewn from translucent green silk, with every door handle and window frame. It can be folded into a suitcase and hung in any gallery. It is a picture of what it feels like to carry home with you when you live far away.
artistBio: Do Ho Suh was born in Seoul in 1962 and has lived in the United States and London. His fabric houses and rooms, sewn in many colors, have been shown around the world. They come from his own experience of moving between countries.

title: Woven Works
medium: Beads, rope, wire, string and fabric
about: Large hangings woven from glass beads, rope and wire that look like maps or worn floors. Some trace the paths people make walking across open ground in his neighborhood. Others use the pattern of old linoleum floors from family homes. They are about memory, faith and the marks people leave on places.
artistBio: Igshaan Adams was born in 1982 in Cape Town and grew up in Bonteheuwel, a neighborhood created under apartheid. His work draws on his family, his Muslim faith and his community. He has had major exhibitions in South Africa, Europe and the United States.

title: Trapunto Paintings
medium: Stitched and stuffed painted canvas with beads, mirrors and buttons
about: Huge, bright paintings stitched and padded so they puff out from the wall, covered with buttons, shells, mirrors and sequins. Some show masks and patterns from the many countries she lived in. Others tell the stories of refugees and migrants. They mix painting and textile into something joyful and serious at once.
artistBio: Pacita Abad (1946–2004) was born in the Philippines and lived in more than a dozen countries. She learned textile techniques from local artisans wherever she went. A major retrospective toured from SFMOMA in 2023.

title: Silk Collages
about: Scenes of everyday life made from pieces of raw silk sewn by hand: a woman cooking, bathing her child, looking out at the city. Zangewa shows the quiet work of caring for a home and family as something worthy of art. The shining silk gives these ordinary moments a calm dignity.
artistBio: Billie Zangewa was born in Malawi in 1973 and grew up in Botswana. She lives in Johannesburg. She often uses herself and her son as subjects. Her work is shown internationally.

title: The Overlord Embroidery
artist: Sandra Lawrence and the Royal School of Needlework
about: Thirty-four panels telling the story of D-Day and the Normandy landings in 1944, from the planning to the battle. Inspired by the Bayeux Tapestry, it is even longer, at about 83 meters. It shows soldiers, ships, factories and civilians, honoring the many people behind the invasion.
artistBio: Lord Dulverton commissioned it. Sandra Lawrence designed it, and a team at the Royal School of Needlework made it over about five years. It is displayed at the D-Day Story museum in Portsmouth.

title: The Great Tapestry of Scotland
about: One hundred and sixty panels telling the history of Scotland, from the Ice Age to the present: saints, kings, miners, poets, football and oil rigs. It is one of the longest embroideries in the world. Each panel was stitched by volunteers from the area it describes, so the nation tells its own story.
artistBio: The novelist Alexander McCall Smith had the idea. The artist Andrew Crummy designed the panels, and around a thousand volunteers stitched them. It now has a permanent home in Galashiels, in the Scottish Borders.

title: The Keiskamma Altarpiece
medium: Embroidery, appliqué, beadwork, wire and photographs
about: A huge folding altarpiece modeled on the Isenheim Altarpiece in France, which was made for a hospital treating people with a skin disease. In this version, the suffering is HIV and AIDS in a South African village. Local grandmothers, widows and children appear, stitched in thread. It mourns, and it also shows a community holding on to hope.
artistBio: The Keiskamma Art Project was started by the doctor and artist Carol Hofmeyr to create income for women in the village of Hamburg. Around 130 people worked on the altarpiece. It has been shown in churches and galleries in South Africa, Europe and North America.

title: The Changi Quilts
about: Quilts made of squares, each embroidered by a different woman with her name, a flower, a symbol or a message. They were made by women held prisoner by the Japanese in Singapore and were sent to the men's camp, supposedly for the wounded. In fact they were a secret way for wives to let husbands know they were alive.
artistBio: Ethel Mulvany, a Canadian internee, organized the project. Dozens of women of many nationalities each stitched a square. Three quilts are known to survive. One is at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra.

title: The Rajah Quilt
about: A large patchwork quilt made by women prisoners being transported from England to Van Diemen's Land, today's Tasmania. An embroidered message at the bottom thanks the ladies who gave them sewing supplies. It is a rare object from the lives of convict women, who left very few records of their own.
artistBio: Elizabeth Fry's society gave each woman sewing materials for the long voyage. Kezia Hayter, a free woman traveling with them, organized the quilt. Most of the makers' names are lost. It is at the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra.

title: Manto da Apresentação
medium: Embroidery on cloth, using thread from unraveled uniforms
about: A cloak embroidered inside and out with names, words and small images. He made it to wear on the Day of Judgment, so he could present the world to God. The names are of people he knew. He unraveled hospital uniforms to get blue thread. The cloak is a record of a whole world, stitched by one man.
artistBio: Arthur Bispo do Rosário (c. 1909–1989) spent about fifty years in a psychiatric hospital in Rio de Janeiro. There he made more than 800 objects from whatever he could find. His work was shown at the Venice Biennale in 1995 and is now celebrated in Brazil.

title: The Lady of Shalott
about: In Tennyson's poem, the Lady of Shalott is cursed to weave a tapestry of the world she may see only in a mirror. When she looks at the real world, she must leave. Here she sits in a boat drifting toward Camelot, her woven tapestry trailing in the water. It is about the price of art, longing and leaving safety.
artistBio: John William Waterhouse (1849–1917) was a British painter influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites, known for women from myth and legend. He painted the Lady of Shalott three times. This version is at Tate Britain in London.
f: John William Waterhouse - The Lady of Shalott - Google Art Project (derivative work - AutoContrast edit in LCH space).jpg

title: Penelope and the Suitors
about: In Homer's Odyssey, Penelope waits twenty years for her husband to return. She tells her suitors she will choose one when she finishes weaving a shroud, then secretly unpicks her work every night. Here she bites a thread at her loom while the men try to win her over. Weaving becomes her way of resisting.
artistBio: John William Waterhouse often painted women from myth. This was one of his late works. It is at Aberdeen Art Gallery in Scotland.
f: Penelope and the Suitors - John William Waterhouse - ABDAG003035.jpg

title: Young Mother Sewing
about: A woman bends over her sewing while a little girl leans on her lap and looks straight at us. The painting is about ordinary closeness: a child resting against a busy parent. Cassatt shows women's daily work and love without sentimentality. The loose brushwork keeps it fresh and alive.
artistBio: Mary Cassatt (1844–1926) was an American painter who lived in France and showed with the Impressionists. She is known for paintings of women and children. This work is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

title: The Ambassadors
about: Two French diplomats stand beside a table covered with an Anatolian carpet, globes, a lute and scientific tools. The carpet is painted so carefully that this type of rug is now called a "Holbein carpet." Across the floor lies a strange stretched shape that, seen from the side, becomes a skull. Wealth and learning are set beside death.
artistBio: Hans Holbein the Younger (c. 1497–1543) was a German painter who worked at the court of Henry VIII. He was one of the greatest portrait painters of his time. The painting is at the National Gallery in London.

title: The Syndics of the Drapers' Guild
about: Officials of the Amsterdam cloth makers' guild sit around a table covered with a rich red rug. Their job was to check the quality of dyed cloth. They look up as if someone has just walked in. Rembrandt makes a business meeting feel like a living moment, and shows the importance of the cloth trade to the city.
artistBio: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669) is one of the greatest painters in history. This was one of his last group portraits, painted when he was in financial trouble. It is at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

title: The Romanian Blouse
about: A woman in a white embroidered Romanian blouse sits against a flat red background. Matisse reworked the painting many times, simplifying it until the embroidered sleeve became a few bold marks. It shows his love for textiles. He kept a collection of fabrics from many countries and used them in his paintings.
artistBio: Henri Matisse (1869–1954) was a French painter and one of the leaders of modern art. He grew up in a weaving town in northern France. The painting is at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

title: The Cotton Pickers
about: Two young Black women stand in a field of cotton, carrying heavy sacks. Painted ten years after the Civil War, it shows them as strong, thoughtful people, not as background figures. Cotton was the fiber that drove the economy and the slave system. Homer gives the people who picked it their dignity.
artistBio: Winslow Homer (1836–1910) was an American painter known for scenes of the sea and rural life. He visited Virginia in the 1870s and painted the people he met there. The painting is at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

title: Women Mending Nets
about: Women sit on a windswept dune mending fishing nets, while one stands looking out to sea. Nets are fiber work too, essential to fishing families. The painting shows hard labor in a bleak landscape, with quiet strength. Perhaps the standing woman is waiting for someone to come home.
artistBio: Max Liebermann (1847–1935) was a German painter who often worked in the Netherlands. He became a leading figure in German art, until the Nazis forced him out of his positions. The painting is at the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

title: The Lace Maker
about: A young woman sits with her back to a plain wall, absorbed in her lace pillow. Her shoes lie on the floor. The bare setting focuses all attention on her work and stillness. Dutch paintings often presented lace making as a sign of a good and orderly home.
artistBio: Caspar Netscher (c. 1639–1684) was a Dutch painter who trained with Gerard ter Borch. He was known for small, finely painted scenes. This painting is in the Wallace Collection in London.

title: The Knitting Lesson
about: A mother sits beside her young daughter, guiding her hands as she learns to knit. The room is plain and warm. Millet often painted farm families at work, treating ordinary labor with seriousness and tenderness. Passing down a skill is shown as an act of love.
artistBio: Jean-François Millet (1814–1875) was a French painter known for scenes of peasant life, such as The Gleaners. He painted this subject in several versions. One is at the Saint Louis Art Museum.

title: Tapestry Weaving
about: In tapestry, the weaver passes colored weft threads back and forth only where each color is needed, packing them down so tightly that the warp threads disappear. The picture is built line by line from the bottom up, often while looking at the back. It is slow, careful work, and a skilled weaver may finish only a small area in a day.
artistBio: Tapestry is found in ancient Egypt, the Andes, China and medieval Europe, each developing it on its own. The great European workshops of Brussels, Arras and Paris made tapestries more valuable than paintings. Today, artists around the world still weave tapestry by hand.

title: Ikat
about: Before any weaving, bundles of thread are tied tightly in places with fiber or plastic, then dyed. The tied parts resist the dye. Untie, retie and dye again for more colors. When the threads go on the loom, the pattern appears, with its typical soft, feathered edges. The word comes from a Malay word meaning to tie.
artistBio: Ikat was developed independently in many places: Indonesia, India, Central Asia, Japan, Guatemala and West Africa. Warp ikat dyes the lengthwise threads, weft ikat the crosswise ones, and double ikat, the hardest, dyes both.

title: Shibori
about: Cloth is folded, twisted, bound, stitched or wrapped around a pole before it goes into the dye. Wherever the cloth is squeezed or covered, the dye cannot reach. Each method makes its own pattern, from tiny dots to spider-web rings to diagonal stripes. No two pieces come out exactly the same.
artistBio: Shibori is the Japanese name, and Japan developed dozens of methods, especially in the town of Arimatsu near Nagoya. Similar techniques exist worldwide, such as bandhani in India and adire in Nigeria. Indigo is the most traditional color.

title: Sashiko
about: Sashiko means "little stabs." It is a simple running stitch in white thread on indigo cloth, used to strengthen and patch fabric. The stitches form geometric patterns like waves, hemp leaves and interlocking circles. It began as practical mending and has become an art of slow, visible repair.
artistBio: Rural women in northern Japan used sashiko to layer and reinforce work clothes and to make cloth warmer. It is closely linked to boro. Today, sashiko is popular worldwide as part of the visible mending movement.

title: Felting
about: Felt is made without spinning or weaving. Wool fibers have tiny scales. When wool is wet, warm and rubbed or rolled, the scales lock together into a dense cloth. Nomads roll felt in reed mats, sometimes behind a horse. Felt is warm, windproof and can be shaped into hats, boots, rugs and whole tents.
artistBio: Felt may be the oldest fabric. The frozen tombs of Pazyryk held felt saddle cloths and hangings. Kyrgyz and Kazakh felt carpets, called shyrdak and syrmak, remain strong traditions, and artists today use felting for sculpture and fashion.

title: Bobbin Lace
about: The lace maker works on a firm pillow with a paper pattern pinned to it. Threads are wound on dozens of small wooden or bone bobbins, which she crosses and twists in sequence, holding the work in place with pins. The bobbins click softly as they move. Patterns can need hundreds of bobbins.
artistBio: Bobbin lace grew in Italy and Flanders in the 1500s and spread across Europe. Towns such as Bruges, Honiton and Le Puy became famous for their styles. Vermeer's Lacemaker shows a woman at this exact work.

title: Ruth Asawa
about: Ruth Asawa was born in California to Japanese immigrant farmers. During the Second World War, her family was sent to internment camps. She later studied at Black Mountain College with Josef Albers, and settled in San Francisco, where she raised six children while working as an artist.
artistBio: On a trip to Mexico, she learned a looping technique used to make wire egg baskets. She turned it into hanging sculptures of looped wire, forms inside forms that cast shadows like drawings. Her method is close to knitting and crochet. She also fought for arts education in San Francisco's public schools.
f: Untitled Looped Wire Sculpture, Ruth Asawa, De Young Museum Permanent Collection.jpg

title: Rosie Lee Tompkins
about: Rosie Lee Tompkins was the name used by Effie Mae Howard, who grew up in rural Arkansas and learned to quilt from her mother. She lived quietly in Richmond, California, and was a deeply religious woman. She avoided publicity and preferred that her real name not be used.
artistBio: Her quilts are bold and unpredictable, made of velvet, fake fur, printed T-shirts and bright scraps. Some include Bible verses. A major retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum in 2020 established her as one of the great American artists of her time.

title: Candace Wheeler
about: Candace Wheeler was an American designer who saw that many women needed a way to earn money from their skills. In 1877 she helped found the Society of Decorative Art in New York to help women sell needlework and crafts. She worked alongside Louis Comfort Tiffany before running her own company.
artistBio: Her firm, Associated Artists, run entirely by women, designed textiles and interiors, including work for the White House. She invented a needle-woven tapestry technique and designed printed silks with American plants. She was one of the first women to succeed as a professional interior designer in the United States.

title: Ethel Mairet
about: Ethel Mairet spent years in Sri Lanka and India, where she studied local crafts and saw how industrial cloth was harming village weavers. Back in England, she wrote a book on vegetable dyes and became a leader of the hand-weaving revival.
artistBio: At her workshop, Gospels, in Ditchling, Sussex, she trained many weavers who went on to teach across Britain and abroad. She believed hand weavers should experiment and work with industry, not just copy the past. Her book Vegetable Dyes is still read today.

title: Hosteen Klah
about: Hosteen Klah was a Diné healer, or hataałii, who knew many long and complex ceremonies. He was nádleehi, a person of a recognized gender role in Diné tradition, and he learned weaving, usually women's work, as well as ceremonial knowledge, usually men's.
artistBio: Klah made the controversial choice to weave sacred sandpainting images into permanent tapestries, so the knowledge would not be lost. With Mary Cabot Wheelwright, he founded what is now the Wheelwright Museum of the American Indian in Santa Fe to preserve Diné ceremonial knowledge.

title: Indigo
about: Indigo gives the deep blue of jeans, boro and adire. It comes from the leaves of plants such as Indigofera and woad. The dye is not water-soluble, so it must be put in a special vat. Cloth comes out of the vat yellow-green and turns blue before your eyes as the air touches it.
artistBio: Indigo was used in ancient Peru, Egypt and India. It was so valuable that it was called "blue gold." In colonial times it was grown by enslaved people in the Americas. Since 1897, most indigo has been synthetic, but natural indigo dyers work around the world today.

title: Cochineal
about: Cochineal is a brilliant red from tiny insects that live on prickly pear cactus. The insects are dried and crushed. Depending on what is added, the dye can give pinks, scarlets, crimsons and purples. It colored Teotitlán rugs, Andean textiles and Zapotec clothing.
artistBio: Indigenous farmers in Mexico and Peru bred the insects for centuries. After the Spanish conquest, cochineal became one of Mexico's most valuable exports and colored European paintings and the red coats of British soldiers. It is still used today, including in foods.

title: Tyrian Purple
about: Tyrian purple came from the glands of sea snails. Thousands of snails were needed to dye a single garment, and the process smelled terrible. The color shifts between purple and red and does not fade easily. Because it was so costly, it became the color of emperors and was often restricted by law.
artistBio: It was made in Phoenician cities such as Tyre, in today's Lebanon. Roman and Byzantine rulers used it as a sign of power. Production largely ended after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and the word "purple" still suggests royalty.

title: Madder
about: Madder red comes from the roots of the madder plant, dried and ground. With different mordants it gives warm reds, oranges, pinks and browns. Turkey red, a bright and very fast madder color, took a long and secret process. It is the red of many Turkmen carpets and Indian chintzes.
artistBio: Madder-dyed cloth has been found in ancient Egypt and the Indus Valley. For centuries, it was one of the world's most important crops. In 1868, chemists made its coloring agent synthetically, and madder fields declined almost overnight. Natural dyers still grow it today.

title: The Drop Spindle
about: A spindle is a stick with a weight, called a whorl, near one end. The spinner twists fiber onto it and lets it spin and drop, so it pulls and twists the fiber into yarn. It is simple, portable and can be used while walking or herding animals. For most of human history, all thread was spun this way.
artistBio: Spindle whorls are among the most common finds in archaeology, from the Andes to China. Spindles are still used daily in many places, and handspinners around the world use them for fine, controlled yarn.

title: The Backstrap Loom
medium: Sticks, cord and the weaver's body
about: One end of the loom ties to a tree or post, and the other to a strap around the weaver's hips. She controls the tension by leaning back or forward, so her body is part of the loom. It rolls up and can be carried anywhere. Some of the most complex textiles in the world are made on it.
artistBio: Backstrap looms were used by the Maya, the Inca and peoples across Asia. Maya women in Guatemala and weavers in the Andes and Southeast Asia still use them every day.
f: Woman on a backstrap loom in Oaxaca.jpg

title: The Spinning Wheel
about: A spinning wheel turns a spindle with a large wheel, driven by hand or foot. It spins much faster than a hand spindle. Later wheels added a flyer that twists and winds the yarn at the same time. Many homes had one, and the image of a woman at her wheel became a symbol of home life.
artistBio: The spinning wheel probably developed in India or China and reached Europe in the Middle Ages. Gandhi made the charkha, a small spinning wheel, a symbol of India's independence movement and self-reliance. Handspinners today still use wheels, many made new.

title: The Jacquard Loom
about: The Jacquard loom uses a chain of punched cards to control which threads lift for each row. That made complex patterns, even portraits, possible on a machine. It was one of the first programmable machines, and it inspired early computer pioneers such as Charles Babbage and Ada Lovelace.
artistBio: Joseph Marie Jacquard developed it in Lyon, a center of silk weaving. Weavers feared it would take their jobs, and some attacked it. It changed the textile industry, and today computerized Jacquard looms weave much of the patterned cloth we buy.

title: The Woolsack
about: In the House of Lords sits a large red cushion stuffed with wool, called the Woolsack. It is said to have been introduced under Edward III in the 1300s, when wool was England's most important export, as a reminder of where the kingdom's wealth came from. The person who chairs the House of Lords still sits on it.
artistBio: In 1938 it was discovered that the Woolsack was stuffed with horsehair. It was then refilled with wool from across Britain and the Commonwealth, as a sign of unity. Medieval wool money also built many of England's great "wool churches."

title: The Luddites
about: Skilled textile workers in Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Lancashire broke into mills at night and smashed new machines, such as stocking frames and power looms. They were not simply against technology. They were protesting low pay, cheap poor-quality goods and the loss of their trade. They signed letters in the name of a made-up leader, Ned Ludd.
artistBio: The government sent thousands of soldiers and in 1812 made machine-breaking a crime punishable by death. Many Luddites were hanged or transported to Australia. Today "Luddite" means someone who resists new technology, but historians see a more complex story about work and dignity.

title: Spinning Bees and the Daughters of Liberty
about: When Britain taxed imported goods, American colonists began boycotting British cloth. Women gathered for public spinning bees, sometimes dozens at a time, often at a minister's house, to spin yarn for homespun cloth. Wearing homespun became a political statement. Spinning, usually private household work, became a public act.
artistBio: Groups of women known as the Daughters of Liberty organized many of these events, and newspapers reported on them to encourage others. The boycott pressured Britain to repeal most of the taxes. It was one of the first times American women took a visible part in politics.

title: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
about: A fire broke out on the upper floors of a factory that made women's blouses. Many doors were locked, and the fire escape collapsed. 146 garment workers died, most of them young Jewish and Italian immigrant women. Crowds watched helplessly from the street. It was one of the deadliest workplace disasters in the city's history.
artistBio: The disaster led to major new laws on fire safety and working conditions in New York and helped build the labor movement. Frances Perkins, who witnessed it, later became U.S. Secretary of Labor. Each year the dead are remembered by name.

title: The Stole and Maniple of Saint Cuthbert
about: These two long, narrow strips were made to be worn by a priest at Mass. They are embroidered in colored silk and gold thread with standing prophets, saints and popes, each named in Latin beside him. The figures are calm and upright, framed by leafy plants. Gold thread was laid on the surface and tied down with tiny stitches, so very little of the precious metal was hidden on the back.
artistBio: Inscriptions say Queen Ælfflæd ordered the work for Frithestan, Bishop of Winchester. The names of the stitchers are not recorded. Some years later King Æthelstan gave the pieces to the shrine of Saint Cuthbert. They were found in the saint's coffin in 1827 and are now kept at Durham Cathedral. They are among the oldest English embroideries to survive.
c: St Cuthbert stole maniple embroidery Durham

title: The Butler-Bowdon Cope
medium: Silk and silver-gilt thread on velvet
about: A cope is a large half-circle cloak worn by clergy for processions. This one is cut from deep red velvet and embroidered with scenes from the life of the Virgin Mary, set under rows of slender Gothic arches. Lions' faces, leaves and birds fill the gaps. Working fine stitches through thick velvet was hard, and the embroiderers did it with great control.
artistBio: English church embroidery of this period was famous across Europe and was called opus anglicanum, English work. It was made in professional workshops, many in London, by both men and women. The cope takes its name from the Butler-Bowdon family, who kept it for centuries. It is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

title: The Star Mantle of Emperor Henry II
about: This deep blue cloak is covered with gold embroidery of the heavens: stars, signs of the zodiac, Christ in majesty, angels and saints. Latin inscriptions explain the figures. Whoever wore it was wrapped in the whole cosmos, a clear message about the emperor's place under God. An inscription also names a man called Ismahel, who is thought to have ordered it as a gift for Henry.
artistBio: The embroiderers are unknown. The mantle passed to Bamberg Cathedral, which Henry founded. In the fifteenth century the worn original was carefully cut out and sewn onto new silk, so the gold work we see today sits on a later ground. It is kept in the cathedral's museum in Bamberg.

title: The Battle of Pavia Tapestries
about: This set of seven large tapestries shows the battle of 1525 in which the army of Emperor Charles V defeated the French and captured King Francis I. Each panel is crowded with horses, pikes, guns and fleeing soldiers, with real commanders picked out among them. The weavers kept the scale and detail of a painting while working in wool and silk.
artistBio: Bernard van Orley was court painter in Brussels and one of the leading tapestry designers of his time. The tapestries were presented to Charles V. They later came to the d'Avalos family of Naples, descendants of one of the commanders, and are now in the Museo di Capodimonte in Naples.

title: L'Histoire du Roy (The Story of the King)
about: This series of fourteen tapestries tells the reign of Louis XIV as a run of triumphs: his coronation, royal weddings, sieges and even a visit to the Gobelins workshops. That last panel shows workers carrying in silver, carpets and tapestries for the king to admire. The scenes are large, busy and carefully staged, like theater.
artistBio: Charles Le Brun was first painter to the king and director of the royal Gobelins Manufactory, which gathered weavers, cabinetmakers and goldsmiths to furnish the palaces. The series was woven several times. Tapestries from it are in French national collections, including Versailles. The Gobelins still weaves today as part of the Mobilier national.
c: Histoire du Roy tapestry Gobelins Le Brun

title: Tunic Roundels and Bands from Late Roman Egypt
artist: Weavers of Egypt (often called Coptic textiles)
about: Linen tunics in late Roman Egypt were decorated with woven purple or colored wool roundels on the shoulders and knees and bands running down from the neck. They show dancers, hunters, vines, birds and later Christian crosses. The decoration was woven right into the tunic while it was on the loom, often in tapestry technique with a fine linen thread used for outlines.
artistBio: These textiles survive because people were buried in their clothes in the dry sand of Egypt. Many were cut from tunics by dealers in the nineteenth century, so museums often hold only the decorated pieces. The weavers were Egyptians of many faiths. Large collections are in Paris, London, Berlin and New York.

title: Textiles of the Noin-Ula Burials
artist: Xiongnu, Chinese and Central Asian makers
about: The royal tombs at Noin-Ula held textiles from across Asia. There were Chinese silks with clouds and characters, felt carpets with animal combat scenes, and wool hangings embroidered with men's faces and horsemen that look Central Asian or Greek in style. Together they show how goods traveled along trade routes long before anyone called them the Silk Road.
artistBio: The Xiongnu were a nomadic confederation north of China. The tombs were excavated in 1924 and 1925 by an expedition led by Pyotr Kozlov. Some of the textiles were made locally and others came as trade or diplomatic gifts. Most are in the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.

title: Clothing of the Egtved Girl
about: A young woman was buried in an oak coffin wearing a short woven wool top with elbow sleeves and a skirt made of twisted wool cords hanging from a band. A belt held a round bronze disc at her waist. The cord skirt would have swung as she walked. It is one of the best preserved outfits from Bronze Age Europe.
artistBio: The coffin was found in a burial mound in 1921. Acid water in the mound dissolved her bones but kept wool, hair and skin. Her clothing was spun and woven by people whose names we will never know. It is now in the National Museum of Denmark in Copenhagen.
c: Egtved Girl clothing National Museum Denmark

title: The Thorsberg Trousers
artist: Iron Age weavers of northern Germany
about: These are a pair of full-length wool trousers, woven in a diamond twill and tailored with a seat gusset and sock-like feet. They were found in a bog together with weapons, tunics and cloaks left as offerings. The fit and finishing show skilled tailoring, and they look surprisingly modern.
artistBio: The makers belonged to Germanic peoples living along the Baltic in the Roman period. The bog kept the wool for well over a thousand years. The trousers are now in the archaeology museum at Schloss Gottorf in Schleswig, along with other finds from the same moor.

title: Sakyamuni Preaching on Vulture Peak
about: This large embroidered hanging, well over two meters tall, shows the Buddha standing on a mountain in red robes, flanked by disciples and bodhisattvas. Below kneel the men and women who paid for it, offering it as a pious act. The whole surface is filled with tight satin stitch, so it glows like a painting.
artistBio: It was found sealed in the Library Cave at the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, where thousands of manuscripts and paintings had been hidden around the year 1000. Aurel Stein acquired it in 1907. It is now in the British Museum in London. It is one of the largest Chinese embroideries of its age.
c: Sakyamuni Vulture Peak embroidery British Museum

title: Tenjukoku Shūchō Mandala
artist: Court embroiderers for Princess Tachibana no Ōiratsume
about: This embroidery was made to show the Land of Heavenly Longevity, where Prince Shōtoku was believed to dwell after his death. Only fragments survive. They show small figures, buildings, the moon with a rabbit, and turtles carrying characters on their shells, which once spelled out the story of the piece.
artistBio: The prince's widow had it made after he died in 622. It is one of the oldest embroideries in Japan. In the thirteenth century a copy was made, and surviving pieces of both were later mounted together. It belongs to the nunnery of Chūgū-ji next to Hōryū-ji and is a National Treasure.

title: Karaori Noh Robe
about: Karaori robes are worn by Noh actors playing women. The patterns, often autumn grasses, fans or flowers on blocks of color, look embroidered, but they are woven. Long floats of glossy colored silk lie on the surface, held only at their ends. On stage, under lamplight, the floats catch the light as the actor moves slowly.
artistBio: The name means Chinese weaving, a nod to the Chinese silks that inspired it. These robes were woven in the Nishijin district of Kyoto and collected by warrior families who sponsored Noh. Theater companies kept them for generations. Fine examples are in the Tokyo National Museum and in museums abroad.

title: Miao Festival Embroidery
about: Miao women in the hills of Guizhou decorate jackets, collars, sleeves and baby carriers with dense embroidery. Each area has its own style: tiny cross stitch, braided silk couched down in coils, or folded and pleated work. Butterflies, dragons, fish and birds come from Miao stories of how the world and people began.
artistBio: Girls learn from their mothers and grandmothers and spend years making the clothes they will wear at festivals and their weddings. Because the Miao had no traditional written script, embroidery has been called a way of carrying history. Today some women work for cooperatives, while machine-made imitations are sold in markets.

title: Suzhou Double-Sided Embroidery
about: Suzhou embroidery is famous for its fineness. A single silk thread can be split into many thinner strands, and stitches are blended so smoothly that fur and feathers seem real. In double-sided work, the embroiderer hides every knot and thread end so that a cat or goldfish looks finished from both sides of a sheer gauze screen.
artistBio: Su embroidery is counted among the four great regional embroideries of China, with those of Hunan, Guangdong and Sichuan. The city has been a silk center for centuries. In the early twentieth century, the embroiderer Shen Shou became known for realistic portraits in thread. Workshops and an embroidery research institute keep the craft going in Suzhou today.

title: Chikankari
medium: White cotton thread on fine muslin
about: Chikankari is white embroidery on sheer cotton. Flowers and vines are worked in many small stitches. In the best known one, the thread crosses behind the cloth so the motif shows through as a soft shadow from the front. Tiny knots and raised dots add texture. Held up to the light, a kurta looks like it has been drawn in breath.
artistBio: A popular story links it to the Mughal court, and it flourished in Lucknow under the Nawabs of Awadh. Today most of the work is done by women at home in and around Lucknow, often through middlemen. The fabric is first printed with removable blue designs, then embroidered, washed and finished.

title: Toda Embroidery (Pukhoor)
artist: Toda women of the Nilgiri Hills
medium: Red and black wool on white cotton
about: Toda women decorate a thick white cotton shawl, the puthukuli, with bands of red and black wool. They work from the back of the cloth, counting threads, so the geometric patterns appear on the front with a raised, almost woven look. The designs have names drawn from their surroundings, such as flowers and buffalo horns.
artistBio: The Toda are a small pastoral community in the Nilgiri Hills of southern India, whose life has long centered on buffalo herding. The shawl is worn by both men and women and is used in important rites. Women now also embroider bags and table linens for sale, which helps keep the skill alive.

title: Suzani
place: Bukhara, Samarkand and Shahrisabz, Central Asia
about: A suzani is a large hanging covered with bold round flowers, suns and moons, curling stems and leaves. The name comes from the Persian word for needle. Designs were drawn onto several strips of cotton, which were then embroidered by different women and sewn together. Small mismatches where the strips meet are part of their charm.
artistBio: Suzanis were made as dowry pieces by a bride and her female relatives, and hung in the home or over the marriage bed. Each town had its own color and pattern style. Many fine nineteenth-century examples left Central Asia in the twentieth century, and today Uzbek workshops make new ones with natural dyes.

title: Anatolian Kilim
artist: Village and nomadic women of Anatolia
about: A kilim is a rug with no pile. Colored wool wefts are beaten tightly over the warp, and where two colors meet in a vertical line, small slits are left open. This is why kilim patterns are full of stepped diamonds and zigzags. Motifs carry names, such as the figure with hands on hips, elibelinde, often read as a sign of womanhood and fertility.
artistBio: Kilims were woven by women for their own households and dowries, as floor covers, bags, cushions and tent dividers. Designs passed from mother to daughter and varied by region and group. Old kilims were long overlooked by collectors in favor of pile carpets and are now widely studied and valued.

title: Aso Oke
about: Aso oke means top cloth. It is woven in narrow strips on a horizontal loom, and the strips are sewn edge to edge into wrappers, caps and robes. The three classic kinds are sanyan, woven from beige wild silk; alaari, with deep red; and etu, a dark indigo blue with fine lines. It is worn for weddings, funerals and festivals.
artistBio: Traditionally men wove aso oke on narrow looms, while women wove wider cloth on upright looms. Iseyin and Oyo are well known weaving towns. Families and friends often agree to wear matching cloth, called aso ebi, at a celebration. Weavers today use shiny synthetic yarns along with cotton and silk.

title: Kanga
about: A kanga is a printed rectangle of cotton with a bold border, a central design and a saying printed in Swahili. The two pieces of a pair are cut apart and worn as a wrap, a head cloth or a baby sling. The saying matters most. A woman may choose a kanga to send a message of love, advice or a pointed remark to a neighbor.
artistBio: Kangas appeared on the Swahili coast, around Zanzibar and Mombasa, in the late nineteenth century, when women are said to have stitched printed handkerchiefs together. Later the cloth was printed in Europe and India, and now largely in East Africa. Sayings change with the times, from proverbs to political slogans.

title: Ethiopian Tibeb Cloth
about: Ethiopian dress cloth is fine white cotton, soft and slightly sheer, woven on a pit loom. Along the edges runs a colored woven border called tibeb, made of crosses, diamonds and bands. A netela shawl or a long habesha kemis dress is worn to church, weddings and holidays, and the border is often the most noticed part.
artistBio: Handloom weaving has a long history in Ethiopia. The Dorze people of the south are among the best known weaving communities, and many work in Addis Ababa. Cotton was traditionally spun by women and woven by men. Designers today use tibeb borders in modern fashion.

title: Ugandan Barkcloth
medium: Beaten bark of the mutuba tree
about: Barkcloth is made from the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree. The bark is stripped in one piece, softened, and beaten for hours with grooved wooden mallets until it spreads into a broad, soft sheet. Left in the sun, it turns a warm terracotta brown. The tree is not cut down and grows new bark.
artistBio: Barkcloth has long been worn and used in Buganda for coronations, funerals and ceremonies, and makers once served the royal court. Cotton cloth replaced it for daily wear, but it is still made for rites and by artists. UNESCO lists Ugandan barkcloth making as intangible cultural heritage.

title: Harrania Tapestries
artist: Weavers of the Ramses Wissa Wassef Art Centre
about: These tapestries show village life along the Nile: palm trees, birds, fields, donkeys and water buffalo, in bright naturally dyed wool. There is no drawing or cartoon behind them. Each weaver composes the picture directly on the loom, working from memory and imagination, so every piece is unlike any other.
artistBio: The architect Ramses Wissa Wassef and his wife Sophie Habib Gorgy started the center in the village of Harrania in the 1950s. They believed children could make art if taught the craft but left free to invent. Some of the first children became lifelong weavers, and a younger generation continues the work today.

title: Chancay Gauze and Painted Cloth
about: Chancay weavers made airy cotton gauze, where pairs of warps cross and lock the weft into an open net, and they embroidered or brocaded birds, fish and cats into it. They also painted large cloths in brown and ochre, and made small figures of cane wrapped in cloth and thread, placed in burials.
artistBio: The Chancay culture flourished in the valleys north of present-day Lima before the Inca took over the region. The desert coast preserved many of their textiles in cemeteries. They are found in museums in Lima, and in collections around the world. Their cloth is valued today for its playful animals and open, airy weaves.

title: Wari Feathered Panels
medium: Macaw feathers knotted to cotton cloth
about: These large rectangular panels are covered in rows of blue and yellow macaw feathers. Each feather was folded over a cotton string and tied, and the strings were sewn to the cloth so the feathers overlap like shingles. Most panels are split into two or four simple color blocks. The effect is bold and modern looking, and the colors are still bright.
artistBio: The macaws lived in the Amazon rainforest across the Andes, so the feathers came over long trade routes. A group of these panels was found rolled up in large jars in a remote valley of southern Peru, apparently left as an offering. Panels from the find are now in museums in Peru, the United States and Europe.

title: Ravenstail Robe
artist: Northern Northwest Coast weavers; revived by Cheryl Samuel and others
about: Ravenstail is a twined weaving style with bold black, white and yellow geometric patterns: zigzags, diamonds and bars. It is woven on an upright frame, with the weaver twisting pairs of weft strands around each warp by hand. Robes have long fringes that sway when the wearer dances.
artistBio: It is older than Chilkat weaving and was made by Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. By the nineteenth century it had nearly disappeared, and only a few robes survived, mostly in museums. In the 1980s the weaver and researcher Cheryl Samuel studied them and taught the method, and today Native weavers make Ravenstail robes again.

title: Hopi Wedding Robe
about: When a Hopi woman marries, the men of the groom's family weave her wedding garments of white cotton, including a large robe and a smaller one, and a long braided sash. The weaving takes many weeks. The white robe is later used for important ceremonies, and it is said to go with the woman at the end of her life.
artistBio: Among the Hopi, weaving is men's work, often done in the kivas, the underground ceremonial rooms. Cotton has been grown and woven in the Southwest for well over a thousand years. Hopi weavers also make sashes, kilts and embroidered mantas for ceremonies, and the knowledge passes from older men to younger ones.

title: Cherokee Double-Weave Rivercane Basket
medium: Split rivercane dyed with walnut and bloodroot
about: A double-weave basket is really two baskets in one. The weaver begins at the bottom, weaves up the inside wall, folds the strips over the rim and weaves back down the outside, so each surface has its own pattern. The cane is split into thin strips and dyed dark brown with black walnut or red-orange with bloodroot.
artistBio: Rivercane baskets are among the oldest Cherokee arts. Rivercane has become scarce as wetlands were drained, and weavers and land groups now work to replant it. In the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians in North Carolina, families pass the skill down, and the Qualla Arts and Crafts Mutual has sold members' work since the 1940s.

title: Sweetgrass Baskets
medium: Coiled sweetgrass, bulrush, pine needles and palmetto
about: These baskets are coiled, not woven. Bundles of sweetgrass and bulrush are wrapped and stitched together with strips of palmetto leaf, using a sewing tool once made from a spoon handle or bone. A wide, flat fanner basket was used to toss rice and blow away the chaff. Today the shapes range from small bowls to tall lidded forms.
artistBio: The craft came with Africans who were enslaved and forced to grow rice on Carolina plantations, and it matches coiled baskets in West Africa. Their Gullah Geechee descendants kept it alive. Basket makers in Mount Pleasant have long sold their work from stands along Highway 17, though development threatens the places where sweetgrass grows.

title: Ñandutí Lace
about: Ñandutí means spider web in Guaraní. The lacemaker stretches threads across a frame like the spokes of a wheel and then knots and weaves patterns between them, making round motifs that look like webs or flowers. Many circles are joined into collars, shawls and table pieces. Modern pieces are often brightly colored.
artistBio: It grew from a type of Spanish sun lace brought to South America and took its own form in Paraguay. The town of Itauguá is its home, and most makers are women who learned at home. Ñandutí is now a national symbol in Paraguay and appears on dresses for folk dance.

title: Wayuu Mochila
about: A mochila is a round shoulder bag crocheted in tight single stitches. The finest are made with one strand, so dense they hold their shape. The patterns are called kanaas and come from things in Wayuu life, such as the tracks of animals, parts of a loom or stars. A large bag can take weeks.
artistBio: The Wayuu live on the dry Guajira Peninsula across the Colombia–Venezuela border. In their stories, a spider woman named Wale'kerü taught women to weave. Girls traditionally learned during a period of seclusion at coming of age. The bags are now sold worldwide, which brings income but also cheap copies.

title: Hardanger Embroidery
medium: White cotton or linen thread on evenweave
about: Hardanger is counted whitework. Blocks of satin stitches, usually five over four threads, are worked on even-weave linen. Then threads inside the blocks are cut and pulled out, leaving an open grid that is wrapped or needle-woven into bars and filled with little lace stitches. The result is geometric and crisp, with light shining through.
artistBio: The style is named for the Hardanger region on Norway's west coast, where it decorated aprons, collars and cuffs of women's festival dress. It is still seen on the bunad, Norway's regional folk costume. Norwegian emigrants carried it to North America, where it remains a popular needlework.

title: Aran Sweater
about: An Aran sweater is knitted in thick cream wool, called báinín, with raised panels of cables, diamonds, honeycomb and moss stitch running up the body and sleeves. The textured stitches make a warm, dense fabric. Many stitches have folk names, such as the tree of life and the lobster claw.
artistBio: Islanders on Inis Mór, Inis Meáin and Inis Oírr knitted them for family, and they became widely known in the mid-twentieth century when they were sold abroad. A popular story says each family had its own pattern to identify drowned fishermen, but historians find little evidence for it. Hand-knitted Arans are still made in Ireland.

title: Orenburg Gossamer Shawl
about: The finest Orenburg shawls, called gossamer or pautinka, are knitted from down combed from local goats and spun nearly as thin as thread. A large shawl is so fine it can be pulled through a wedding ring. Patterns of diamonds, cat's paws and peas are built from small lace motifs, and edges are knitted on separately with points.
artistBio: Goats on the steppes near the Ural River grow especially fine down in the cold winters. Peasant women in villages around Orenburg made the shawls, and they won fame at exhibitions in the nineteenth century. A shawl was often a family treasure. Knitters in the region, and many abroad, still make them.

title: Kalocsa Embroidery
about: Kalocsa embroidery is dense with flowers: roses, tulips, paprika pods and leaves in bright reds, blues, yellows and greens, stitched in satin stitch so close it covers the cloth. It decorates blouses, aprons, pillows and table linens. The same flowers are painted on walls and furniture in local homes.
artistBio: Kalocsa, a town near the Danube known for paprika, developed this colorful style in the late nineteenth century, growing out of earlier white embroidery. Women known as painting women drew the designs and others stitched them. It became one of the best known Hungarian folk arts and is still made for costumes and for sale.

title: Lefkaritika
medium: Linen embroidery with cutwork and drawn thread
about: Lefkaritika is embroidered work on white or ecru linen. Stitchers combine satin stitch, cutwork, hemstitching and needle-made fillings into geometric patterns, often zigzags, triangles and a central star. Large table cloths can take months. The patterns are counted, and each design has a name. The thread is traditionally white, ecru or brown, giving the work a calm, even look.
artistBio: It comes from the mountain villages of Lefkara, where women worked outside their doors while men traveled abroad to sell the work. A well-loved local legend says Leonardo da Vinci visited and bought an altar cloth for Milan Cathedral, though there is no record to confirm it. UNESCO lists Lefkara embroidery as intangible cultural heritage.

title: Point d'Alençon Lace
about: Alençon lace is made with a needle and thread alone, stitch by stitch, over a pattern drawn on parchment. Flowers are outlined with a raised cord stitched in horsehair, then filled with fine stitches, and joined by a tiny net ground. Each step was done by a different specialist, so one piece passed through many hands.
artistBio: In 1665 the French minister Colbert set up royal lace workshops, including in Alençon, so France could stop buying Venetian lace. The town's lace became a luxury of the court. The craft nearly died out, but a small workshop kept it going, and UNESCO lists Alençon needle lace as intangible heritage. A single piece can take years.

title: Toile de Jouy
about: Toile de Jouy is cotton printed in a single color, often red, blue or purple, on a pale ground. The scenes are fine line pictures of country life, myths, balloon flights and current events, repeated across the cloth. They were printed from engraved copper plates, which allowed more detail than wood blocks.
artistBio: Oberkampf, born in Germany, opened his printworks near Versailles in 1760, soon after France lifted its ban on printed cottons. The painter Jean-Baptiste Huet designed many of its best known scenes. The factory closed in 1843. Today a museum in Jouy-en-Josas shows its fabrics, and the name is used for any printed cloth in this style.

title: Berlin Woolwork
artist: Amateur needleworkers across Europe and America
medium: Wool on canvas in tent and cross stitch
about: Berlin woolwork was stitched in bright wool on canvas, following printed charts in which each square stood for one stitch. Roses, parrots, lapdogs and Bible scenes covered slippers, cushions, footstools and bell pulls. New chemical dyes later in the century made the colors louder. Some pieces added beads or raised plush stitches.
artistBio: The charts were first published in Berlin in the early nineteenth century and sold with soft merino wools. The craze spread to Britain and America and filled middle-class parlors. Critics of the time called it mechanical, but it gave many women a creative pastime. Pieces survive in large numbers in homes and museums.

title: Jane Bostocke's Sampler
medium: Silk and metal thread on linen, with pearls and beads
about: This is the earliest known dated English sampler. At the top are animals, including a dog with a collar, and below are bands of patterns and an alphabet. An inscription records the birth of a girl named Alice Lee in 1596, so the sampler may have been a gift for her. It includes many stitches, some worked with seed pearls and beads.
artistBio: Jane Bostocke stitched her name into it, but little else is known of her. Samplers were first a way to keep a record of stitches and patterns, before printed pattern books were common. Later they became schoolwork for girls. This sampler is in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

title: ʻIe Toga (Samoan Fine Mat)
about: An ʻie toga is a mat woven from pandanus leaves split into strips so thin it feels like cloth. A fine one can take a weaver many months or longer. It is soft, flexible and edged with red feathers. Fine mats are not used on floors. They are wealth, given and received at weddings, funerals and the bestowing of chiefly titles.
artistBio: Fine mats have been central to Samoan exchange for centuries, and old mats carry the history of every occasion they were given at. Over time many mats became coarser and quicker to make. In recent decades women's groups and the government have encouraged a return to the finest traditional weaving.

title: Bilum
about: A bilum is a looped string bag, made with a single needle and no knots, so it stretches to hold almost anything. Women carry them with the strap across the forehead, loaded with garden food, firewood or a sleeping baby. Patterns in stripes and zigzags can show where a woman comes from.
artistBio: Bilums were traditionally made from plant fiber rolled into string on the thigh. Now many are made of bright acrylic yarn. The bilum is so closely linked with women's care and work that it stands for motherhood in some places. Makers sell them across the country and abroad, and designers use them in fashion.

title: Tīvaevae
about: Tīvaevae are large quilts made by groups of women. In appliqué tīvaevae, a big flower design is cut from one color and stitched onto another. In piecework, hundreds of small squares or diamonds are joined into flowers. Hibiscus, frangipani and breadfruit leaves are favorite motifs, often outlined with fine embroidery.
artistBio: The craft grew from sewing taught by missionaries, but the designs and use are Cook Islands. Women gather to make them together. Tīvaevae are given at important moments, such as weddings, a boy's first haircut, twenty-first birthdays and funerals, and they are treasured and passed down.

title: Crocheted Installations
about: Ernesto Neto makes soft, body-sized spaces that people can walk into, lie on or smell. Early works hung stretchy fabric sacks heavy with spices like turmeric and clove. Later he crocheted huge colorful nets and tunnels, some suspended from ceilings in museums and train stations. They are meant to be felt as well as seen.
artistBio: Neto was born in Rio de Janeiro in 1964 and still works there. His studio crochets the large works together. He has collaborated with the Huni Kuin people of the Brazilian Amazon, and his work has been shown at the Venice Biennale and in major museums around the world.

title: Woods of Net
about: Woods of Net is a huge crocheted play structure, hung inside a wooden building in a sculpture park. Children climb, bounce and tumble through its bright netted pockets and hammocks. The work is fiber art that is meant to be used. The open nets move and stretch with each child.
artistBio: Toshiko Horiuchi MacAdam is a Japanese textile artist who studied weaving and worked with hand-crocheted forms. She began making play nets after children climbed on one of her gallery pieces. She has made playgrounds in Japan and abroad, and the timber pavilion here was built to house this net.
c: Woods of Net Hakone Horiuchi MacAdam

title: She Changes
medium: Net sculpture on steel ring and poles
about: She Changes is a giant net that floats over a seaside roundabout, held up by a steel ring and three poles. It moves constantly with the wind. Its colors and shape were chosen to recall the town's fishing past. From below, it looks like a shape drawn in the sky that never stays still.
artistBio: Janet Echelman is an American artist who turned to netting after working with fishermen in India in the 1990s. She now makes huge outdoor net sculptures using industrial fibers and computer modeling. She Changes was one of her first permanent large works and honors the fishing industry of Matosinhos.

title: Deconstructed Carpets
about: Faig Ahmed starts with the patterns of traditional Azerbaijani carpets and then breaks them. In his pieces the pattern seems to melt and drip onto the floor, dissolve into pixels or twist like a digital glitch. It makes you see the old designs again by showing what happens when their rules are bent.
artistBio: Ahmed was born in Azerbaijan in 1982 and lives in Baku. He designs the works, and they are woven by hand by skilled carpet weavers, which can take many months. His carpets have been shown widely, including at the Venice Biennale, and he is one of the best known artists working with the rug today.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait
about: A merchant and a woman stand hand in hand in a room in Bruges. Cloth is everywhere: her huge green wool gown lined with fur, with sleeves cut into scalloped edges, his dark fur-trimmed cloak, the deep red bed hangings and a small patterned rug by the bed. The amount of fine wool in her dress alone shows great wealth.
artistBio: Jan van Eyck was one of the great painters of fifteenth-century Flanders and worked for the Duke of Burgundy. The man is usually identified as a member of the Arnolfini family, Italian merchants in Bruges, and cloth was the heart of that city's trade. The painting is in the National Gallery in London.

title: Sewing the Sail
about: In a shady courtyard by the sea, women and a man sit mending a huge white sail that spills across the whole canvas. Sunlight comes through the leaves and falls in patches on the cloth and the flowers. The sail is the real subject: a great sheet of heavy canvas, folded and gathered, worked on by hand.
artistBio: Joaquín Sorolla was a Valencian painter known for light, beaches and working people of the Mediterranean coast. He painted fishermen and their families many times. This painting was shown internationally and is now in the Ca' Pesaro modern art gallery in Venice. He worked outdoors whenever he could, painting quickly to catch the light.
c: Sorolla Sewing the Sail Cosiendo la vela

title: Sunlight in the Blue Room
about: A girl sits by a window in a blue-walled room, bent over her crochet. Sunlight pours through the curtains and lands on the floor and her chair in warm squares. The room is quiet and simple. It is a picture about light, but also about the calm, absorbed time of handwork.
artistBio: Anna Ancher was born in Skagen, a fishing town at the tip of Denmark that drew a colony of painters. Unlike most of them, she was a local. She often painted women at home and the changing light of interiors. The girl is her daughter Helga. The painting is in the Skagens Museum.
c: Anna Ancher Sunlight in the Blue Room

title: The Millinery Shop
about: A young woman sits in a hat shop, holding up a hat and studying it. In front of her, finished hats on stands crowd the table in bright greens, oranges and blues, trimmed with ribbons and feathers. She may be a milliner at work. Degas shows her close and from an angle, as if we have just walked in.
artistBio: Degas made a group of pictures of Paris milliners in the 1880s, interested in their skill and in the business of fashion. Hats were made by hand in many small workshops in the city. He reworked this canvas over years. It is in the Art Institute of Chicago.

title: The Two Fridas
about: Two Fridas sit side by side holding hands under a stormy sky. One wears a white European-style dress trimmed with lace, the other a Tehuana outfit from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. Their exposed hearts are joined by a vein. The clothes do much of the speaking here, setting two sides of one identity next to each other.
artistBio: Frida Kahlo painted it around the time of her divorce from Diego Rivera. She often wore Tehuana dress in daily life, and her clothing is now treated as part of her art. The painting is in the Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexico City. It is one of her largest paintings.

title: Nålebinding
medium: Looped yarn with a single needle
about: Nålebinding means binding with a needle. The maker uses a flat needle with one eye and short lengths of yarn. Each new loop passes through loops already made, often around the thumb as a guide. When the yarn runs out, a new length is felted onto the end. The fabric is thick, stretchy and does not unravel if cut.
artistBio: It is older than knitting and was used for socks, mittens and hats. Famous finds include Egyptian socks with split toes from the late Roman period and many Viking-age pieces. In Scandinavia, mittens were still made this way into the twentieth century, and reenactors and knitters have revived it.

title: Tablet Weaving
about: In tablet weaving, warp threads pass through holes in a stack of small square cards, one thread at each corner. Turning the cards a quarter turn twists the threads and opens a new space for the weft. Changing the direction of turning, or the colors in the holes, makes patterns. The result is a narrow, very strong band.
artistBio: Tablet woven bands are known from Iron Age Europe and were used for belts, straps and the edges of cloth. The Viking-age Oseberg ship burial in Norway held a band still on its tablets. Similar bands were made in Egypt, Iceland, Asia and beyond. Today, many weavers use tablets because they need no loom.

title: Sprang
about: Sprang is made only from warp threads stretched on a frame. There is no weft. The maker twists neighboring threads around each other row by row with the fingers, and the same twists form at the other end in mirror image. A stick holds each row until the middle is secured. The fabric is very elastic.
artistBio: Sprang is found in Bronze Age Denmark, where a woman's hairnet survives, in Coptic Egypt for caps and in ancient Peru. It was used for hairnets, stockings and bags. It nearly vanished in Europe, survived in a few folk traditions, and has been revived by textile researchers and makers.

title: Couched Goldwork
about: Gold thread is usually a thin strip of metal wrapped around a silk core. It is too stiff and precious to pull through cloth, so the embroiderer lays it on the surface and ties it down with tiny stitches of silk, called couching. In or nué, gold threads are laid side by side and covered with colored silk stitches, closely or sparsely, to shade a picture.
artistBio: Couched gold appears in Chinese, Byzantine, Islamic and European embroidery. Or nué reached its height in Burgundy and the Netherlands in the fifteenth century, on church vestments. Goldwork is still made for regalia, uniforms and church use, and embroidery schools teach it today. Because the metal stays on the surface, very little gold is wasted on the back.

title: Kumihimo
about: Kumihimo is Japanese braiding. Threads are wound on weighted bobbins and hung over a stand, the most familiar being the round marudai with a hole in the center. The braider moves the bobbins in a set order, and the braid grows down through the hole. Different stands and moves make round, square or flat braids.
artistBio: Braids were used in Japan to tie Buddhist objects and court robes, and later to lace samurai armor and wrap sword hilts. Today kumihimo is best known in the obijime, the cord tied around a kimono's obi. Many makers outside Japan use foam discs for simpler versions.

title: Supplementary Weft Brocade
about: In brocade, the weaver adds extra pattern threads to an ordinary woven cloth. These supplementary wefts float on the surface where the pattern should show and hide on the back or are cut away elsewhere. They can run edge to edge or be worked by hand only in small areas. Gold and silver threads are often used.
artistBio: Brocade is found across Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas. Malay songket, Banarasi saris and Maya huipils all use it in their own ways. Hand weavers pick each pattern by hand, while draw looms and later Jacquard looms made the work faster. A brocaded cloth can look embroidered, but the pattern is woven in at the same time as the cloth.

title: Judith Scott
about: Judith Scott was born in Ohio with Down syndrome, and her deafness went unrecognized for years. At seven she was sent to an institution, apart from her twin sister Joyce, for about thirty-five years. In 1986 Joyce became her guardian and brought her to California, where she began attending Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland.
artistBio: After a fiber workshop there, Scott found her art. She wrapped found objects, sticks and chairs in layer after layer of yarn, string and fabric, making dense cocoon-like forms with no words to explain them. She worked daily until her death in 2005. Her sculptures are now in major museums, and the Brooklyn Museum held a large retrospective in 2014.

title: Elizabeth Zimmermann
about: Elizabeth Zimmermann was born in England, studied art, and moved to the United States in the late 1930s, later settling in rural Wisconsin. She knitted constantly and grew impatient with patterns that told knitters exactly what to do. She preferred knitting in the round and wanted people to understand their sweaters well enough to design their own.
artistBio: Her book Knitting Without Tears came out in 1971, followed by others and by television programs. She created the Baby Surprise Jacket, which knits as a strange flat shape and folds into a little coat. With her daughter Meg Swansen she ran Schoolhouse Press, which still publishes her work. Her friendly, practical voice changed how many people knit.

title: Märta Måås-Fjetterström
about: Märta Måås-Fjetterström grew up in southern Sweden and trained as a textile artist. She studied Swedish folk weaving and older rugs from the Middle East and drew on both. In 1919 she opened her own workshop in Båstad, on the coast of Skåne, where weavers made her designs by hand.
artistBio: Her rugs, in flat weave and knotted pile, use bold, simple shapes and deep plant-like colors, with names drawn from Swedish nature. They became some of the most admired Scandinavian textiles of the twentieth century. The workshop in Båstad still operates and continues to weave her designs and those of later artists.

title: Ed Rossbach
about: Ed Rossbach taught textiles at the University of California, Berkeley, for decades and was married to the textile artist Katherine Westphal. He was fascinated by how things are made and studied baskets and textiles from around the world, writing books such as Baskets as Textile Art.
artistBio: He made baskets and woven pieces from whatever caught his eye: newspaper, plastic wrap, rice paper, foil and even images of Mickey Mouse. The work was playful but rooted in old techniques like twining and plaiting. His teaching and experiments helped turn basketry into a field of contemporary art in the United States.

title: Kay Sekimachi
place: San Francisco Bay Area, United States
about: Kay Sekimachi was born in San Francisco to Japanese immigrant parents. During the Second World War she and her family were held in incarceration camps. Afterward she studied at the California College of Arts and Crafts and later with the weaver Trude Guermonprez. She married the woodturner Bob Stocksdale.
artistBio: She is known for hanging forms woven from clear nylon monofilament on a multi-harness loom, which open into layered tubes that seem to float. She also made small, delicate vessels from paper, linen and leaves. Her quiet, precise work is in many American museums. Her weaving combines careful planning on the loom with a light, almost transparent result.

title: The Calico Acts
about: In the late 1600s, light, washable printed cottons from India became wildly popular in England. Wool and silk weavers feared for their jobs. Parliament responded in 1700 by banning the import of printed calicoes, and in 1721 went further, largely banning the wearing and use of printed cotton cloth. Weavers had even attacked women in the street for wearing it.
artistBio: The laws protected wool for a time but also pushed English makers to spin and weave cotton themselves. When the bans were lifted in 1774, a home cotton industry was ready to grow. That shift helped start the Industrial Revolution and changed the fortunes of Indian weavers, whose trade later suffered.

title: The Canut Revolts
about: The canuts were the silk weavers of Lyon, many working Jacquard looms in tall apartments on the Croix-Rousse hill. In 1831, after merchants refused to honor an agreed minimum price for their cloth, they rose up and briefly took control of the city under the motto Live working or die fighting. They rose again in 1834, and both revolts were put down by the army.
artistBio: The canut revolts are often called among the first workers' uprisings of the industrial age. They showed that skilled craft workers could organize against falling pay. The tall windows of the Croix-Rousse buildings, made to light the looms, still mark the neighborhood, and a silk weaving workshop museum operates there.

title: Woad
about: Woad is a yellow-flowered plant whose leaves hold the same blue compound as indigo, though less of it. The leaves were crushed, formed into balls and fermented, then used in a vat where the dye dissolves. Wool comes out of the vat yellow-green and turns blue as it meets the air. Repeated dips give deeper shades.
artistBio: Woad was Europe's main blue for centuries. Whole regions grew rich on it, including the area around Toulouse in France and Thuringia in Germany. In the seventeenth century, cheaper and stronger indigo from Asia and the Americas replaced it, despite laws against indigo. Natural dyers grow it again today.

title: Weld
about: Weld is a tall plant with spikes of small yellow-green flowers. The whole plant is dried and simmered to give a clear, bright and lasting yellow, best on wool or silk mordanted with alum. Dyers often call it the best natural yellow because it fades less than most.
artistBio: Weld was used in ancient Rome and throughout medieval Europe. Dyeing cloth first with woad and then with weld produced greens, including the famous Lincoln green of English cloth. It remained important until synthetic dyes arrived in the nineteenth century, and it is a favorite in natural dye gardens today.

title: The Warp-Weighted Loom
about: The warp-weighted loom leans against a wall. The warp threads hang down from a top beam, gathered in bunches tied to heavy weights of clay or stone that keep them tight. The weaver stands, passes the weft across, and beats it upward, so the cloth grows from the top down. A wide loom could make large blankets and sails.
artistBio: Loom weights are among the most common finds at ancient sites, from Neolithic Europe to classical Greece, where vase paintings show these looms. Vikings wove sailcloth and clothing on them. In parts of Norway and Iceland they were used into the twentieth century, and today they are rebuilt by museums and weavers.

title: Hand Cards
about: Hand cards are a pair of flat paddles covered with rows of small bent wire teeth. A tuft of washed wool is spread on one card, and the other is drawn across it until the fibers are opened and lined up. The wool is then rolled off into a soft rolag, ready to spin into a light, airy yarn.
artistBio: Before wire cards, people used teasel heads to open fibers. Hand cards became common in medieval Europe. In the eighteenth century, carding machines with rotating drums were developed, and Richard Arkwright improved them for factories. Hand cards and small drum carders are still the tools of many spinners and shepherds today.

title: The Oseberg Tapestry
about: The Oseberg ship burial held two women and a great deal of cloth. Among it were narrow woven bands showing a long procession: horses, wagons, warriors with spears and figures in long dresses, all moving one way. The pieces were found crushed and broken. Patient work by conservators and drawings by copyists let us read the scene today. It may show a real ritual journey, perhaps a funeral.
artistBio: The weavers are unknown, but the burial shows how central textiles were to Viking life. The ship also held tools for spinning and weaving, including tablet-weaving gear. The burial was dug out in 1904 and 1905. The fragments are in the collections of the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History. They are among the very few Viking Age pictures made in cloth.

title: Felt Swans from Pazyryk
about: These are swans made of felt, stuffed with deer hair, with colored felt for the wings and beak. They were found in a frozen burial mound in the Altai, where ice kept wool and wood from rotting. They probably decorated a funeral wagon or a canopy. Even after more than two thousand years, the birds look light and alert, as if ready to lift off.
artistBio: The Pazyryk people were horse-riding herders who kept sheep and moved with the seasons. Felt was their everyday cloth: tents, rugs, saddle covers and clothing.
