The same burials gave us the famous Pazyryk Carpet and a large felt hanging of a horseman. The swans are now in the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.

title: The Valois Tapestries
artist: Netherlandish weavers after drawings by Antoine Caron
medium: Wool, silk, silver and gold thread
about: This set of eight large tapestries shows the festivals of the French royal court: water pageants, mock battles, an attack on an elephant, dancing in the open air. Courtiers in fine clothes fill the front, and Catherine de' Medici, the queen mother, appears in black widow's dress. The scenes were built on drawings by Antoine Caron, with portraits of royal family members added.
artistBio: The weavers worked in the Southern Netherlands, the great tapestry center of the age. The set probably came to Florence with Christine of Lorraine, Catherine's granddaughter, when she married Ferdinando I de' Medici in 1589. The tapestries are now in the Uffizi Galleries in Florence. Historians still study them for clues about court politics of the time.

title: The Gideon Tapestries
artist: Flemish weavers; bought by Bess of Hardwick
about: This large set tells the Bible story of Gideon, a farmer who became a leader of Israel. The panels line the Long Gallery at Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire, where they have hung for over four hundred years. Look closely at the coats of arms. They were changed: Bess of Hardwick covered the old owner's arms with painted cloth showing her own.
artistBio: The set was made for Sir Christopher Hatton. After his death, Bess of Hardwick bought it in 1592 for her new house. It still hangs where she placed it. Centuries of light and dust weakened the wool, and the National Trust has spent years cleaning and repairing each panel. It is one of the largest tapestry sets still in its original setting in England.

title: The Bradford Table Carpet
about: In the 1600s, a 'carpet' often meant a cloth for a table. This one is worked in tiny tent stitches in silk. The center is a grapevine with leaves and fruit. The wide border is the fun part: a strip of English country life with hunters, fishermen, castles, houses, animals and trees, seen as if in a long walk around the edge.
artistBio: The makers are unknown, likely professional embroiderers working for a wealthy household. The carpet is named after the Earls of Bradford, who once owned it. It is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. Its colors have survived well, so it gives a rare clear view of how bright English embroidery looked around the time of Shakespeare.
c: Bradford Table Carpet Victoria and Albert Museum

title: The Girdlers' Carpet
artist: Weavers of Lahore for Robert Bell
about: This long carpet was ordered from the royal workshops of Lahore by an English merchant. It mixes two worlds. The border has Mughal flowers and leaves. In the field are the coat of arms of the Girdlers' Company of London and the initials and arms of the man who gave it. It is one of the earliest dated carpets made for an English buyer.
artistBio: Robert Bell, a director of the East India Company and a master of the Girdlers' Company, commissioned the carpet and gave it to his guild. The weavers' names are not recorded. Remarkably, the carpet is still owned by the Girdlers' Company in London. It shows how quickly Indian carpets became prized goods in Europe through the new trading companies.

title: Yamantaka Mandala
about: This large silk tapestry shows a mandala, a sacred diagram used in Tibetan Buddhist practice. At its center is Yamantaka, a fierce form who conquers death, surrounded by circles and gateways. In the bottom corners are small portraits of the people who paid for it: two Mongol emperors on one side, and their wives on the other.
artistBio: It was woven in an imperial workshop of the Yuan dynasty, when Mongol rulers governed China and supported Tibetan Buddhism. Kesi is a slit-tapestry technique, and this piece is one of the largest and finest known. It is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. It shows Chinese, Tibetan and Mongol traditions meeting in one cloth.

title: Kogin-zashi
artist: Farm women of the Tsugaru region
medium: White cotton stitching on indigo hemp
about: Kogin is a counted stitch worked in white cotton thread on indigo-dyed hemp cloth. Each stitch passes over an odd number of threads, building small diamond shapes. These units, called modoko, join into larger patterns across the back and shoulders of a work jacket. The thick stitching made the thin hemp warmer and much stronger for farm work in a cold climate.
artistBio: In the Edo period, rural people in northern Japan were often barred from wearing cotton cloth, so they wore hemp. Women of Tsugaru turned the rule into an art. The craft faded with modern clothing but was revived in the twentieth century, partly through the folk craft (mingei) movement. Today it is stitched on bags, cushions and clothing far beyond Aomori.

title: Pichhwai
about: A pichhwai is a large painted cloth hung behind the image of Shrinathji, a child form of Krishna, in temples. The word means 'hanging at the back.' Paintings show cows, lotus ponds, the full moon, and gopis, the cowherd women who loved Krishna. Different hangings are put up for different festivals and seasons, so the temple's look changes through the year.
artistBio: The tradition grew around the Shrinathji temple at Nathdwara, a center of the Pushtimarg devotional path. Families of painters there have passed down the work for generations, grinding mineral and plant colors by hand. Older pichhwais are now in museums worldwide. Painters in Nathdwara still make them today, both for temples and for collectors.

title: Baluchari Sari
about: A Baluchari sari tells stories on its end panel, the pallu. Small woven boxes hold scenes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, or figures from daily life: riders, musicians, boats. Older pieces even show Europeans and trains. The figures are woven into the silk, not printed, so each scene is built up thread by thread on the loom.
artistBio: The style is named after Baluchar, a village in Murshidabad district where it grew in the eighteenth century. After floods and hard times, weaving there declined. In the twentieth century, the craft was revived in Bishnupur, a town known for its terracotta temples. Many of the woven scenes echo the temple carvings. Bishnupur weavers still make Baluchari saris today.

title: Bandhani
artist: Khatri dyers and binders of Gujarat and Rajasthan
about: Bandhani is made by pinching tiny points of cloth and binding each one tightly with thread. When the cloth goes into the dye, the bound points stay pale. Thousands of dots can form flowers, dancers, elephants and borders. Untied, the cloth keeps small puckers, a sign that it was done by hand. Bright red and yellow bandhani are worn at weddings.
artistBio: Bandhani is closely linked to Khatri families in Kutch, though many communities practice it in Gujarat and Rajasthan. The tying is often done by women at home, and the dyeing in family workshops. Bhuj, Mandvi and Jamnagar are well known centers. Modern bandhani appears in fashion around the world, while traditional wedding cloths like the gharchola are still made.

title: Shyrdak
about: A shyrdak is a felt rug made like a puzzle. Two sheets of felt in strong colors, often red and dark blue, are stacked and cut along the same curling pattern, like ram's horns. The pieces are swapped and sewn back together, so each color fills the other's shape. A cord sewn along every seam outlines the design. The rug is then quilted for strength.
artistBio: Kyrgyz herding families have made shyrdaks for their yurts for generations, from the wool of their own sheep. The work is shared by women, from washing and felting to cutting and sewing. A good shyrdak can last decades. In 2012 UNESCO listed Kyrgyz felt carpet making as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding, and cooperatives now teach younger makers.

title: Dragon Carpets
about: Dragon carpets have a large lattice of jagged leaves dividing the field into diamonds. Inside, there are strong, angular creatures. The 'dragons' are so stylized that they can look like plants or zigzags at first. Other animals, such as lions and birds, and big palmette flowers fill the gaps. The carpets are long, made for large rooms, and their reds and blues are bold.
artistBio: Where exactly they were woven is still debated. Both Armenian and Azerbaijani traditions claim them, and the Karabakh region is often named. The designs may come from older Persian animal carpets. Surviving examples are prized by museums, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Textile Museum in Washington. They are among the most studied of all Caucasian rugs.

title: Al Sadu Weaving
medium: Warp-faced weaving in sheep, goat and camel hair
about: Sadu is the weaving of Bedouin women, done on a narrow ground loom staked out in the sand. They spin wool from sheep, hair from goats and camels, and dye some of it red, black and other colors. The cloth is warp-faced and very tough. Bands of geometric pattern carry names for things in desert life, like eyes, combs and stars.
artistBio: Sadu cloth made the Bedouin tent: walls, dividers, rugs, and decorated camel bags. With settled life, fewer women learned it. UNESCO lists Al Sadu as heritage needing urgent care, with entries from the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. In Kuwait, Sadu House has worked since the 1970s to record patterns and teach the craft to new weavers.

title: Adinkra Cloth
about: Adinkra cloth is printed with stamps carved from pieces of calabash gourd. The ink is made by boiling the bark of the badie tree into a thick dark paste. The cloth is divided into squares with a comb, and each square gets a symbol. Each symbol has a name and a proverb, such as Gye Nyame, 'except God,' or Sankofa, 'go back and get it.'
artistBio: Adinkra comes from the Asante (Ashanti) people of Ghana. Older cloths were dark, worn mainly at funerals and for mourning. Today they come in many colors and are worn at festivals too. The town of Ntonso near Kumasi is known for its stampers. The symbols are now used far beyond cloth, on buildings, logos and jewelry across Ghana and the diaspora.

title: The Linen Garments of Tutankhamun
medium: Linen, some with tapestry and embroidery
about: When Tutankhamun's tomb was opened in 1922, archaeologists found chests of clothing: tunics, shawls, loincloths, gloves, and sashes. Most were fine white linen. A few were richly decorated, with woven tapestry bands and small embroidered patterns. Some garments were sized for a child, perhaps kept from the king's youth. They show what a royal wardrobe of the period was really like.
artistBio: Linen was Egypt's main cloth, spun from flax and woven by skilled workers in temple and palace workshops. Many tomb textiles were in poor condition and needed long study. Researchers have since reconstructed some garments. The collection is held in Cairo, where much of the tomb's contents have been moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum.

title: Mapuche Ponchos (Makuñ)
about: Mapuche weavers make ponchos, belts and blankets on an upright loom called a witral. Many ponchos are warp-faced with bold stepped crosses and diamonds. Some use ikat, where warp threads are tied and dyed before weaving to make blurry-edged patterns. Weaving a poncho takes weeks. A fine one was a mark of standing for a lonko, or chief.
artistBio: The Mapuche are the largest Indigenous people of Chile. After sheep came with the Spanish, wool became the main fiber. Weaving is passed from mother to daughter and is seen as women's knowledge. Mapuche ponchos were traded widely in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Today weavers' groups keep the craft alive, using both natural and synthetic dyes.

title: Jalq'a Weaving
about: Jalq'a weavers make dark cloth, mostly black or brown, crowded with red creatures. These are khurus, wild beings from the inner world below the earth. Some look like animals, some are strange mixes, some are upside down. There is no top or bottom and no neat rows. The women's overskirt, the aqsu, is the main place these designs appear.
artistBio: The Jalq'a live in the hills west of Sucre. Their style is very different from the ordered designs of neighboring Tarabuco. In the 1980s, a project working with anthropologists helped weavers sell their work and keep fine techniques. Examples are shown at the Museo de Arte Indígena in Sucre. Women still weave it, and each woman's creatures are her own.

title: Rebozo
artist: Rebozo weavers and knotters of Mexico
place: Santa María del Río, San Luis Potosí, and other towns, Mexico
medium: Ikat-dyed cotton or silk with knotted fringe
about: A rebozo is a long shawl. Women use it to carry babies and loads, to cover the head, or to dress up. The finest are made with ikat: the threads are tied and dyed before weaving, so patterns look softly blurred. The long ends are knotted into fringes called rapacejos, sometimes forming words or tiny figures. A fine silk one, people say, can pass through a ring.
artistBio: The rebozo grew from Indigenous, Spanish and Asian influences in colonial Mexico. Santa María del Río is famous for silk rebozos, and Tenancingo for cotton ones. Weaving and fringe knotting are often done by different people. Frida Kahlo wore them often. Today the rebozo is a symbol of Mexican identity and is still worn and given as a treasured gift.

title: Rio Grande Blankets
artist: Hispano weavers of northern New Mexico
place: Chimayó and the upper Rio Grande, New Mexico, USA
about: These blankets were woven on heavy treadle looms brought by Spanish settlers. Most early ones have simple stripes in natural white, brown and indigo blue. Later pieces add a central diamond and serrated shapes borrowed from Mexican Saltillo sarapes. They were made for daily use and for trade. Two narrow pieces were sometimes sewn together for a wide blanket.
artistBio: Spanish colonists brought churro sheep to New Mexico, a hardy breed with long, low-grease wool. Weaving became a family trade in villages like Chimayó, where families such as the Ortegas and Trujillos still weave. Churro sheep almost disappeared in the twentieth century but have been brought back by breeders. Their wool is again used by local weavers.

title: Wabanaki Brown Ash Baskets
place: Maine, USA and the Maritimes, Canada
about: Wabanaki basketmakers start with a brown ash log. They pound it with a mallet until the growth rings separate into long, thin layers. These are split, shaved and woven into baskets. Some are sturdy pack baskets for potatoes or fish. Others are fancy baskets with curls, braided sweetgrass trims and small fitted lids. The best ones are both strong and very fine.
artistBio: The Wabanaki nations include the Maliseet, Mi'kmaq, Passamaquoddy and Penobscot. Basketry has supported families for generations. The Maine Indian Basketmakers Alliance, founded in 1993, helped train young makers. Now the craft faces a new threat: the emerald ash borer, an insect killing ash trees. Basketmakers are working with scientists to save seed and protect the trees.

title: Victorian Crazy Quilt
artist: Women quiltmakers in America and Britain
medium: Silk, velvet and satin patchwork with embroidery
about: A crazy quilt is made of irregular scraps of silk, velvet and satin pieced without a set pattern. Every seam is covered with fancy embroidery stitches. Makers added painted flowers, spiders and webs, fans, names, dates and bits of ribbon from special events. Most were not bed covers. They were shown on sofas and pianos, as proof of skill and taste.
artistBio: The craze swept through American and British homes in the 1880s. It is often linked to the Japanese art shown at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia. Magazines sold patterns and packets of silk scraps. Because they hold personal keepsakes, many crazy quilts are family records. Today they are in museums and are still made by quilters who love embellishment.

title: The Abraham Tapestry of Halberstadt
about: This long, narrow hanging tells the story of Abraham from the Bible, including his welcome of three angelic visitors and the near-sacrifice of Isaac. The figures stand stiffly under arches, with simple faces and bold outlines. It was made to hang along the walls of the cathedral choir on feast days. Its colors are faded now, but the story is still easy to follow.
artistBio: The weavers are unknown. They may have worked in a convent or church workshop in Saxony, a region with a strong textile tradition. It belongs to the cathedral treasury of Halberstadt, which also keeps other Romanesque hangings, including a Christ and the Apostles tapestry. Together they are among the oldest surviving woven wall hangings in Europe, older than the great Gothic tapestry sets.

title: The Tristan Embroideries of Wienhausen
about: These large embroidered hangings tell the love story of Tristan and Isolde in rows of scenes, with captions stitched along the bands. The figures are worked in wool in a dense stitch that covers the whole linen ground. It may seem odd that nuns stitched a romance. But stories of courtly love were widely known, and the convent's women came from noble families.
artistBio: Wienhausen is one of the Lüneburg convents, a group of Protestant women's houses in Lower Saxony that kept their medieval treasures through the centuries. The embroideries are fragile and light-sensitive. They are kept in the dark and shown to the public only for a short time each year. They are among the finest examples of German medieval wool embroidery.

title: Honiton Lace
medium: Bobbin lace in fine linen or cotton thread
about: Honiton lace is bobbin lace made in small pieces, called sprigs: flowers, leaves, ferns and birds. Each sprig is worked separately on a pillow, then the sprigs are joined with a mesh or with plaited bars. Because the motifs are made one at a time, many lacemakers could work on one large piece. The finished lace is soft and full of detail.
artistBio: Lacemaking grew in East Devon from the late 1500s. In 1840 Queen Victoria chose Honiton lace for her wedding dress, made by lacemakers in and around the village of Beer. That brought fame, but machine lace later cut into the trade. Today Honiton lace is kept alive by teachers, guilds and hobbyists, and Allhallows Museum in Honiton shows historic pieces.

title: Irish Crochet Lace
artist: Irish women and girls, taught by nuns and teachers
about: Irish crochet imitates costly needle lace, using only a hook and fine thread. Makers crochet raised roses, shamrocks, leaves and scrolls, some padded over a thicker cord. Then the motifs are joined with a crocheted mesh. Because each motif can be made by a different person, families and whole villages worked together on collars, cuffs and even full dresses.
artistBio: The craft spread during the Great Famine of the 1840s, when convents and charitable women taught it as a way to earn money. Ursuline nuns at Blackrock, near Cork, are often credited with starting it. Clones in County Monaghan became a center. Irish crochet was sold across Europe and America. Today makers and teachers keep it alive in Ireland and abroad.

title: Latvian Patterned Mittens
about: Latvian mittens are knitted in two or more colors with fine wool on thin needles. Patterns cover every inch, often with old symbols such as the sun, stars, the cross of Auseklis (the morning star) and zigzags. Cuffs may have fringe or scalloped edges. Each region had its own colors and motifs, so a mitten could show where its maker came from.
artistBio: Mittens played a big part in Latvian weddings. A bride filled her dowry chest with dozens or even hundreds of pairs, which she gave to her new family and guests. Mittens also appeared at funerals and other turning points. Many old pairs are in the Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum and other collections. Knitters still use the patterns today.

title: Bohus Stickning
artist: Knitters of Bohuslän, led by Emma Jacobsson
medium: Stranded knitting in fine wool and angora
about: Bohus sweaters have round yokes of small, shimmering patterns in many close colors. The yarn often mixed fine wool with angora rabbit, so the colors seem to blur and glow. Purl stitches were used inside the colorwork to add texture, which was unusual. Each pattern had its own name. They were bought by fashionable women in many countries.
artistBio: In the 1930s, many families in Bohuslän were poor because the stone quarries had little work. Emma Jacobsson started a knitting cooperative in 1939 so women could earn income at home. Designers including Anna-Lisa Mannheimer Lunn and Kerstin Olsson created the patterns. The cooperative closed in 1969. Its designs are now reproduced as kits, and the original sweaters are collected.

title: Selbu Mittens
about: Selbu mittens are knitted in black and white wool, with an eight-pointed star, the Selbu rose, on the back of the hand. The palm has a small checked or spotted pattern, and the cuff is often a band of bold motifs. Two colors carried together make the mittens thick and warm. They became one of the best-known images of Norwegian knitting.
artistBio: Local tradition says a young woman, Marit Gulsethbrudet Emstad, first knitted two-color mittens in Selbu in the 1850s and wore them to church. Soon many women in the valley knitted them, and selling mittens became an important source of income for farm families. Selbu mittens were sold throughout Norway and abroad. They are still knitted there and by knitters worldwide.

title: Gansey (Guernsey) Sweaters
artist: Fishing families of the British Isles
place: Channel Islands and the coasts of Britain
medium: Worsted wool, knitted in the round
about: A gansey is a fisherman's working sweater, knitted very tightly from twisted wool so it sheds wind and spray. It is made in the round on fine needles, with no side seams. Underarm gussets give room to move. The plain body is topped with textured patterns of knit and purl near the chest: ladders, cables, anchors and diamonds.
artistBio: The name comes from the island of Guernsey, which had a knitting trade for centuries. In the 1800s, wives, mothers and professional knitters along many coasts knitted ganseys for men who fished. Each village had favorite patterns. It is often said they helped identify drowned sailors, though this is hard to prove. Knitters today still follow old ganseys stitch by stitch.

title: Pag Lace
about: Pag lace is a needle lace made with only a needle and thread over a small cushion. It begins with circles of thread like a spider's web, and the maker builds up wheels, triangles and stars. The lace is stiff, white and very fine. Round pieces are used as small table covers. The patterns are mostly kept in the makers' memory, not in drawings.
artistBio: The women of the town of Pag have made this lace for centuries, adding it to their folk dress. In the late 1800s and early 1900s it began to be sold well beyond the island. In 2009 UNESCO listed lacemaking in Croatia, including Pag lace, as intangible heritage. Older women still teach girls the craft.

title: Ghost Net Sculptures
artist: Indigenous artists of Erub, Pormpuraaw and other communities
about: Ghost nets are fishing nets lost or dumped at sea. They drift for years, trapping turtles, fish and birds, and wash up on northern Australian beaches. Artists cut them free, then weave, knot and wrap the old nets into new forms: turtles, sharks, rays, jellyfish and crocodiles, some very large. Bright plastic colors give the sculptures a strong, cheerful look with a serious message.
artistBio: The movement grew with art centers like Erub Arts in the Torres Strait and the Pormpuraaw Art Centre in Cape York. Artists draw on long traditions of weaving and of caring for sea country. Their works have been shown in Australian museums and abroad. Each piece both cleans a beach and tells about the life of the reefs.

title: Tukutuku Panels
medium: Lattice of stems and wooden slats laced with flax and kiekie
about: Tukutuku are woven lattice panels set between the carved posts inside a wharenui, a Māori meeting house. A frame of upright stems is crossed by thin horizontal slats. Strips of harakeke (flax) and kiekie, dyed or natural, are laced through to make patterns. Two people often work together, one on each side of the panel, passing the strips back and forth.
artistBio: Each pattern carries meaning. Poutama, a stepped design, speaks of growth and climbing toward knowledge. Other patterns recall stars, flounder, or the ribs of ancestors. Panels and carvings together tell a tribe's history. Tukutuku are still made by Māori weavers for new and restored meeting houses, often as a community project shared by many hands.

title: Knitted Pictures
about: Rosemarie Trockel began making 'knitted pictures' in the mid-1980s. She designed patterns on a computer and had them machine-knitted in wool, then stretched them like paintings. The patterns repeat signs from public life: the Playboy bunny, the hammer and sickle, the Woolmark logo. Placing these signs in knitting raises questions about women's work, mass production and what counts as art.
artistBio: Trockel was born in 1952 and lives in Cologne. She works across drawing, sculpture, ceramics and video, but the knitted works made her name. She chose machine knitting on purpose, to avoid the idea of a cozy handmade object. Her work is in many major museums. She represented Germany at the 1999 Venice Biennale.

title: The Dinner Party
artist: Judy Chicago and hundreds of collaborators
medium: Embroidered runners, ceramic plates, porcelain tiles
about: The Dinner Party is a huge triangular table set for 39 women from history and myth, from ancient goddesses to Georgia O'Keeffe. Each place has a painted ceramic plate and a long runner embroidered in needlework styles that echo her time and place. The floor below is inscribed with 999 more women's names.
artistBio: Judy Chicago, born in 1939, led the project with hundreds of volunteers, many of them needleworkers who taught and stitched. It was a deliberate claim that 'women's crafts' belonged in museums. The work drew crowds and fierce debate on its tour. Since 2007 it has been on permanent view at the Brooklyn Museum in New York.
c: The Dinner Party Judy Chicago Brooklyn

title: Embroidered Paintings
about: Ghada Amer paints with thread. She stitches outlines of women's figures onto canvas, often repeated many times, then leaves long loose threads hanging over the surface. From far away, the work looks like an abstract painting full of drips and tangles. Up close, the figures appear. Her early works also stitched texts and images about women's daily tasks.
artistBio: Amer was born in Cairo in 1963 and moved to France as a child. She studied painting in Nice, where she felt the field was dominated by men, and turned to embroidery, long seen as women's work, as her answer. She later moved to New York. Her work questions how women are seen, in both Western and Middle Eastern cultures.

title: Agnes Richter's Jacket
about: This is a plain grey linen jacket that its maker took apart and resewed to fit her own body. She then covered it inside and out with embroidered words in old German handwriting, layered so densely that much is hard to read. Some lines are clear, such as 'I' and phrases about her jacket and her life. It is a diary worn on the body.
artistBio: Agnes Richter was a seamstress from Dresden who was confined to a psychiatric hospital at Hubertusburg in the 1890s. Little else is known about her. Her jacket came into the Prinzhorn Collection in Heidelberg, a collection of art by psychiatric patients. It is often shown now and has inspired textile artists, writers and researchers who try to read her words.

title: Needle Paintings
about: Mary Linwood copied famous oil paintings in embroidery so closely that visitors could hardly tell them apart. She used fine worsted wool, dyed specially for her, and long, varied stitches to follow brushstrokes. Her subjects included old master paintings and works by her contemporaries, such as Gainsborough. The results look like paintings until you stand very near.
artistBio: Linwood (1755–1845) lived and ran a school in Leicester. For many years her needle paintings were shown in a gallery in Leicester Square, London, a popular stop for visitors. She was famous in her lifetime, but after her death many works were sold and scattered. A few survive in museum collections. She was among the best-known needlewomen of her age.

title: The Leek Replica of the Bayeux Tapestry
artist: Leek Embroidery Society, led by Elizabeth Wardle
about: This is a full-size copy of the Bayeux Tapestry, stitched from hand-colored photographs. The women matched the wools as best they could and signed their names under the sections they worked. A few changes are telling: some naked figures in the original borders were given underclothes. Seeing the whole length in one room gives a clear sense of the original's scale.
artistBio: Elizabeth Wardle, wife of the silk dyer Thomas Wardle, who worked with William Morris, organized the project with women of the Leek Embroidery Society. It toured Britain and abroad. Since 1895 it has belonged to the town of Reading, and it is shown at Reading Museum. It is a record of both the medieval embroidery and Victorian women's ambition.

title: The Tristan Quilt
about: This white linen quilt tells the story of Tristan in raised pictures. The scenes were outlined with stitching, then stuffed from behind with cotton or cord so the figures stand up from the surface. There are ships, knights, castles and battles, with captions in Sicilian. With no color, the whole story is made from light and shadow on the quilted ridges.
artistBio: It is one of the oldest surviving quilts in Europe. The quilt was later divided: one part is in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, and another is in the Bargello in Florence. Its stuffed technique is related to what later came to be called trapunto. Its quiet, all-white surface still rewards a slow look, scene by scene.

title: Jamdani
artist: Jamdani weavers of the Dhaka region
medium: Fine cotton with hand-inserted supplementary weft
about: Jamdani is sheer cotton cloth with patterns that seem to float. As the plain weave grows, the weaver adds extra threads by hand, one motif at a time, using small bamboo or wooden sticks instead of a mechanism. Flowers, vines and geometric shapes appear in white, gold or color. The patterns are kept in memory, not drawn out. Saris can take months.
artistBio: Jamdani grows from the fine muslin tradition of Bengal, prized at the Mughal court. Weaving families around Dhaka, especially in Narayanganj, pass the skill down, often father to son. In 2013 UNESCO listed the traditional art of Jamdani weaving. It is still worn for weddings and special events across Bangladesh and India.

title: Kalaga Tapestries
medium: Appliqué, padding and sequins on velvet or wool
about: A kalaga is a glittering wall hanging. Figures are cut from cloth, padded so they stand out, and covered with sequins, glass beads and metallic thread. Scenes come from the Buddha's past lives, the Ramayana, and court life, often with dancers, elephants and peacocks. Kalagas were hung in palaces and monasteries and used as curtains or screens.
artistBio: The craft flourished at the royal court in Mandalay in the nineteenth century. After the end of the monarchy, workshops kept making kalagas for monasteries, then for visitors and collectors. Mandalay is still the main center. The work is slow, and a large piece can take many weeks of close needlework by a team.

title: Piña Cloth
about: Piña is cloth woven from fibers scraped out of pineapple leaves. The fibers are cleaned, knotted end to end by hand and woven on a simple loom. The cloth is light, stiff and slightly shiny, like fine paper. It is often embroidered with flowers in white thread. Piña is used for the barong Tagalog, the formal shirt worn by Filipino men.
artistBio: Piña weaving grew under Spanish rule and was prized in Europe in the nineteenth century. Machine-made cloth later took its place. In recent decades, weavers in Kalibo and other towns of Aklan revived it. It remains costly because of the slow work. Piña is worn at weddings and state events, and the Philippines has sought to protect it as national heritage.

title: Ship Cloth (Palepai)
about: A palepai is a long, narrow cloth showing one or two great ships. On their decks are people, animals, houses and trees. The ship carries the idea of passage: from one stage of life to another, or to the world of the dead. Palepai were hung at weddings, births and funerals, and only certain noble families had the right to use them.
artistBio: Ship cloths were woven in the southern Sumatran province of Lampung. Production seems to have stopped around the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Surviving examples are rare and held by museums and collectors. Smaller ship cloths, called tampan, were used more widely. Scholars still study their meanings with Lampung communities.

title: The Quaker Tapestry
artist: Anne Wynn-Wilson and thousands of stitchers
place: Made worldwide; shown in Kendal, England
about: The Quaker Tapestry is a series of more than seventy embroidered panels telling the history of the Quakers, from George Fox in the 1600s to modern peace work. Panels show the abolition of slavery, prison reform, science and industry. A new stitch, called Quaker stitch, was invented for the lettering. Each panel is a mix of picture, words and border.
artistBio: The idea came from Anne Wynn-Wilson, a Quaker in Somerset, in 1981, as a way to share Quaker history through stitching. Thousands of people in many countries took part, many of them new to embroidery. The panels are on display in the Quaker Tapestry Museum in Kendal, Cumbria. It is one of the largest community embroideries ever made.

title: Penelope with the Suitors
about: Penelope sits at her loom, waiting for her husband Odysseus to come home. In the story she weaves by day and secretly unravels by night, to delay the suitors who want to marry her. Young men crowd in at the door. A cat at her feet plays with a ball of yarn, and through the window you can see Odysseus's ship and his adventures.
artistBio: Pinturicchio was a painter from Perugia known for bright, detailed frescoes. He painted this scene for the palace of Pandolfo Petrucci, the ruler of Siena. Later, the fresco was taken off the wall and moved to canvas. It is now in the National Gallery in London. It shows a woman at a loom, with every part of the warp and shuttle in view.
c: Pinturicchio Penelope with the Suitors National Gallery

title: Winding the Skein
about: Two girls in loose ancient Greek dress sit on a sunny rooftop above the sea. One holds a loose skein of yarn while the other draws it off and winds it into a ball. It is a quiet, everyday task, the kind every spinner knows. Leighton makes it graceful, with flowing cloth and soft light.
artistBio: Frederic Leighton was one of the leading painters of Victorian Britain and president of the Royal Academy. He loved classical subjects and painted many scenes of figures at rest in warm Mediterranean light. Winding the Skein was bought for the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney, where it still hangs and is one of the gallery's best-loved works.

title: The Sleeping Spinner
about: A young woman has fallen asleep in her chair beside a spinning wheel. Her head tips to one side, and her hand still rests near the distaff, which is loaded with fiber. The painting is honest about tiredness. It shows a working woman in a private, unguarded moment, not a pretty idea of spinning.
artistBio: Gustave Courbet was a leader of Realism in French painting, known for painting ordinary people at full size and with full seriousness. He showed this work at the Paris Salon in 1853. It is now in the Musée Fabre in Montpellier. The detail of the wheel and fiber shows how common spinning still was in country homes of his time.

title: The Embroiderer
about: A young woman sits with her back to us at a window, bent over her embroidery frame. The room is calm and nearly bare, with plain walls and very few objects. Light falls on her work. There is no story here, only concentration. It is one of the gentlest images of needlework in European painting, and it treats quiet handwork as worth a picture.
artistBio: Kersting was a German painter of the Romantic period and a friend of Caspar David Friedrich. He specialized in small interiors showing people reading, writing or working, often friends he knew. The woman here is the painter Louise Seidler. The painting is in Weimar. Kersting later worked as a painting supervisor at the Meissen porcelain factory.

title: Portrait of Giovanni della Volta with his Wife and Children
about: A Venetian merchant, his wife and their two children gather around a table. Many viewers look first at the tablecloth: it is a knotted carpet from Anatolia, with a yellow lattice pattern on red. Lotto painted it so carefully that rug experts still use it as evidence for how and when such carpets were made.
artistBio: Lorenzo Lotto was a Venetian painter with an unsettled career and an intense, personal style. He painted this type of Turkish carpet so often that it is now called a 'Lotto carpet,' even though he did not make them. The painting is in the National Gallery in London. It shows how prized Anatolian carpets were in Renaissance Venice.
c: Lotto Giovanni della Volta portrait National Gallery

title: Pile Knotting
place: Central Asia, Middle East and worldwide
medium: Wool, silk or cotton knots on a woven foundation
about: A pile rug is made on a loom strung with warp threads. The weaver ties a short piece of yarn around warp threads, cuts it, and moves on, knot by knot, across the row. Then a few rows of weft are beaten down to lock the knots in place. The symmetrical knot wraps two warps; the asymmetrical knot wraps one and leaves an end open. Finally, the pile is sheared even.
artistBio: The oldest known knotted carpet, the Pazyryk Carpet from Siberia, is over two thousand years old. Pile weaving spread across Anatolia, Persia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, India and China, and north to Scandinavia as the shaggy rya. The two knots are often called Turkish and Persian, but both are used in many regions. Fine knotting can take a weaver months or years.

title: Crewelwork
about: Crewelwork is embroidery done with crewel wool, a fine two-ply worsted yarn, on a sturdy linen or linen-and-cotton cloth. Stitchers use stem stitch, chain stitch, long-and-short shading, French knots, and laid threads held down in lattices. The wool is thicker than silk, so the stitches stand out and cover ground quickly. Curving branches, leaves and birds fill the cloth.
artistBio: Crewelwork became popular in seventeenth-century England for bed curtains, often with a 'tree of life' design. Some patterns show the influence of Indian painted cottons coming through trade. Settlers carried the craft to New England, where lighter, more open designs developed. Around 1900 a revival began, including the Deerfield Society of Blue and White Needlework in Massachusetts.

title: Tatting
about: Tatting is lace made of knots. The tatter holds a small shuttle wound with thread and makes a series of double stitches, each one two half hitches, over a core thread. Pulling the core closes the stitches into a ring. Rings and arcs called chains are joined to build edgings, collars and doilies. Small loops called picots add a lacy edge and serve as joining points.
artistBio: Tatting grew out of an older pastime called knotting, popular with fashionable women in the 1700s, who used large shuttles to make knotted cord. In the mid-1800s, tatting as we know it took shape, and pattern writers such as Mlle Riego de la Branchardière helped popularize it. Later tatters also use a long needle instead of a shuttle. Tatting guilds keep the craft going today.

title: Rug Hooking
medium: Fabric strips or yarn pulled through a backing
about: Rug hooking uses a tool like a small crochet hook set in a wooden handle. The backing cloth is stretched on a frame. From underneath, the maker holds a strip of fabric or yarn, and the hook pulls loops up through the backing, one by one, close together. The loops stand on their own. Shading comes from careful choice of strip colors, often from old clothes.
artistBio: Hooked rugs became common in the 1800s in Atlantic Canada and New England, when burlap from sacks became easy to find. Rural women used worn-out wool clothing, which made the craft thrifty and widely shared. Some communities, like those of the Grenfell Mission in Labrador, sold their rugs. Today hooking is popular again, with hand-dyed wool and both traditional and modern designs.

title: Double Weave
place: Andes, North America, Europe and beyond
medium: Two interlocked layers of woven cloth
about: In double weave, two separate layers of cloth are woven on the same loom at once, one on top of the other. By trading which threads are on top, the weaver can swap the layers to make a pattern. The design then shows in reverse on the back. Double weave can also make tubes, pockets, or a cloth twice as wide as the loom, folded open later.
artistBio: Ancient Andean weavers made double cloth with bold animal and bird designs. The same principle shows up in Cherokee rivercane baskets. In Europe and North America, double-woven coverlets were common in the nineteenth century, many made on Jacquard looms by professional weavers. Modern handweavers use double weave on floor looms for blankets, pictures and sculptural pieces.

title: Macramé
about: Macramé makes textiles by knotting cords, with no loom or needle. The two main knots are the square knot and the half hitch. By repeating and combining them, makers build nets, spirals, flat panels and raised patterns. Beads, rings and wood can be worked in. Fine thread gives fringes and lace. Heavy cord gives wall hangings and the familiar plant hanger.
artistBio: Decorative knotting has long histories in many places. The word is often said to come from Arabic for a fringed cloth. Sailors were famous for knotting on long voyages, making covers, belts and bell pulls. Victorian homes used macramé fringes, and the 1970s brought a huge craze. A new generation of fiber artists has made it popular again.

title: Peter Collingwood
about: Peter Collingwood trained and worked as a doctor. After the Second World War he decided to weave instead, learning in the workshops of Ethel Mairet and others. He set up his own workshop in Suffolk, where he wove rugs and wall hangings for decades. He taught widely around the world and was known for his clear thinking, humor and generosity to students.
artistBio: His best-known works are macrogauzes: tall hangings of linen threads that cross each other in the middle, held by metal rods, so they look like weaving drawn in the air. He also wrote standard books on rug weaving, sprang, and tablet weaving, built from close study of old textiles. Weavers still use these books. His work is in many museum collections.

title: Jessie Newbery
about: Jessie Newbery started embroidery classes at the Glasgow School of Art in 1894, where her husband, Fra Newbery, was the director. She believed embroidery should be for everyone, not only the rich. She taught students to use plain linen, simple stitches and appliqué, and to design their own work. She also cared about everyday dress and designed clothes for herself.
artistBio: Her work helped shape the 'Glasgow Style,' with stylized roses, long stems and lettering, related to the work of Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret Macdonald. Her student Ann Macbeth carried her ideas forward and later led the department. Her embroidered collars, cushions and panels survive in Scottish museum collections. Her approach shaped embroidery teaching well beyond Glasgow.

title: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay
about: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay was an activist in India's freedom movement, a leader for women's rights, and later the great champion of Indian crafts. After independence, she traveled across the country to find weavers, dyers, embroiderers and potters whose skills were dying out. She worked to find them markets, fair pay and respect. She believed craft was a living source of income and identity.
artistBio: She led the All India Handicrafts Board and founded the Crafts Council of India, among many other institutions for craft and the arts. Many handloom traditions that survive today, from saris to rugs, were helped by her efforts. She also wrote books on Indian crafts and textiles. In India she is remembered as one of the key figures in craft revival.

title: Mariano Fortuny
about: Mariano Fortuny was born in Granada, Spain, and lived most of his life in Venice. He was a painter, photographer and stage-lighting inventor, but he is best known for cloth. His studio in a Venetian palace was filled with fabrics, lamps and experiments. He worked closely with his wife, Henriette Negrin, who was central to the textile work.
artistBio: Their most famous design is the Delphos gown, a column of fine pleated silk inspired by ancient Greek dress. It slipped over the head and clung softly, with no corset. Fortuny also printed velvets and cottons with patterns drawn from Renaissance and Asian textiles. His palace is now the Museo Fortuny, and his Giudecca factory still produces Fortuny fabrics.

title: Dorothy Liebes
place: San Francisco and New York, USA
about: Dorothy Liebes was an American weaver who brought bold color and surprising materials into modern interiors. She mixed yarns with metallic threads, wood slats, bamboo and other unexpected materials. Her studio in San Francisco wove fabrics for architects and designers. She was famous for color combinations that seemed to clash yet worked beautifully, full of shine and texture.
artistBio: Liebes later moved her studio to New York. She worked with big companies, helping them design machine-made fabrics and synthetic yarns that kept a handwoven look. That brought her ideas into millions of homes in mid-century America. Her work shows a link between the handloom and industry. Her textiles and swatches are in American museum collections.

title: Silkworms Come to Byzantium
about: For centuries, China kept the secret of how silk was made, and the Roman world paid high prices for imported silk. According to the Byzantine historian Procopius, around the 550s some monks came to Emperor Justinian and offered to bring back silkworms. They returned with eggs, which were hatched and fed on mulberry leaves. A later account says the eggs were hidden in hollow canes.
artistBio: With silkworms in hand, the Byzantine Empire began its own silk industry. Imperial workshops in Constantinople wove some of the most valued cloth of the Middle Ages, used as gifts and in church treasures. Silk making later spread to Italy, Spain and France. The story shows how much a single craft secret could be worth.

title: The Mesta
about: The Mesta was a powerful association of sheep owners in Castile, given a royal charter by King Alfonso X in 1273. Each year, huge flocks of merino sheep walked hundreds of miles between summer pastures in the north and winter pastures in the south. They used protected routes called cañadas reales. The Mesta defended these routes and the owners' rights, often against farmers.
artistBio: Merino wool was soft and fine, and Spain grew rich selling it. For centuries Spain did not allow merino sheep to leave the country. When they finally spread in the eighteenth century, merinos were bred across Europe, then Australia and the Americas. The Mesta was abolished in 1836. Shepherds still drive sheep through the center of Madrid in an annual festival.

title: Mauveine
about: Mauveine was the first synthetic dye to be made in a factory. In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an eighteen-year-old chemistry student, was trying to make quinine, the malaria medicine, from coal tar. Instead he got a dark sludge that dyed silk a strong purple. The color was called mauve. It did not fade quickly, and it was cheaper than older purples.
artistBio: Perkin patented the dye and opened a factory with his family. Mauve became the fashion color of the late 1850s, worn by Queen Victoria and Empress Eugénie. Within years, chemists made a flood of new synthetic dyes. They changed textiles worldwide. Natural dyes faded from common use, and many traditional dyers had to adapt or stop.

title: Kermes
about: Kermes is a red dye made from the dried bodies of small scale insects that live on the kermes oak, a shrubby tree of the Mediterranean. Gatherers picked the insects by hand, then dried and ground them. With a mordant, kermes dyes wool and silk deep, clear reds. The words 'crimson' and 'carmine' both come from the name of this dye.
artistBio: Kermes was used in the ancient world and was one of the most valued dyes of medieval Europe. The finest red woolens, scarlets, were dyed with it, and they cost a fortune. After Spanish ships brought cochineal from the Americas in the sixteenth century, kermes was slowly replaced, because cochineal gave more color for less effort.

title: The Flying Shuttle
medium: Loom shuttle with wheels and picker
about: On older looms, a weaver passed the shuttle by hand from one side to the other. Wide cloth needed two weavers. John Kay's flying shuttle ran on small wheels in a track. The weaver jerked a cord attached to 'pickers' at each side, which knocked the shuttle across the warp. One weaver could now make wide cloth, much faster than before.
artistBio: Kay patented the shuttle in 1733. Weavers adopted it but many refused to pay him, and he faced anger from those who feared losing work. He later went to France. Faster weaving created a shortage of yarn, which pushed inventors to build spinning machines. The flying shuttle is still used on many handlooms today.

title: The Niddy-Noddy
about: A niddy-noddy is a simple hand reel for making skeins. It is a central stick with a short crossbar at each end, set at right angles to each other. The spinner winds yarn from the bobbin around the four ends in a fixed path, rocking the tool with a nodding motion. Each wrap is a known length, so counting wraps tells how much yarn you have.
artistBio: Hand reels like this appear in many old pictures of spinning. In the past, a skein of a set length was a unit of trade and work, so reeling was important. Niddy-noddies were made by hand from wood. Today spinners still use them, in wood or plastic pipe, to wind, measure and set the twist in handspun yarn.

title: The Gunthertuch
about: The Gunthertuch is a large Byzantine silk woven in tapestry technique. It shows an emperor on a white horse at the center,. Two women in crowns stand on either side and offer him crowns. They probably stand for two cities greeting the ruler after a victory. Which emperor it shows is still debated. The colors have faded, but the purple and gold design is still clear.
artistBio: The cloth was made in Byzantine imperial or court workshops. Bishop Gunther of Bamberg probably received it while traveling to Jerusalem. He died on the way home in 1065 and was buried wrapped in it. The silk was found long afterward, when his tomb in Bamberg Cathedral was opened. It is kept today in the Diocesan Museum in Bamberg.

title: The Nine Heroes Tapestries
about: In medieval Europe, the Nine Heroes (or Nine Worthies) were three pagan, three Hebrew and three Christian leaders, held up as models of courage. These tapestries show the heroes enthroned in Gothic architecture, surrounded by small figures of courtiers, musicians and soldiers. Five of the heroes survive, among them Joshua, David and King Arthur. Every niche is crowded with lively, busy detail.
artistBio: The tapestries are among the very few large tapestries to survive from around 1400. Coats of arms in them suggest they were made for Jean, Duke of Berry, a famous patron of the arts. They came down in pieces and were later reassembled from many fragments. They hang today at The Met Cloisters in New York.

title: The Trivulzio Tapestries of the Months
about: This set of twelve tapestries shows the months of the year. In each, a figure standing for the month poses above a scene of the season's work, such as harvesting, pressing grapes or slaughtering pigs. The sign of the zodiac and the sun appear above. The scenes are calm and orderly, with solid, sculptural figures, very different from the dense Gothic tapestries of the north.
artistBio: Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, a powerful Milanese general, ordered the set. The painter Bartolomeo Suardi, called Bramantino, made the designs, and the weaver Benedetto da Milano wove them in a workshop at Vigevano. It is one of the few complete tapestry sets made in Renaissance Italy. The tapestries are now in the Castello Sforzesco in Milan.

title: The Hunts of Maximilian
medium: Wool, silk, gold and silver thread tapestry
about: These twelve tapestries follow a year of hunting, one month to a panel, with the zodiac sign shown at the top. Riders, hounds and huntsmen chase stags and boar through the forest of Soignes near Brussels. Real buildings and views of the area appear in the backgrounds. The scenes are full of movement, weather and light, and the dogs are drawn with great care.
artistBio: Bernard van Orley was court painter in Brussels and one of the leading tapestry designers of his time. The set was woven in Brussels, then the center of European tapestry. The name links it to Emperor Maximilian I, who loved hunting, though he had died before it was made and the name came later. The tapestries are in the Louvre in Paris.

title: The Noble Women Hangings
artist: Embroiderers working for Bess of Hardwick
medium: Appliqué of silk, velvet and cloth of gold
about: These tall hangings show heroines of the ancient world, each standing in an arch between two figures who stand for her virtues. Penelope, Lucretia, Zenobia, Artemisia and Cleopatra appear. Penelope is shown with Patience and Perseverance. The figures are made of cut pieces of rich fabric sewn onto a ground. Much of the fabric came from medieval church vestments, cut up and reused.
artistBio: Bess of Hardwick, one of the richest women in Elizabethan England, had the hangings made, probably for her house at Chatsworth. After the dissolution of the monasteries, old copes and vestments were available, and her embroiderers used them as material. The hangings have stayed together and are at Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire, cared for by the National Trust.
c: Hardwick Hall Noble Women hangings Penelope

title: The Emperor's Carpet
about: This large carpet is filled with scrolling vines and blossoming trees on a deep red field. Among the plants are lions, deer, birds and mythical creatures, some fighting, some at rest. Cloud bands and flowers fill the dark border. The pile is very fine, so the drawing is crisp and curving. It shows how far Persian court weaving had moved from simple repeating patterns toward painting.
artistBio: The carpet was woven in a Safavid court workshop in Iran. It belonged to the Habsburg emperors in Vienna, which gave it its name; tradition says it arrived as a diplomatic gift. A closely matching carpet is in the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna. This one is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

title: Polonaise Carpets
artist: Safavid weavers of Isfahan and Kashan
medium: Silk pile with silver and gold brocading
about: Polonaise carpets have a silk pile, with areas woven in silver and gold thread that catch the light. Their designs are flowing flowers, palmettes and arabesques. Many were made in bright greens, pinks, yellows and blues, which have now faded to soft tones. They were luxury objects, meant to impress, and many went to Europe as royal gifts or purchases.
artistBio: These carpets were woven in Safavid court workshops in Iran. Some came to Poland in the 1600s, and a few carried Polish coats of arms. When pieces from the Czartoryski collection were shown at the 1878 Paris exhibition, people thought they had been made in Poland, and the French name 'polonaise' stuck. Examples are in museums in Europe, the United States and Iran.

title: Mamluk Carpets
about: Mamluk carpets are made of many small geometric shapes that fit together like a kaleidoscope. A large central octagon or star is surrounded by smaller stars, cypress trees and papyrus-like plants. The colors are few: mainly crimson, green and light blue. When you look closely, the shapes seem to move and shimmer. They feel very different from Persian and Turkish carpets.
artistBio: These carpets were woven in Cairo under the Mamluk sultans. They were exported to Europe, especially to Venice, where they were prized. After the Ottomans took Egypt in 1517, Cairo workshops began making carpets in Ottoman style as well. A famous large example, the Simonetti carpet, is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

title: Lotto Carpets
artist: Anatolian weavers of the Ushak region
about: A Lotto carpet has a yellow lattice of angular leaves and arabesques laid over a red field. The pattern repeats without a center, so it seems to run on past the edges. Borders often show a pattern based on Arabic script. The bold yellow and red, sometimes with touches of blue, make these carpets easy to spot, even at a distance in old paintings.
artistBio: The carpets were woven in western Anatolia and exported to Europe in large numbers. They are named after the Venetian painter Lorenzo Lotto, who painted them in several pictures, including his portrait of Giovanni della Volta and his family. The name was given by later scholars, not by the weavers. Examples are in museums in Istanbul, Europe and North America.

title: Gabbeh Rugs
about: A gabbeh is a thick, soft rug with a long pile. Several rows of weft are packed between each row of knots, so the rug is loose and heavy. The designs are simple: open fields of color, a few rectangles, a small animal, tree or human figure. Weavers made them for their own families, to use as bedding and floor covers in tents.
artistBio: Gabbehs come from the nomadic and village peoples of southwest Iran, especially the Qashqai and Luri. Women did the weaving, often from their own flocks' wool. For a long time they were seen as rough household rugs. From the late twentieth century, collectors and buyers came to love their freedom and color, and many are now made for export.

title: Tibetan Tiger Rugs
about: These rugs show a tiger, either as a flat pelt with head and paws spread out, or simply as orange and black stripes filling the field. Tiger skins were rare and costly, and stood for power and protection. A woven version gave the same meaning. Many are small, sized for a seat or a cushion, and the stripes are often drawn with wit and freedom.
artistBio: Tibetan weavers used a looped knotting method that is different from Persian and Turkish knots. Tiger rugs were used by people of rank and by some lamas, and are linked with meditation and protective rites. Old examples are rare and sought by collectors. Tibetan weavers working in Nepal and India still make tiger rugs today.

title: Akwete Cloth
medium: Handwoven cotton, raffia or synthetic thread
about: Akwete cloth is woven by women on a wide upright loom. Unlike the narrow strips of many West African weavers, the loom makes a broad panel that can be worn as a wrapper. Patterns are woven in with extra threads, making raised motifs in rows and grids. Each motif has a name, and some are said to have belonged to particular families.
artistBio: The town of Akwete in southeastern Nigeria has been known for this cloth for a long time, and weaving skills are passed from mother to daughter. Cotton was once the main fiber, with raffia used too; today weavers also use bright synthetic and metallic threads. Akwete cloth is worn for weddings and other important events.

title: Fez Embroidery (Tarz al-Fassi)
medium: Silk embroidery on cotton or linen
about: Fez embroidery is counted, worked by following the threads of the cloth, and it looks the same on both sides. Usually only one color is used, often deep red or blue silk. The designs are geometric: stylized flowers, trees, birds and stars, built from small straight stitches. The work is even and exact, and the back of a good piece is as neat as the front.
artistBio: Women in Fez have made this embroidery for generations, often for a bride's household linens: towels, cushions, tablecloths and headscarves. Girls once learned it from older women at home or with a teacher. It remains one of Morocco's best-known embroideries and is still taught and sold in the city today.

title: Oya
medium: Needle lace, crochet, tatting or beads
about: Oya is a tiny, three-dimensional lace made into flowers, leaves and fruit, sewn along the edge of a headscarf. In needle oya, the lace is built with a sewing needle and silk thread, knot by knot. There are also crochet, tatting and beaded kinds. The flowers can be so fine that they look real. Colors and flowers were said to send messages about the wearer.
artistBio: Women and girls in Anatolia made oya for their own scarves and for their trousseaus, and each region had its own forms. Some say particular flowers showed whether a woman was happy, longing or newly married. Oya is still made and worn, though fewer young women learn needle oya now. Groups in Turkey work to keep it alive.

title: Arraiolos Rugs
medium: Wool embroidery on linen or jute canvas
about: An Arraiolos rug looks like a knotted carpet but is actually embroidered. Wool yarn is stitched onto a strong canvas with a slanted cross stitch, row by row, until every bit of the ground is covered. Older rugs show the influence of Persian and Turkish carpets, with medallions and animals. Later rugs use bold flowers, birds and Portuguese folk designs in strong colors.
artistBio: The town of Arraiolos in southern Portugal has made these rugs since at least the seventeenth century. For a long time the work was done at home, mostly by women. Today the rugs are a recognized Portuguese craft, made in local workshops and sold widely. The stitch is so linked with the town that it is often called the Arraiolos stitch.

title: Ryijy Rugs
about: A ryijy is a rug with a long, shaggy pile, knotted on a woven ground. Early ryijys were practical: they were used as warm covers on beds and in boats, with the pile turned toward the body. Later they became decorative. Wedding ryijys were hung on the wall and often show the couple's initials, a date, hearts, trees of life and flowers.
artistBio: Ryijys were made across Finland and Sweden, where they are called rya. In the twentieth century, Finnish designers and the Friends of Finnish Handicraft revived them as modern art textiles, with bold abstract color fields. Ryijy became a symbol of Finnish design. Old and new examples are in Finnish museums, and many people still knot them at home.

title: Haapsalu Lace Shawl
about: A Haapsalu shawl is a large lace shawl knitted from very fine wool. Its patterns of leaves, flowers and lily-of-the-valley are often scattered with nupps: small raised bobbles made by working several stitches into one, then gathering them. The shawl is knitted, then the edging is added and the whole piece is stretched to dry. A good one is said to pass through a wedding ring.
artistBio: Women in the seaside town of Haapsalu began knitting these shawls in the nineteenth century, when the town was a fashionable spa and visitors bought them. Patterns were passed down and collected. In recent decades Estonian knitters have published the traditional patterns, and nupps have become loved by lace knitters around the world. The town now has a shawl museum.

title: Lopapeysa (Icelandic Sweater)
about: A lopapeysa is a thick sweater knitted in the round from lopi, a lightly twisted, unspun Icelandic wool. Its mark is the round yoke around the shoulders, patterned in bands of geometric shapes in natural sheep colors: white, grey, brown and black. Icelandic fleece has two layers, a long, tough outer coat and a soft, fine undercoat, which together make the yarn warm, light and water-resistant.
artistBio: Icelanders have knitted for centuries, but the yoke sweater appeared in the mid-twentieth century, when knitters drew on many sources and the design caught on. It was soon a symbol of Iceland. Lopi yarn is still made from the fleece of Icelandic sheep, a breed brought by Norse settlers. Many sweaters are still knitted by hand, and the pattern changes with every maker.

title: Setesdal Lusekofte
about: The lusekofte, or 'lice jacket', is a black and white sweater named for the small scattered dots knitted across its body. Near the top, the dots give way to bands of eight-pointed stars and other patterns. The neck and cuffs are often trimmed with embroidered or woven bands, and closed with silver or pewter clasps. The plain lower part was once hidden under a man's trousers or vest.
artistBio: The sweater comes from the Setesdal valley in southern Norway, where it was worn by men as part of local dress. In the twentieth century it became a national favorite and a ski-sweater classic, made in factories as well as at home. The pattern has inspired countless Norwegian sweaters, and many Norwegians still own one.

title: North Country Wholecloth Quilts
artist: Quilters and quilt markers of Durham and Northumberland
about: A wholecloth quilt is made from plain fabric, not patchwork. All the beauty is in the quilting: rows of tiny running stitches that hold the layers together and draw feathers, roses, fans, twisted cables and hearts across the surface. Light falls on the raised and sunken lines, so the pattern shows best at a slant. Many were made in strong single colors or two-colored 'strippy' layouts.
artistBio: Quilting was a home skill in the mining and farming villages of Durham and Northumberland. Some people worked as professional markers, drawing designs on the cloth for others to quilt; George Gardiner of Allendale and his apprentice Elizabeth Sanderson were well known. In the hard years between the world wars, a government scheme helped quilters sell their work. Examples are at the Beamish Museum and the Bowes Museum.

title: Lambani Embroidery
place: Karnataka and other parts of India
medium: Embroidery with mirrors, shells and coins
about: Lambani embroidery is bold and dense. Women work patterns in red, orange, yellow, white and black thread on dark cotton, using many kinds of stitches together. They add small mirrors, cowrie shells, coins, beads and tassels. The work covers skirts, blouses, headcloths and bags. On a whole outfit, the weight of the embroidery and ornaments can be considerable.
artistBio: The Lambani, also called Banjara, were once traveling traders who moved goods with cattle across India. Their women's embroidery is linked with that history and with their identity. Today many Lambani live in settled villages, and women's groups make embroidery for sale. The Lambani embroidery of Sandur in Karnataka has a Geographical Indication to protect its name.

title: Kanchipuram Silk Sari
medium: Mulberry silk with zari (gold or silver thread)
about: Kanchipuram saris are heavy silk saris with wide, contrasting borders and a rich end piece (pallu), woven with zari. Motifs include temple towers, peacocks, parrots, mango shapes and checks. In the traditional method, the body, border and pallu are woven separately in different colors and then interlocked on the loom so firmly that they will not come apart.
artistBio: Kanchipuram is an old temple town, and silk weaving there is closely tied to its temples. Many weaving families belong to communities that have done this work for generations. A Kanchipuram sari is a favored bridal sari in South India and is often kept as an heirloom. The name is protected by a Geographical Indication.

title: Paithani Sari
medium: Silk and zari, tapestry woven borders
about: A Paithani is a silk sari with a gold border and a gold end piece (pallu). Its borders and pallu are woven with a tapestry method, where each colored thread is worked only across its own area. That is why the motifs, especially peacocks, parrots and lotus flowers, have clean, solid shapes. Some Paithanis are woven so the two sides of the cloth look the same.
artistBio: The sari is named for Paithan, an old town on the Godavari River. It was prized by royal families, and weaving flourished under the patronage of the Peshwas in the eighteenth century. Today most Paithanis are woven in Yeola, as well as Paithan. A handwoven Paithani can take months, and many families keep one for weddings.

title: Ajrakh
artist: Khatri block printers of Sindh and Kutch
medium: Resist and mordant block printing on cotton
about: Ajrakh is a block-printed cloth of deep indigo blue and madder red, with black and white. Its patterns are geometric: stars, rosettes and grids, set in borders and centered layouts. The cloth goes through many stages: washing, printing with resists and mordants, dyeing in indigo, printing again and dyeing in red. Each side of the cloth may be printed, so it can take weeks.
artistBio: Ajrakh is worn as a shawl, turban or wrapper by men in Sindh and by herders in Kutch, and is a strong sign of Sindhi identity. The Khatri printers of Kutch carried the craft on; after the 2001 earthquake some families settled in a new village, Ajrakhpur. Many printers have returned to natural dyes, and their work is sought worldwide.

title: Srikalahasti Kalamkari
about: Kalamkari means 'pen work'. The artist draws with a kalam, a bamboo pen wrapped with a pad of cloth, on cotton treated with myrobalan and milk. Lines are drawn in black, then areas painted with alum mordant, so that the red dye takes only there. Blue, yellow and green follow. The cloths tell long stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and other sacred texts, in panels with written captions.
artistBio: Srikalahasti is a temple town, and its kalamkari began as hangings and story cloths for temples and festivals. The style is free-hand, unlike the block-printed kalamkari of Machilipatnam. In the twentieth century the craft nearly died out, but was revived with support from Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay's crafts programs, and painters still work in the town today.

title: Tsujigahana
medium: Stitched resist dyeing, ink painting and gold on silk
about: Tsujigahana textiles combine stitch-resist dyeing with painting. Dyers stitched around shapes and drew the threads tight, so that dye could not reach those areas. Inside the reserved shapes, artists painted flowers, leaves and pine needles in fine black ink, sometimes adding gold leaf or small embroidery. The result is a soft, dreamy look, with patches of color floating on the silk.
artistBio: Tsujigahana flourished in Japan's Muromachi and Momoyama periods and was worn by warriors and the wealthy. It disappeared in the early seventeenth century, as new methods replaced it, and much about it remains unknown. Fragments survive in Japanese and foreign museums. In the twentieth century the dyer Itchiku Kubota spent years trying to recreate it, inspiring his own famous kimono.

title: Bashōfu (Banana Fiber Cloth)
about: Bashōfu is cloth made from the fibers of the Japanese fiber banana plant. The stalks are cut and stripped into layers. The inner layers give the finest thread. Fibers are boiled with ash, scraped, split by hand, and knotted end to end into long threads. The cloth is crisp, light and airy, well suited to Okinawa's heat, and is often patterned with simple ikat in brown and indigo.
artistBio: Bashōfu was once worn by everyone in the Ryukyu Islands, from royalty to farmers. After the Second World War it nearly disappeared. In the village of Kijoka, Taira Toshiko led its revival and was named a Living National Treasure. Making a single garment takes many months of work, from growing the plants to weaving.

title: Kesa (Buddhist Patchwork Robe)
about: A kesa is the outer robe of a Buddhist monk, worn over one shoulder. It is pieced from many rectangles arranged in columns, recalling the rule that monks should dress in cloth made from discarded rags. In Japan, though, many kesa were sewn from fine donated silks: brocades, old kimono and even Noh costumes. The result is a humble form made from beautiful fabric.
artistBio: The kesa comes from the kasaya robe of early Indian Buddhism and traveled with the religion through China to Japan. Donating fine cloth for a kesa was a way for lay people to earn merit. Many old kesa are kept in temples and museums, and they preserve fabrics that might otherwise have been lost.

title: Mandarin Squares (Rank Badges)
about: Mandarin squares were badges sewn on the front and back of an official's robe to show his rank. Civil officials wore birds, with the crane for the highest rank. Military officials wore animals, such as lions, tigers and leopards. The creature stands on a rock in the waves, often looking toward a red sun, framed by clouds and lucky symbols.
artistBio: Rank badges were set by rules early in the Ming dynasty and continued in the Qing. Officials had to buy or commission their own, so quality varies widely. In the Qing, the front badge was usually split down the middle, because the surcoat opened at the front. The system ended with the fall of the Qing in 1912, and many badges went to collectors.

title: Pua Kumbu
medium: Warp ikat cotton on a backstrap loom
about: A pua kumbu is a ritual blanket woven with warp ikat: the warp threads are tied in patterns and dyed before weaving. The colors are deep reddish brown, black and cream. Designs show spirits, crocodiles, plants and human figures, linked together in dense, rhythmic patterns. Some designs are powerful and may only be woven by experienced women. Pua are used in important rituals and as shelters for sacred ceremonies.
artistBio: Among the Iban, weaving was women's path to honor. The mordanting stage, called ngar, was dangerous and secret, and it was compared to men's warfare. A master weaver held high status. Designs are said to come to weavers in dreams. Pua kumbu are still woven today in Sarawak longhouses, and old pieces are treasured family heirlooms.

title: Sampot Hol and Pidan
about: Hol is Cambodian weft ikat: the weft threads are tied and dyed in sections before weaving, so the pattern appears as they are woven in. The silk is woven in an uneven twill that shows more color on one side. A sampot hol is a wrap skirt with fine, small repeating patterns. A pidan is a larger hanging with pictures of temples, Buddhas, elephants and trees, made for pagodas and ceremonies.
artistBio: Silk weaving is an old Khmer tradition, carried on mostly by women in villages. Under the Khmer Rouge in the 1970s, weaving nearly stopped and many skilled weavers died. Since then, projects such as the Institute for Khmer Traditional Textiles, founded by Kikuo Morimoto, have helped older weavers teach younger ones, and natural dyes have returned.

title: Kiribati Coconut Fiber Armour
medium: Knotted coconut fiber cord (sennit), porcupinefish skin
about: Warriors of Kiribati wore full suits of armour made of thick cord twisted from coconut husk fiber. The cord was knotted into a dense, stiff fabric covering the legs, body and arms, with a tall panel rising behind the head to guard the neck. Some suits have patterns worked in dark and light cord, or human hair. Helmets were made from the dried, spiny skin of a porcupinefish.
artistBio: On low coral islands without metal, coconut palm was the main material for almost everything, including weapons and armour. The armour protected against swords and spears edged with sharks' teeth. Many suits reached museums in Europe, America and Oceania in the nineteenth century. Today they are admired as a remarkable use of plant fiber.

title: Unangax̂ Grass Baskets
medium: Twined wild rye grass, sometimes with silk or wool thread
about: Unangax̂ women made baskets from wild rye grass that grows on Aleutian beaches. The grass was cut, cured and split into very thin strands, then twined so finely that the best baskets feel like cloth. Many are small lidded baskets with knob handles, decorated with colored silk or wool worked into the twining. Weavers from the island of Attu were especially famed for fineness.
artistBio: The baskets were used at home and, from the late nineteenth century, sold to collectors and travelers. The Second World War brought great loss: the people of Attu were taken prisoner to Japan, and other Unangax̂ were moved to camps in Southeast Alaska. Weaving almost stopped. Since then, weavers and teachers have worked to revive the craft.

title: Haitian Vodou Flags (Drapo)
artist: Haitian flag makers, including Myrlande Constant
medium: Sequins and beads sewn on satin or velvet
about: Drapo are ceremonial flags covered in thousands of hand-sewn sequins and beads, so they glitter when moved. Older flags often show the vèvè, the drawn symbol of a spirit (lwa), or a Catholic saint linked with that spirit. Flags are carried at the start of a ceremony to greet the spirits. Newer works can be very large, with crowded scenes of people, history and the spirit world.
artistBio: Flag making grew from Vodou practice, and makers were often linked with temples. From the mid-twentieth century, collectors began buying drapo as art. Myrlande Constant, who once worked in a wedding dress factory, began making flags in the 1990s with large, detailed scenes in tiny beads. She is one of the best-known Haitian artists working today.

title: The Star-Spangled Banner
artist: Mary Pickersgill, with Caroline Pickersgill, family members and Grace Wisher
about: This huge garrison flag has fifteen stars and fifteen stripes. It was made to fly over Fort McHenry in Baltimore, big enough to be seen from far off. In September 1814, after a night of British bombardment, it was raised over the fort. Francis Scott Key saw it and wrote the poem that became the United States national anthem. Pieces were later cut off as souvenirs.
artistBio: Mary Pickersgill was a Baltimore flag maker. She made the flag with her daughter Caroline, other relatives and Grace Wisher, a young African American girl bound to her household as an apprentice. They worked for weeks, finishing it on a brewery floor because it was too big for the house. The flag is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

title: Wrapped Reichstag
medium: Polypropylene fabric with aluminum surface, blue rope
about: For two weeks in the summer of 1995, the Reichstag building in Berlin was wrapped in silvery fabric tied with blue rope. The fabric hung in deep folds that changed with the sun and wind, so the heavy stone building looked soft and alive. Millions of people came to see it. Then everything was taken down and recycled, as the artists always planned.
artistBio: Christo and Jeanne-Claude worked together on large, temporary projects using fabric. They spent about twenty-four years seeking permission to wrap the Reichstag, until Germany's parliament voted to allow it. As with all their works, they paid for it themselves by selling Christo's drawings. Sewing teams prepared the fabric panels, and climbers installed them.

title: Unikko
about: Unikko, Finnish for 'poppy', is a pattern of huge, flat, rounded flowers in bold colors, often red and pink with black centers on white. There are no outlines or shading, just simple shapes repeated large. It was printed on cotton by the meter and used for dresses, curtains and bags.
