It still looks fresh and is one of the best-known printed fabrics in the world.
artistBio: Maija Isola designed hundreds of prints for Marimekko. The company's founder, Armi Ratia, had said Marimekko would not print floral patterns. Isola answered with a set of flower designs, including Unikko, and Ratia accepted them. Unikko has been printed ever since in many colorways. Isola's work is in design museums, and she is honored as a leader of Finnish design.

title: Matyó Embroidery
medium: Embroidery on cotton, wool or silk
about: Matyó embroidery is covered in large, bright flowers: roses, peonies, tulips and buds, crowded together in red, pink, yellow, blue, green and black. Petals are often worked in satin stitch, so they shine. The flowers decorate aprons, shirt sleeves, cushions and household linens. Over time the designs grew denser and the colors brighter, until whole garments were covered.
artistBio: The Matyó are a Catholic community around Mezőkövesd in northeastern Hungary. Embroidery was done by women and was central to their festive dress. Patterns were often drawn by skilled 'pattern writers' and stitched by others. Matyó embroidery became a symbol of Hungarian folk art, and its folk art traditions are listed by UNESCO.

title: Blaudruck (Blueprint Cloth)
place: Germany, Austria, Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia
about: Blaudruck means 'blue print'. Printers press a sticky resist paste onto white cloth with carved wooden blocks. Then the cloth is dipped in an indigo vat again and again. When the paste is washed away, the printed areas stay white against deep blue. Patterns include small flowers, dots, leaves and stripes. The cloth was used for aprons, skirts, tablecloths and bedding.
artistBio: Blueprinting spread in Central Europe in the eighteenth century, as indigo became available, and most towns had a blue dyer. Factory printing later replaced most workshops. A few family workshops still carry on, some using blocks a century or more old. In 2018 UNESCO listed the craft as shared heritage of Austria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary and Slovakia.

title: St. Gallen Embroidery
artist: Embroiderers and manufacturers of St. Gallen
medium: Hand and machine embroidery on cotton and other fabrics
about: St. Gallen embroidery is fine white and colored work on cotton, often with cutwork and open areas that look like lace. It began as hand embroidery done at home in eastern Switzerland. In the nineteenth century, embroidery machines took over, first hand-operated, later the large Schiffli machines, which stitch with hundreds of needles at once. The patterns are delicate and very even.
artistBio: St. Gallen had been a linen-trading town since the Middle Ages. By the early twentieth century, its embroidery was among Switzerland's largest exports, and the city was a world center for it. The industry collapsed after the First World War but recovered in a smaller form. Today St. Gallen firms supply lace and embroidery to Paris fashion houses. The Textilmuseum St. Gallen holds its history.

title: Paisley Shawl
medium: Woven wool, silk or cotton, sometimes printed
about: Paisley shawls were large shawls covered in curving teardrop shapes called boteh, with wide patterned borders. They copied the costly hand-woven shawls of Kashmir, which were fashionable in Europe. Weavers in Paisley used drawlooms and later Jacquard looms to make them faster and cheaper. The teardrop shape became so linked with the town that it is still called the paisley pattern.
artistBio: Paisley was a busy weaving town near Glasgow. Its weavers were skilled and known for being well read and politically active. When fashion changed in the 1870s and shawls went out of style, the trade collapsed. Paisley Museum holds a large collection of shawls, pattern books and looms that tell the story.

title: Ayrshire Whitework
medium: White cotton embroidery with needle lace on fine muslin
about: Ayrshire work is white embroidery on very fine white muslin, done with tiny satin stitches and eyelets. Its special mark is the needle-lace fillings: small areas are cut away and filled with delicate lace stitches. It was used on christening gowns, baby caps, collars and cuffs. The best pieces are so fine that they look almost transparent.
artistBio: The style is credited to a Mrs. Jamieson of Ayr, who is said to have copied the lace fillings from a French christening robe. Thousands of women in Ayrshire and northern Ireland did the work at home for agents and merchants. It declined in the 1860s as machine embroidery spread and fashions changed. Many christening gowns survive as family heirlooms.

title: Carrickmacross Lace
medium: Appliqué of cambric or organdie on fine net
about: Carrickmacross lace is made by laying a fine cotton fabric over net, then outlining a design of flowers, leaves and scrolls with a thick thread couched down with tiny stitches. The extra fabric is cut away, leaving the solid shapes on the clear net. Small loops and filling stitches add texture. The finished lace is crisp and clean, with strong shapes.
artistBio: The craft is said to have begun in the 1820s when Mrs. Grey Porter taught local women a method she had seen in Italy. During the Great Famine, lace schools gave women a way to earn money. The St. Louis nuns of Carrickmacross later kept it going. The lace on the Duchess of Cambridge's 2011 wedding dress was made with the Carrickmacross method.

title: Termeh
about: Termeh is a fine woven cloth with small, dense patterns, especially the curved boteh (the paisley shape), set in rows on a deep red, green or black ground. It is woven with many colored weft threads, which the weaver selects for each part of the pattern. Termeh is used for covers and tablecloths, and was once worn as clothing.
artistBio: Termeh weaving was famed in Iran from at least Safavid times, with centers in Kerman and Yazd. Traditional termeh was woven on a drawloom, with an assistant above pulling the pattern cords. Only a few hand weavers remain today, mostly in Yazd, and most termeh is now made by machine. Iranian families often bring termeh out for Nowruz tables and weddings.

title: Afghan War Rugs
artist: Afghan weavers, including Baluch and Turkmen families
place: Afghanistan and refugee communities in Pakistan
about: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, weavers began knotting weapons into their rugs. Tanks, helicopters, rifles, grenades and fighter jets replace or sit among the old flower and medallion patterns. Some rugs include maps or words. From a distance, a rug may look traditional; up close, it is full of war. Later rugs also show events after 2001.
artistBio: War rugs were woven by families in Afghanistan and in refugee camps in Pakistan, often by women and children. Some recorded what weavers lived through; others were made because soldiers and foreign buyers wanted them. They raise hard questions about witness and commerce. Collectors and museums now keep them as a record of a long conflict seen by weavers.

title: Tiraz Textiles
artist: Weavers and embroiderers of state workshops (dar al-tiraz)
place: Egypt, Iraq, Yemen and other Islamic lands
medium: Linen or cotton with silk inscription bands
about: Tiraz are textiles with bands of writing woven or embroidered in silk across them. The inscriptions usually name the ruling caliph, give a blessing, and sometimes say where and when the cloth was made. The writing is in Arabic script, often in elegant Kufic letters. Many surviving pieces are fine linen from Egypt with a single band near the edge.
artistBio: Rulers ran special workshops called dar al-tiraz. Garments with tiraz bands were given as robes of honor to officials and guests, linking the wearer with the ruler. Many fragments survive from Egyptian burials, especially from the Fatimid period. Because they carry dates and names, they help scholars date other Islamic textiles.

title: Textiles from the Hallstatt Salt Mines
about: Deep in the salt mines of Hallstatt, miners left behind worn-out clothing, used as rags and lost in the tunnels. The salt preserved hundreds of wool fragments. They include fine twills, checks, stripes and narrow bands woven on tablets. Some still show their colors, blue, red, yellow and brown. Together they show how skilled and color-loving these early Europeans were.
artistBio: Hallstatt gave its name to a whole period of early Iron Age Europe. The textile finds have been studied for decades and have taught scholars a great deal about prehistoric spinning, weaving and dyeing. Many fragments are kept at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Weavers have made reconstructions of the bands and cloths.

title: The Diligent Mother
about: A mother sits in a quiet room with her sewing things around her. Her young daughter stands beside her and shows her a piece of needlework, and the mother points to something in it, perhaps a mistake. A dog rests on the floor. Nothing dramatic happens. Chardin paints soft light, worn furniture and the calm work of teaching a child to sew.
artistBio: Chardin was a French painter known for still lifes and small scenes of everyday home life. He showed this picture at the Paris Salon of 1740, with its companion, Saying Grace, and both were presented to King Louis XV. The painting is now in the Louvre. Prints after it made the image widely known in the eighteenth century.

title: Weaver's Workshop
about: Decker painted the inside of a weaver's cottage again and again. A big wooden loom fills the dim room, and the weaver sits at it working the treadles and beater. Light comes through a small window. Often a woman or child sits nearby winding bobbins, with baskets and tools scattered about. The pictures show weaving as everyday family work at home.
artistBio: Cornelis Decker worked in Haarlem, a center of Dutch linen weaving and bleaching. He is best known for landscapes with cottages and for these weaver interiors, which survive in several versions in Dutch and other European museums. Few painters of his time took such interest in the working loom, so his pictures are valued by textile historians as well as art lovers.

title: The Dressmaking Studio
about: Women bend over their sewing in a small, crowded room. The patterns of their dresses, the cloth on the table and the wallpaper all blend together, so the figures seem to melt into the space. Faces are barely shown. Vuillard paints the soft hum of a working room, where fabric is everywhere and hands are always busy.
artistBio: Vuillard grew up among cloth and seamstresses. His mother ran a small corset-making and dressmaking workshop in the family apartment in Paris, and he painted it many times. He was a member of the Nabis, a group of young painters who loved flat patterns and decorative surfaces. Several versions of the dressmakers theme are in museums and private collections.

title: The Seamstress
about: A woman in a dark dress sits in profile on a chair, her body still and her work in her lap. The background is plain and the colors are muted greys and browns. Everything unneeded has been taken away. The painting is simple and quiet, and gives the seamstress a calm dignity, as if she were a figure in a much older painting.
artistBio: Helene Schjerfbeck is one of Finland's most admired painters. After years of travel, she lived quietly with her mother in the small town of Hyvinkää, where she painted local women, often working women, in a pared-down style. The Seamstress, also called The Working Woman, is in the Ateneum Art Museum in Helsinki.

title: The Spinner
about: A young barefoot woman stands in a sunny landscape, holding a distaff loaded with fiber in one hand. With the other she draws out the thread to the hanging spindle. She looks straight at us. The picture is polished and sweet, but it shows real hand spinning: the fiber on the distaff, the twist running down, the spindle turning.
artistBio: Bouguereau was one of the most successful French academic painters of the nineteenth century, famous for smooth finish and idealized figures. He painted many young women from Italian and French countryside life, often with spinning or other handwork. His reputation fell in the twentieth century, but his skill is again widely admired today.

title: Blackwork
medium: Black silk embroidery on white linen
about: Blackwork is embroidery in black thread on white or pale linen. Most of it is counted: the stitcher follows the threads of the cloth to make small, repeating geometric patterns that fill shapes like lace. The main stitch is double running, also called Holbein stitch, which goes along a line and back, filling the gaps. Done well, it looks the same on both sides.
artistBio: Blackwork was very fashionable in Tudor England, on shirts, collars, cuffs and caps. It is often linked with Catherine of Aragon and Spain, and was sometimes called Spanish work. Holbein's portraits show it on clothing in fine detail, which is why one stitch is named after him. Today embroiderers use blackwork for samplers, pictures and modern geometric designs.

title: Stumpwork (Raised Embroidery)
about: Stumpwork is embroidery that stands up from the surface. Shapes are padded with felt or wool, or built over carved wood. Petals, wings and leaves are worked in detached buttonhole stitch, sometimes over wire, so they can lift free of the ground. Beads, seed pearls, metal threads and tiny pieces of mica add sparkle. The result is a small, three-dimensional world.
artistBio: Raised work was popular in England between about 1650 and 1690. Girls often made it as a final test of their skill, after samplers, covering boxes, caskets and mirror frames with scenes from the Bible, kings and queens, gardens and animals. The name stumpwork came later, in the nineteenth century. Embroiderers today still use the methods for flowers and insects.

title: Soumak
about: Soumak is a way of wrapping weft yarn around warp threads instead of simply passing it over and under. A common form goes forward over four warps and back under two, again and again. This makes a strong, slightly raised surface with a fine braided look. Plain wefts are usually woven between soumak rows to hold it firm. The back is left with loose yarn ends.
artistBio: Weft wrapping is old and found in many places. The name soumak is often linked with Shemakha, a town in Azerbaijan, and Caucasian soumak rugs are especially famous. Weavers in Iran, Anatolia and Central Asia use it for rugs, bags and animal trappings. Modern tapestry and rug weavers use it to add texture and outline shapes.

title: Smocking
about: In smocking, fabric is gathered into many tiny, even pleats. Then the stitcher embroiders across the tops of the pleats with stitches such as cable, stem and honeycomb, holding them in patterns. The gathered fabric stays stretchy, so it can fit closely and still move. The stitches form bands of zigzags, diamonds and waves across a chest, cuffs or waist.
artistBio: English farmworkers in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries wore smock frocks: loose linen overgarments with smocked panels. Some say the patterns showed a worker's region or trade, though this is not certain. Later, smocking moved into fashion, especially for children's dresses, and became a favorite home sewing skill. It is still widely used today.

title: Ply-Split Braiding
place: Rajasthan and Gujarat, India, and elsewhere
medium: Twisted cords split by other cords
about: In ply-split braiding, the maker works with firm, plied cords. One cord is pushed through another, splitting it between its plies, using a hooked tool called a gripfid. By choosing which cords split which, the maker builds patterns and structures. The result is very strong and can be flat, tubular or sculptural. Two colors of cord make bold graphic designs.
artistBio: Herders in Rajasthan and Gujarat have long used the method to make camel girths and other gear, with striking patterns. The English weaver Peter Collingwood studied these girths and wrote about the method, bringing it to weavers in Europe and America. Today fiber artists use ply-split braiding for baskets, sculpture and jewelry.

title: Inkle Weaving
medium: Warp-faced bands on an inkle loom
about: Inkle weaving makes narrow, strong bands. On an inkle loom, warp threads are wound around pegs in a loop. Every other thread passes through a fixed string heddle; the rest are free. Lifting or pushing down the free threads opens the shed. Since the warp covers the weft completely, the pattern comes from how the colored warps are arranged: stripes, checks and small motifs.
artistBio: 'Inkle' is an old English word for a narrow linen tape. Shakespeare mentions inkles among a peddler's wares. Bands like these were used for ties, straps and trims. The simple table inkle loom became popular with hand weavers in the twentieth century and is still a favorite beginner's loom, used for belts, guitar straps and lanyards.

title: Otti Berger
place: Zmajevac (now Croatia); Dessau and Berlin, Germany
about: Otti Berger was born in a village that is now in Croatia and studied art in Zagreb. She lost much of her hearing as a child. In 1927 she came to the Bauhaus and joined the weaving workshop, where she soon stood out. She felt fabric with her hands and thought about cloth through touch. Later she ran her own studio in Berlin.
artistBio: Berger designed fabrics for industry, studying structure, sound absorption and feel, and she patented some of her designs. As a Jewish woman she was barred from working under the Nazis. She went to London but returned to Yugoslavia to care for her mother. In 1944 she was deported to Auschwitz and murdered. Her fabrics and samples are kept in Bauhaus collections.

title: Jack Lenor Larsen
about: Jack Lenor Larsen grew up in the Pacific Northwest and studied architecture and weaving before turning fully to cloth. He studied at Cranbrook Academy of Art, then moved to New York. In 1952 he started his own company. One of his first big jobs was the casement fabric for Lever House, a new glass office tower. He loved travel and handwork from around the world.
artistBio: Larsen's company made fabrics with the texture and life of handweaving, produced on power looms, and brought in methods from many cultures. He also wrote books, including one with Mildred Constantine that helped define fiber as art. His home and gardens in East Hampton, New York, became LongHouse Reserve, open to the public.

title: Claire Zeisler
about: Claire Zeisler was born in Cincinnati and lived most of her life in Chicago. She came to fiber art in middle age, after studying weaving and other arts. She soon left the flat loom behind and began making free-standing sculptures, tying, knotting and wrapping by hand. She was also a serious collector of art, which shaped her eye.
artistBio: Zeisler's best-known works are tall forms of knotted jute or wool, with masses of loose fiber spilling down onto the floor like hair or water. Bright reds were among her favorite colors. She was a leading figure in the fiber art movement of the 1960s and 1970s, and the Whitney Museum gave her a retrospective in 1979.

title: Yvonne Koolmatrie
about: Yvonne Koolmatrie is a Ngarrindjeri weaver from the lower Murray River region of South Australia. In the early 1980s she took a weaving workshop with the elder Dorothy Kartinyeri, one of the few people still keeping the old method alive. Koolmatrie decided to carry it on. She gathers river sedge, prepares it, and coils it with great patience.
artistBio: Koolmatrie makes traditional forms such as fish and eel traps and baskets, and also sculptures of animals, boats and even aircraft. Her work keeps Ngarrindjeri weaving alive and teaches it to others. In 1997 she represented Australia at the Venice Biennale with Emily Kame Kngwarreye and Judy Watson. Her work is in major Australian museums.

title: Lucienne Day
about: Lucienne Day studied printed textiles at the Royal College of Art in London. She married the furniture designer Robin Day, and the two became one of the best-known design couples of postwar Britain. Her breakthrough came in 1951 with Calyx, a furnishing fabric of spindly lines and cup-shaped flowers, made for the Festival of Britain and sold by Heal's.
artistBio: Calyx won prizes and changed British taste, moving it away from old-fashioned floral chintz toward abstract modern patterns inspired by art and plants. Day designed many fabrics, as well as wallpapers, carpets and ceramics. Later she made 'silk mosaics', wall hangings pieced from small squares of silk. Her work is in the V&A and other museums.

title: The Flax Fibers of Dzudzuana Cave
about: In 2009, scientists reported finding tiny flax fibers in layers of Dzudzuana Cave in the Caucasus mountains of Georgia, about 30,000 years old. Under the microscope, some fibers were twisted, which suggests they had been made into cord or thread. Some appeared to have been colored. The flax was wild; farming had not yet begun.
artistBio: Fibers rot easily, so evidence of very early textiles is rare. These finds suggest that Ice Age people were already twisting plant fiber into string, perhaps for sewing, tying, baskets or simple cloth. Some scholars debate how to read the evidence. Still, the find pushes the story of thread back far beyond the beginnings of weaving and farming.

title: The Lowell Mill Girls
about: Lowell was built as a planned mill town, where water power ran large cotton mills. The owners hired young women from New England farms to run the spinning and weaving machines. They lived in company boarding houses under strict rules and worked long days. Many sent money home or saved for school or marriage. Some wrote for a magazine, the Lowell Offering.
artistBio: When the companies cut wages and raised rents, the women walked out in 1834 and 1836. In the 1840s, led by people such as Sarah Bagley, they petitioned for a ten-hour working day. They were among the first American industrial workers to organize. Later, immigrant workers replaced them in the mills. Their story is told at Lowell National Historical Park.

title: Turkey Red
about: Turkey red is a bright, very fast red on cotton, made with madder. Cotton does not take madder easily, so the process was long: the cloth was treated again and again with oil, alkali, alum and other materials, then dyed and finished. It could take weeks and many stages. The result was a strong, clear red that did not fade in washing or sun.
artistBio: The method came from India and the eastern Mediterranean, and Europeans called it Turkey red. In the eighteenth century, dyers brought it to France and Britain. The Vale of Leven in Scotland became famous for Turkey red cloth, printed with patterns and sold worldwide. After synthetic alizarin was made in 1869, the old madder method slowly ended.

title: Logwood
place: Yucatán, Central America and the Caribbean
medium: Purple, blue and black dye from heartwood
about: Logwood dye comes from the dark red heartwood of a small tree that grows around the Bay of Campeche and in Central America. The wood is chipped and soaked to release its color. Depending on the mordant, it gives purples, greys and blues, and with iron it makes deep, rich blacks. It was one of the most important black dyes for wool, silk and cotton.
artistBio: Spanish ships brought logwood to Europe in the sixteenth century. Early dyes made with it faded, and in Elizabethan England its use was banned for a time; the ban was lifted in the seventeenth century as dyers learned to fix it. Logwood cutting shaped the history of Belize, with hard labor by enslaved Africans. A form of the dye is still used to stain cells in laboratories.

title: The Spinning Jenny
about: The spinning jenny let one person spin several threads at once. A single large wheel, turned by hand, drove a row of spindles. Fiber was held in a sliding carriage that the spinner drew back to stretch the threads, then pushed forward as the yarn wound on. The first jennies had eight spindles; later ones had many more. The yarn was soft, best for weft.
artistBio: James Hargreaves, a weaver in Lancashire, built the jenny in the 1760s and patented it in 1770. Hand spinners feared losing work, and some jennies were smashed. Still, it spread fast in cottages and small workshops. It was soon joined by Arkwright's water frame and then Crompton's mule, which moved spinning into factories.

title: The Charkha
about: The charkha is an Indian spinning wheel, used mostly for cotton. The spinner turns the wheel with one hand, which spins a small spindle at high speed, while the other hand draws out the cotton fiber from a roll. Some charkhas are large and stand on the floor. The box charkha folds into a case and can be carried like a book.
artistBio: Spinning wheels were used in India for centuries. In the 1920s, Mahatma Gandhi made the charkha a symbol of the freedom movement. He asked Indians to spin their own yarn and wear handwoven khadi instead of imported mill cloth. The charkha appeared on the Indian National Congress flag. In the national flag adopted in 1947, it was replaced by the Ashoka wheel.

title: The Hungarian Coronation Mantle
artist: Embroiderers working for King Stephen I and Queen Gisela
about: This mantle began life as a bell-shaped chasuble, a priest's robe. An embroidered inscription says it was made in 1031 and given by King Stephen and Queen Gisela to the church of the Virgin Mary at Székesfehérvár. Rows of gold figures cover the silk: Christ, prophets, apostles and martyrs. It also holds small portraits of Stephen and Gisela, the only ones made in their lifetime.
artistBio: Later the chasuble was cut and reshaped into a coronation mantle, and Hungarian kings wore it when they were crowned for centuries. Tradition links Queen Gisela with its making, though skilled workshop embroiderers almost certainly did much of the stitching. It is now kept at the Hungarian National Museum in Budapest, shown in low light because the old silk is so fragile.

title: The Elephant Silk of Aachen
about: Big elephants stand inside round medallions, each one framed by flowers and vines. They are woven in rich colors on a dark ground, and repeat across the cloth. The silk was found wrapped around the remains of Charlemagne in his shrine at Aachen. It is one of the finest Byzantine silks to survive from this period.
artistBio: A woven Greek inscription ties the cloth to the imperial silk workshops of Constantinople, where weaving fine silk was closely controlled by the state. Silks like this were diplomatic gifts and treasures, sent west to emperors and churches. The Elephant Silk is kept in the treasury of Aachen Cathedral in Germany.

title: The Pienza Cope
medium: Silk and gold thread embroidery on linen
about: A cope is a long semicircular cloak worn by clergy. This one is covered in tiers of small scenes set under arches, telling stories of the Virgin Mary and of saints. Faces are worked in fine split stitch that follows the curves of cheeks and brows. The gold background was couched so the metal threads catch light as the wearer moves.
artistBio: It was made in England, probably in London, when English church embroidery was famous across Europe. Pope Pius II, born in Pienza, gave it to the cathedral of his rebuilt hometown in the 1460s. It is still in Pienza, in the town's diocesan museum, a long way from the workshop where it was stitched.

title: The Story of Abraham Tapestries
artist: Pieter Coecke van Aelst (design), Brussels weavers
medium: Wool, silk, gold and silver thread tapestry
about: This set of huge hangings tells the life of Abraham from the Book of Genesis: his journeys, his meeting with Melchizedek, and the near sacrifice of Isaac. Crowds of figures fill the scenes, with deep landscapes behind. Metal-wrapped threads were woven into the silk and wool so whole areas would shine in candlelight.
artistBio: The designs are by Pieter Coecke van Aelst, a Flemish artist who also worked on prints and books. The set was woven in Brussels and bought by Henry VIII. It still belongs to the Royal Collection and hangs in the Great Hall at Hampton Court Palace, near London, in the room it was made to dress.
c: Story of Abraham tapestry Hampton Court

title: The Story of the Emperor of China
artist: Beauvais Manufactory; designs by Guy-Louis Vernansal, Jean-Baptiste Monnoyer and Jean-Baptiste Belin de Fontenay
about: These tapestries show an imagined Chinese court: an emperor on a throne, astronomers with instruments, a hunt, a harvest, a voyage. Plants, birds and pavilions fill every corner. The scenes mix stories that French readers knew from Jesuit missionaries in China with a lot of invention. They are early examples of the European taste called chinoiserie.
artistBio: The series was designed by a team of French artists and woven at the Beauvais tapestry works north of Paris. It sold well and was rewoven many times for wealthy clients. Panels survive in several museums, including the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. Today they are studied as much for what they get wrong about China as for their skill.
c: Story of the Emperor of China Beauvais tapestry

title: Harris Tweed
about: Harris Tweed is a sturdy wool cloth with flecks of color, woven by hand on the islands of the Outer Hebrides. The wool is dyed and spun on the islands, then woven by islanders at their own homes, often on a pedal-powered loom in a shed beside the house. Finished cloth is stamped with the orb mark that guarantees where it was made.
artistBio: Island families wove tweed for their own clothes long before it was sold abroad. In the 1840s the Countess of Dunmore began promoting Harris cloth to wealthy buyers in Britain. The orb trademark followed in the early 1900s. The Harris Tweed Act of 1993 now defines the cloth in law, so only island-woven tweed may use the name.

title: Pipli Appliqué
about: Pipli work is cut-cloth appliqué in bold colors. Shapes of elephants, parrots, flowers, suns and moons are cut from red, yellow, green, black and white cotton, then stitched onto a contrasting ground, often with tiny mirrors and decorative edging. The look is bright and clear, made to be read from a distance under sun or lamplight.
artistBio: The craft is tied to the Jagannath temple at Puri. Pipli's makers have long sewn the canopies, umbrellas and covers used for the temple's festivals, including the great chariot festival, Rath Yatra. Today the village's shops also sell lanterns, bags and wall hangings, and the work has spread far beyond the temple.

title: Naga Shawls
about: Naga shawls are usually woven in three narrow pieces on a backstrap loom and then sewn together. Each Naga people has its own patterns of stripes and colors, mostly red, black and white. A shawl can show which community a person belongs to, and some designs were kept for people who had earned the right to wear them.
artistBio: Weaving is women's work among the Naga peoples, and girls traditionally learned it at home. Some shawls, such as the Ao warrior's shawl called tsungkotepsu, carry painted or woven figures of animals and people that mark honors. Many families still wear their shawls at festivals, and weaving cooperatives sell them more widely.

title: Muga Silk
about: Muga is a wild silk with a natural golden color. It comes from the cocoons of a moth caterpillar found only in Assam, which feeds outdoors on the leaves of local trees. The silk is never dyed for its gold. It is strong, and the shine is said to grow richer with washing and age.
artistBio: Muga has long been worn by Assamese families for weddings and festivals, especially as the two-piece mekhela chador. The town of Sualkuchi on the Brahmaputra River is known for its many handlooms. Muga silk has a geographical indication in India, which protects its name. Weather and changes to the trees threaten the moths, so supply is small.

title: Kira
about: The kira is a Bhutanese woman's dress: a large rectangle of cloth wrapped around the body, pinned at the shoulders with brooches and tied at the waist with a belt. Woven on backstrap looms in long panels, the finest kiras are covered with tiny patterns made by extra weft threads, picked one by one with the fingers.
artistBio: Weaving is one of Bhutan's most respected arts, and women weave for family, gifts and sale. The Kurtoe area in the northeast is known for kushüthara, a white kira densely patterned in colored silk. Many women now wear a two-piece version for daily life, and the full kira is kept for formal occasions.

title: Tus Kiiz
medium: Chain-stitch embroidery on wool, felt or velvet
about: A tus kiiz is a large embroidered wall hanging that was hung inside the yurt, often behind the bed. Bold curling ram's-horn shapes and flowers spread over a dark ground, worked in chain stitch with a hook or needle. The hanging kept out drafts and made the inside of the home bright.
artistBio: Women made tus kiiz for a daughter's marriage, and they were among the most valued things a bride brought to her new home. Making one could take a long time. The Kyrgyz have a similar hanging. Today women in Kazakhstan still embroider them, and old examples are shown in museums in Almaty and Astana.

title: Kaitag Embroidery
about: Kaitag textiles are covered with strange, lively designs in silk: spirals, stars, birds, rosettes and shapes that are hard to name. The stitch is laid and couched, so long floats of silk lie flat on the surface and shine. Colors are bold reds, blues, yellows and greens on white or blue cotton.
artistBio: They were made by women in the mountain valleys of Kaitag in southern Dagestan, in the Caucasus. They marked life events: covering a newborn, given at weddings, laid over the face of the dead. They were little known outside the region until collectors studied them in the late 20th century, and modern artists have admired their freedom.

title: Pateh
about: Pateh is wool embroidery on a wool ground, so densely stitched that the cloth underneath almost disappears. Patterns are often boteh, the teardrop shape known in English as paisley, along with cypress trees, flowers and borders. The colors are deep and warm, with red, green and gold on dark grounds.
artistBio: Kerman has a long history of fine wool textiles, including shawls woven in imitation of Kashmir. Pateh was traditionally made by women and used as covers, cushions and prayer cloths. Workshops and teaching programs in Kerman keep the craft alive, and it is sold across Iran.

title: Arkilla Kerka
about: An arkilla kerka is a very large wedding blanket made of many narrow strips sewn together edge to edge. Patterns of triangles, diamonds and checks are woven in red, black, white and yellow wool. When hung, it can form a tent-like enclosure around the marriage bed, and it also protected the couple from mosquitoes.
artistBio: Arkilla were woven by specialist Fulani men weavers in central Mali. A wealthy family might commission one for a daughter's wedding, and making one took weeks. The blankets were also kept as family wealth. Today they are prized by collectors, and the related striped blankets called khaasa are still woven.

title: Babban Riga
medium: Cotton or silk with hand or machine embroidery
about: The babban riga, or big robe, is a wide flowing gown worn by Hausa men over trousers and a shirt. Its pride is the embroidery on the chest and a large pocket on the left side. A common pattern is called the eight knives: long pointed shapes beside a spiral, stitched in thread that matches or contrasts with the cloth.
artistBio: Robes like this have been worn by rulers, scholars and wealthy men across West Africa for centuries. The embroidery was traditionally men's work, done by hand by specialists, sometimes over many weeks. Machine embroidery is common now, but hand-stitched robes are still made for weddings, festivals and emirs' courts.

title: Shweshwe
artist: South African cloth printers and dressmakers
about: Shweshwe is a printed cotton with small, crisp patterns of dots, lines and flowers. It was first made in indigo blue, later also in brown and red. The pattern is made by discharge printing: a chemical removes the dye in the design. New cloth is stiff from starch and has a clear smell, both of which wash out.
artistBio: Indigo-printed cloth came to southern Africa in the 19th century with European traders and settlers. It was taken up by Sotho, Xhosa and other communities and became part of their dress for weddings and ceremonies. For many years it has been printed in the Eastern Cape. Fashion designers in South Africa now use it in new ways.

title: Ukara Cloth
artist: Igbo dyers for the Ekpe society
about: Ukara is a large indigo cloth covered in white squares filled with symbols: leopards, crocodiles, hands, and signs from nsibidi, a system of graphic signs used in the Cross River region. The designs are drawn on cotton, stitched or tied tightly, then dyed. When the threads come out, the patterns show pale against the deep blue.
artistBio: The cloth belongs to Ekpe, the men's leopard society found among Igbo, Efik and neighboring peoples. Its signs are meant to be fully understood only by members. Ukara is hung at society houses and worn at important events. Because of its secret meanings, it is treated with care and respect.

title: Montecristi Toquilla Straw Hat
about: These are the hats the world calls Panama hats, though they come from Ecuador. Weavers split toquilla palm leaves into fine straws and plait them by hand, starting at the crown and working outward in a spiral. The finest ones have so many weaves per inch that the brim feels almost like linen and can take months to finish.
artistBio: The name Panama stuck because hats were shipped through Panama and worn by workers building the canal. The weaving towns of Montecristi and Pile in Manabí are famous for the finest grades. In 2012 UNESCO listed the traditional weaving of the Ecuadorian toquilla straw hat as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

title: Hudson's Bay Point Blanket
artist: English wool weavers for the Hudson's Bay Company
about: This is a heavy wool blanket, best known in cream with stripes of green, red, yellow and indigo. Short black lines woven into one edge are the points. They show the blanket's size and weight, so traders could tell its value at a glance. The wool was thick and held warmth even when damp.
artistBio: The Hudson's Bay Company traded point blankets with Indigenous peoples from the late 1700s, often for furs. Many were woven in Witney, England. Indigenous people made them into coats, called capotes, and used them in ceremonies and gift-giving. Their history is mixed, tied to trade, colonization and survival, and the blankets are still made today.

title: Kapa (Hawaiian Bark Cloth)
about: Kapa is cloth made from the inner bark of the wauke, or paper mulberry. The bark is soaked and beaten with wooden beaters until it spreads into a thin sheet. Hawaiian beaters were carved with patterns that pressed a watermark into the cloth. Makers then dyed it and stamped designs with carved bamboo stamps.
artistBio: Before cloth arrived from abroad, kapa was used for clothing, bedding and ceremony across the islands, and Hawaiian kapa was known for its fineness. The craft faded in the 19th century as imported cotton took over. Since the late 20th century, practitioners have studied old pieces and tools to bring the methods back.

title: Masi (Fijian Bark Cloth)
medium: Beaten paper mulberry bark, stencilled pigments
about: Masi is Fiji's bark cloth. Women beat strips of paper mulberry bark into sheets and join them. Many are decorated with stencils, cut from leaves in the past and from card or film today, to print sharp geometric patterns in black and red-brown. The result is crisp and graphic, with fine repeating borders.
artistBio: Islands such as Vatulele and Moce are known for their masi. It plays a key role in weddings, funerals, births and other ceremonies, where large lengths are presented as gifts. Masi was also used for clothing. Fijian makers continue the craft, and masi patterns appear on modern fashion, stamps and airline designs.

title: Burano Lace
about: Burano lace is needle lace, made with a needle and one thread, not with bobbins. The maker outlines the design over a pattern on parchment, then fills it with many tiny buttonhole stitches. Flowers, scrolls and fine mesh grounds take shape stitch by stitch. A single piece may pass through several hands, each worker an expert in one stitch.
artistBio: Women on the small lagoon island of Burano made lace for centuries. After the trade declined, a lace school opened there in 1872 to revive it, and it trained many young women. The Lace Museum on the island now shows historic pieces, and a few local women still make lace by hand.

title: Chantilly Lace
about: Chantilly lace is a bobbin lace best known in black silk. Flowers, vases and scrolls are filled with a soft half stitch that looks like shading, outlined with a thicker thread and set on a fine mesh. The effect is delicate and slightly see-through. It was used for shawls, veils and parasols.
artistBio: The lace takes its name from the town of Chantilly north of Paris. In the 19th century much of the production moved to Normandy, especially to Bayeux. Black Chantilly shawls were high fashion in the mid-1800s. Machine-made copies followed, and the name is now widely used for machine lace in a similar style.

title: Halas Lace
about: Halas lace is a fine needle lace from the Hungarian Great Plain. Its makers use dozens of different filling stitches to give each leaf, petal and animal its own texture, almost like shading in a drawing. Motifs come from Hungarian folk art and from nature, and many pieces are small enough to frame.
artistBio: It was created in the early 1900s by the art teacher Árpád Dékáni, who drew Hungarian designs, and the needlewoman Mária Markovits, who worked out how to stitch them. Lace made in Kiskunhalas won prizes at international exhibitions and was given as state gifts. The Halas Lace House in the town still teaches and makes it.

title: Pavlovo Posad Shawls
about: These are square wool shawls covered in big printed roses, peonies and other flowers, usually on a black, red or cream ground, with a silk or wool fringe. The pattern often frames a central field with a garland border. They are worn over the head or shoulders and are known across Russia.
artistBio: The town of Pavlovsky Posad, east of Moscow, began producing printed shawls in the 19th century. Patterns were first printed by hand with carved wooden blocks, a slow job that needed many separate blocks for each color. Printing methods have changed since, but the manufactory still produces shawls and keeps a museum of older designs.

title: Chiprovtsi Carpets
about: Chiprovtsi carpets are flat-woven wool kilims made on upright looms. Older designs are geometric. Later ones show stylized flowers, trees, birds and vases on red, black or green grounds. Because they are tapestry woven, both sides look almost the same. Weavers work from memory or from paper patterns, beating each row tightly with a comb.
artistBio: Chiprovtsi is a small town in northwest Bulgaria. Carpet weaving became an important trade there and has been passed down mostly among women. In 2014 UNESCO listed the Chiprovtsi carpet-making tradition as Intangible Cultural Heritage. The town has a museum and workshops where women continue to weave and teach.

title: Pirot Kilim
about: Pirot kilims are flat-woven wool rugs with crisp geometric motifs, often in red with black, blue, green and white. Many motifs have names: some look like turtles, combs or little houses. They are tapestry woven so that both faces can be used. A large kilim may take one weaver many months.
artistBio: Pirot, in southeastern Serbia, has been a weaving center for centuries, and its rugs were sold across the Balkans. The kilim is a symbol of the town. Weaving is still practised there, though by fewer women than before, and Pirot kilims are protected as a regional product in Serbia.

title: Castelo Branco Embroidered Bedspreads
about: These bedspreads, called colchas, are embroidered in soft colored silks on handwoven linen. A tree of life often grows up the center, full of flowers, birds, carnations and pairs of lovers. The main stitch is a laid and couched stitch that covers areas smoothly. Some designs show the influence of Indian and Chinese textiles that reached Portugal by sea.
artistBio: The bedspreads were made in the region of Castelo Branco in central Portugal and were often part of a bride's trousseau. After a decline, the craft was revived in the 20th century. The city museum has an embroidery workshop where students learn the stitch and copy old designs.

title: Mountmellick Embroidery
medium: White cotton embroidery on cotton satin
about: Mountmellick is a white-on-white embroidery. Thick matte cotton thread is stitched onto a white cotton satin, so the design stands up in relief. Patterns show local plants: blackberries, ferns, oak leaves, wheat. There is no cutwork or openwork. Pieces like bedspreads and pillow covers were finished with knitted fringes.
artistBio: The work is credited to Johanna Carter, a Quaker woman in the town of Mountmellick, who taught it in the early 19th century to give local women paid work. It was popular for a time and then faded. In the late 20th century local groups revived it, and the Mountmellick Embroidery Museum now keeps examples.

title: Deerfield Blue and White Needlework
artist: Deerfield Society of Blue and White Needlework
about: This embroidery is worked mostly in blue linen thread on white linen, with loose, open designs of flowers, vines, birds and pomegranates. The stitches are simple, such as satin and outline stitch. Pieces include table covers, bed hangings and curtains. Each finished piece was marked with a D inside a spinning wheel.
artistBio: Margaret Whiting and Ellen Miller founded the society in 1896 after studying old crewelwork kept in Deerfield's Memorial Hall. They dyed their own thread and trained local women, who were paid for their work. The group was part of the Arts and Crafts movement and ran for about thirty years. Pieces are kept by Historic Deerfield and other museums.

title: Valkyries
medium: Crochet, knitting, fabric, embroidery and lights
about: Vasconcelos's Valkyries are enormous soft sculptures that hang from ceilings and spread through rooms like huge creatures. They are built from crochet, knitting, patterned fabrics, sequins, tassels and lights. Each one is different. She also covers ceramic animals and other objects in handmade crochet, so familiar things look new.
artistBio: Joana Vasconcelos was born in Paris in 1971 and works in Lisbon with a large studio of makers, many skilled in crochet and needlework. Her art draws on Portuguese crafts and women's domestic work. In 2012 she was the first woman artist given a solo show at the Palace of Versailles.

title: Textile Wall Works
about: Konaté makes huge wall hangings from many strips and pieces of dyed cotton, often Malian bazin. He layers and stitches them into fields of color that shift from deep blue to purple to gold. Some are abstract. Others carry symbols and figures that speak about war, faith, power, health and the environment.
artistBio: Abdoulaye Konaté was born in Diré, Mali, in 1953 and trained as a painter before turning to cloth. He has led Mali's main art school, the Conservatoire des Arts et Métiers Multimédia in Bamako. His work has been shown widely, including at documenta in Kassel, and is held in major museums.

title: Beaded Punching Bags
medium: Everlast punching bags with glass beads, fringe, jingles and trade cloth
about: Gibson takes ordinary punching bags and covers them in glass beads, fringe, metal jingles and bright geometric patterns. Many carry beaded words from song lyrics, poems or slogans. The bags hang like bodies in the gallery. They mix strength and fighting with the beauty and care of Native beadwork.
artistBio: Jeffrey Gibson was born in 1972 and is a member of the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians, of Cherokee descent as well. He trained as a painter and began combining painting, beadwork and textiles. In 2024 he represented the United States at the Venice Biennale, the first Indigenous artist to have a solo show in the US pavilion.

title: Woven Tapestries
medium: Hand-dyed and handwoven cotton and acrylic yarn
about: Brackens weaves tapestries with silhouetted figures, often dark bodies against bright fields, sometimes alongside catfish, birds or water. The images draw on Southern history, folklore, scripture and the lives of Black and queer people. He dyes much of the yarn himself, and the soft edges of the woven shapes give the scenes a quiet, dreamlike feel.
artistBio: Diedrick Brackens was born in Mexia, Texas, in 1989. He studied weaving and textiles, including at the California College of the Arts, and works in Los Angeles. His tapestries have been shown at the New Museum in New York and other museums, and he has won major awards for his work.

title: The Hastings Embroidery
about: The Hastings Embroidery was made to mark 900 years since the Battle of Hastings in 1066. It is a long run of panels, each showing a moment in British history from 1066 to 1966: battles, kings and queens, discoveries and events of the 20th century. It uses appliqué, embroidery and many kinds of thread to bring the scenes to life.
artistBio: It was made by the Royal School of Needlework, the British needlework school founded in the 1870s. Like the Bayeux Tapestry that inspired it, it tells history in stitched pictures, but in bright modern colors. It belongs to the town of Hastings, where it has been displayed in the Town Hall.

title: Apache Burden Basket
medium: Twined willow or sumac, buckskin, tin cones
about: A burden basket is a cone-shaped carrying basket, twined from willow or sumac. It is often banded with color and trimmed with long buckskin fringes ending in tin cones that jingle as the wearer walks. A strap across the forehead or chest held it on the back for carrying firewood, food and other loads.
artistBio: Western Apache women made these baskets for daily use, and they also appear in important ceremonies, including the coming-of-age ceremony for girls. Many Apache families hang a burden basket in the home as a sign of welcome and blessing. Weavers continue to make them, along with tall coiled storage baskets.

title: Tohono O'odham Baskets
medium: Coiled yucca, bear grass and devil's claw
about: These are coiled baskets: bundles of bear grass are wrapped with split yucca and sewn round and round into a spiral. White yucca forms the light ground, black comes from devil's claw seed pods, and red from yucca root. A famous design shows I'itoi, the Man in the Maze, at the entrance to a winding path.
artistBio: The Tohono O'odham, of the Sonoran Desert, have made baskets for food and storage for generations. In the 20th century many women made baskets for sale, and the tribe became known as one of the most productive basket-making nations in North America. Weavers today teach younger generations and sell at markets and museums.

title: Sujani
artist: Women of Bhusura and nearby villages
medium: Running stitch embroidery on layered cotton
about: A sujani is a light quilt made from old saris and dhotis, layered and held together with running stitch. Women outline figures in chain or running stitch and fill them densely, telling stories of daily life, village events and social issues. Traditionally a sujani was made for a newborn baby.
artistBio: Sujani comes from Bihar in eastern India and is related to the kantha of Bengal. In the 1980s, development workers helped women in Bhusura village form groups to sell their work. Since then sujani has become a way to earn income and to speak about subjects like women's rights, health and education.

title: Mashru
artist: Weavers of Gujarat and northern India
about: Mashru is a satin-weave cloth with a silk face and a cotton back. The silk warps float on top, so the outside shines like silk, while the cotton lies against the skin. It is often woven in bright stripes, sometimes with ikat dyed into the warp, and was used for trousers, jackets and linings.
artistBio: The word mashru means permitted. Some Muslim scholars held that men should not wear pure silk against the body, and this cloth was a way to meet that rule while still looking rich. Mashru was woven in several Indian cities and is still made in Gujarat, though fewer weavers continue the craft.

title: Madeira Embroidery
medium: Cotton or linen embroidery with openwork
about: Madeira embroidery is mostly white or blue thread on white linen, cotton or organdy. It mixes satin stitch with eyelets and cut openwork, so flowers and leaves are outlined by small holes. Tablecloths, handkerchiefs and christening gowns are typical. Finished pieces carry an official seal to show they were made on the island.
artistBio: The craft grew as a business in the mid-19th century, helped along by British residents of the island who saw a market for it. Thousands of women embroidered at home, often for merchants who sold the work abroad. The island's institute still certifies pieces, and the embroidery is a well-known symbol of Madeira.

title: Tlingit Spruce Root Baskets
medium: Twined spruce root with false embroidery
about: Tlingit weavers twine fine strands of split spruce root into baskets so tight they can hold water. Bands of geometric designs are added with false embroidery, in which dyed grass and maidenhair fern stems are wrapped around the outer strand only, so the pattern shows on the outside but not inside.
artistBio: Gathering and splitting the roots is slow work, done in spring when they peel easily. Baskets were used for cooking, berry picking and storage, and in the late 1800s many were sold to visitors and collectors. Tlingit weavers today keep the craft going and teach it through classes and cultural programs.

title: Nasij (Mongol Cloth of Gold)
artist: Central Asian and Chinese weavers under the Mongol Empire
about: Nasij is a silk woven so thickly with gold thread that the whole surface glitters. Patterns show winged lions, griffins, birds and flowers in repeating rows. The gold was often strips of gilded leather or paper wrapped around silk thread. It was used for robes, tents and gifts.
artistBio: The Mongol rulers loved gold cloth. When they conquered cities, they moved skilled weavers from Central Asia and Iran to new workshops in their empire. The resulting textiles mix Islamic, Chinese and Central Asian styles. Some were sent to Europe and survive in church treasuries. Others are held by museums such as the Cleveland Museum of Art.

title: Geringsing
about: Geringsing is double ikat: both the warp and the weft threads are tied and dyed before weaving. When the weaver lines them up exactly on the loom, the pattern appears where the colors meet. Colors are deep red-brown, purple-black and natural cream, made with plant dyes that take a long time to build up.
artistBio: It is woven only in the village of Tenganan Pegeringsingan, home of the Bali Aga people, who keep older Balinese traditions. The cloth is believed to protect against illness and harm and is used in ceremonies like tooth filing and temple rites. Double ikat of this kind is made in very few places in the world.

title: Sakiori
medium: Rag weaving with cotton strips on hemp or cotton warp
about: Sakiori means torn and woven. Worn-out cotton cloth was torn into thin strips and used as weft, beaten in tightly on a warp of hemp or cotton. The result is a thick, warm, mottled cloth with short flecks of the old fabric's colors. It was made into work jackets, sashes and bedding.
artistBio: In the cold north of Japan, cotton did not grow and had to be bought. Rural families saved every scrap, and sakiori was one way to use cloth until it was gone. Today weavers in Japan and elsewhere make sakiori again, valued for its texture and for its spirit of thrift.

title: Christ and the Virgin in the House at Nazareth
about: The Virgin Mary sits with her sewing in her lap, a basket of folded linen and scissors beside her. She has stopped stitching to look at her young son. He is weaving a crown of thorns and has pricked his finger. The quiet household scene of needlework carries a foreshadowing of his death.
artistBio: Francisco de Zurbarán worked mainly in Seville and was known for calm, deeply lit religious paintings and careful still-life details. Here the cloth, the basket and the sewing tools are painted with the same attention as the faces. The painting is in the Cleveland Museum of Art in Ohio.
c: Zurbarán Christ and the Virgin in the House at Nazareth

title: Flax Barn at Laren
about: A long, low barn stretches into the distance. Women in dark dresses and white caps walk slowly backward, drawing out flax fibers into yarn, while girls turn the large wheels that twist it. The light falls in through the windows. The painting shows the repetitive, shared labor that turned plants into thread before mill spinning took over.
artistBio: Max Liebermann was a German painter who visited the Netherlands many times and painted Dutch workers, including women mending nets and working in orphanages. He became a leader of German modern painting and head of the Berlin Secession. This painting is in the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

title: The Linen Cupboard
about: Two women stand at a tall carved cupboard, putting away a stack of folded white linen. A child plays with a stick and ball near the open door, which looks out to the street. Clean linen was a sign of a well-run Dutch household and of wealth, and here it is handled with care, almost like treasure.
artistBio: Pieter de Hooch painted calm Dutch interiors and courtyards with light falling through doorways and windows. He worked in Delft and later in Amsterdam, where he painted this picture for richer patrons. The black-and-white floor, the open door and the careful light are typical of his work. The Linen Cupboard is in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
c: Pieter de Hooch Linen Cupboard Rijksmuseum

title: The Parasol
about: A young woman sits on the grass with a small dog in her lap. A young man stands beside her, holding a green parasol to shade her face. The colors are soft and the light bright. This was not meant to hang as a painting but to be copied in wool and silk as a tapestry.
artistBio: Early in his career, Goya painted many full-size designs, called cartoons, for the Royal Tapestry Factory of Santa Barbara in Madrid. Weavers copied them into tapestries for royal palaces. This one was for a dining room at the palace of El Pardo. The cartoon is now in the Museo del Prado in Madrid.

title: Pictures of Tilling and Weaving (Gengzhi Tu)
artist: After Lou Shou; Qing court version by Jiao Bingzhen
date: 12th century original; Qing versions 1690s and later
medium: Ink and color on silk or paper; woodblock prints
about: This set of pictures shows, step by step, how rice is grown and how silk is made. The weaving scenes follow the work from bathing silkworm eggs and feeding the worms mulberry leaves to gathering cocoons, reeling the silk, weaving on a drawloom and finishing the cloth. Each scene is paired with a short poem.
artistBio: The first version was made by Lou Shou, a Song dynasty official, to show the labor that fed and clothed the empire. Later emperors had it remade. The court painter Jiao Bingzhen made a famous version for the Kangxi Emperor, and it was printed as woodblocks. It is a valuable record of silk-making and Chinese looms.

title: Yūzen Dyeing
about: In yūzen, the artist draws the design on silk and then traces its outlines with a fine line of rice paste squeezed from a cone, like icing. The paste keeps colors from spreading. Dyes are brushed inside each shape, then the area is covered and the background dyed. Finally the paste is washed away, leaving thin white lines around every shape.
artistBio: The method is named after Miyazaki Yūzensai, a fan painter in Kyoto around 1700 whose designs became fashionable. It allowed painted, picture-like kimono designs with many colors. Kyoto and Kanazawa, where Kaga yūzen is made, are the main centers. Long silk lengths were once rinsed in Kyoto's rivers to wash out the paste.

title: Bargello (Florentine Work)
about: Bargello is canvas embroidery made with straight upright stitches, each over several threads. The stitches step up and down in rows to form zigzag flames, waves and diamonds. Each row repeats the line of the row above in a new shade, so the colors flow across the canvas. It covers ground quickly and makes hard-wearing upholstery.
artistBio: The name comes from the Bargello palace in Florence, which has chairs covered in this stitch. It is also called Florentine work, flame stitch and Hungarian point. It was popular for chairs, purses and wall hangings in Europe and colonial America, and had a big revival among home stitchers in the 1960s and 70s.

title: Cross-Stitch
about: Cross-stitch is made of small X shapes, each formed by two diagonal stitches crossing. The stitcher counts the threads of an evenly woven cloth so that every X is the same size. Placed side by side like tiles, the Xs build up pictures, letters and patterns. Charts printed on squared paper show where each color goes.
artistBio: Cross-stitch is found in folk embroidery from Palestine to Ukraine, Hungary, China and Mexico. In Europe and America, girls learned it by stitching samplers of letters and numbers. Printed charts spread it widely in the 19th century. Today it is one of the most popular kinds of embroidery, and many stitchers design their own charts.

title: Twining
medium: Plant fiber, grasses, wool or roots
about: In twining, two or more strands, called wefts, twist around each other as they pass across a set of upright strands, called warps. Each twist locks a warp in place. Twining can be done by hand without a loom. It makes firm baskets, mats and bags, and also flexible cloth.
artistBio: Twining is among the oldest textile methods, used long before looms. It appears in early basketry and fiber remains from many parts of the world. Many Native North American basket traditions use it, including the spruce root baskets of the Tlingit and the twined Chilkat robes, and it is still used by basketmakers today.

title: Tambour Embroidery
about: Tambour embroidery uses a fine hook, not a needle. The fabric is stretched tight on a frame. The hook pierces it, catches thread from underneath and pulls up a loop, making a fast, even chain stitch. Workers can also slip beads and sequins onto the thread and fix them in place while working from the back.
artistBio: The technique is old in India, Persia and China, where it is known in different forms, such as the aari work of India. It spread to Europe in the 18th century and was named after the drum-shaped frame, tambour in French. Lunéville in France became known for beaded tambour work, and fashion houses still use it.

title: Needle Lace
about: Needle lace is made with just a needle and thread. The design is drawn on parchment or card, and a few threads are tacked along its outlines. The lacemaker then builds the lace over these lines with rows of buttonhole stitches, filling shapes and linking them with bars or mesh. When done, the tacking is cut and the lace lifts free.
artistBio: It grew out of cutwork in 16th-century Italy, when embroiderers cut away so much linen that the stitches stood alone. Venice called it punto in aria, stitch in the air. Later centers included Alençon in France, Burano near Venice and Halas in Hungary. Each developed its own fillings and grounds.

title: Frida Hansen
about: Frida Hansen was born in Stavanger, Norway. After her husband's business failed in the 1880s, she turned to weaving to support herself, studying old Norwegian tapestry methods and natural dyeing. She opened a weaving studio in Kristiania, now Oslo, trained other women and became one of the leading Norwegian textile artists of the Art Nouveau period.
artistBio: Her tapestries are large and flowing, with women, flowers and swirling shapes in strong colors. She developed a transparent weaving technique in which parts of the warp are left bare, so the hanging is partly see-through. Her best-known work, The Milky Way, shows women in a procession across a dark sky. Her work is in Norwegian museums.

title: Junichi Arai
about: Junichi Arai grew up in Kiryū, an old weaving town, in a family of textile makers. He became one of the most inventive textile designers of his time. He worked with fashion designers including Issey Miyake and Rei Kawakubo, and in 1984 he co-founded the textile company Nuno in Tokyo with Reiko Sudo.
artistBio: Arai mixed old weaving skills with new materials and machines. He used computer-controlled looms, metallic yarns, fibers that shrink or melt, and heat treatments to make cloth that crinkles, glimmers or looks like metal. His fabrics showed that industrial textiles could be as experimental as handmade art, and many are kept in museums.

title: Nike Davies-Okundaye
about: Nike Davies-Okundaye grew up in Ogidi in Nigeria, learning weaving and adire, the Yoruba indigo-resist cloth, from family members. As a young woman she joined the artists' community in Osogbo. She became known for her own textiles and for her energy in teaching and promoting Nigerian crafts.
artistBio: She founded art centers in Osogbo, Ogidi, Abuja and Lagos, where many young people, especially women, have trained in adire, batik and weaving. Her Lagos gallery is one of the largest in West Africa. Her own work uses indigo and wax-resist to show Yoruba stories, everyday life and symbols, and has been exhibited abroad.

title: Jagoda Buić
about: Jagoda Buić was born in Split, on the Croatian coast. She studied art and theater design and worked on costumes and stage sets. In the 1960s she began weaving large forms that broke away from flat wall tapestry. She became one of the key artists of the international movement that turned weaving into sculpture.
artistBio: Her works are tall, heavy hanging forms woven from wool, sisal and other rough fibers, often in black, red, brown and natural colors. They hang in folds or stand like walls and ruins. She showed often at the Lausanne International Tapestry Biennial, where much of the new fiber art was first seen, and her work is in museums in Europe.

title: Trude Guermonprez
about: Trude Guermonprez was born in Danzig and trained in weaving in Germany, where her teachers were linked to the Bauhaus. She worked in the Netherlands, where her husband was killed during the Second World War. She moved to the United States in 1947 and taught at Black Mountain College before settling in California.
artistBio: She taught for many years at the California College of Arts and Crafts and led its crafts department. Her own work ranged from fine fabrics for interiors to woven hangings that explored color, space and image. She trained many weavers who shaped the American fiber art movement.

title: The Lancashire Cotton Famine
about: During the American Civil War, cotton from the Southern states stopped reaching Britain. The mills of Lancashire depended on it. Many closed or cut hours, and hundreds of thousands of workers lost their wages. Families relied on relief committees, soup kitchens and sewing schools. Some mills tried cotton from India and Egypt, which was hard to spin on their machines.
artistBio: Many Lancashire workers still supported the North and the end of slavery, even as they suffered. At the end of 1862, a meeting of working people in Manchester sent a message of support to Abraham Lincoln, and he wrote back to thank them. A statue of Lincoln in Manchester recalls this link.

title: The Lawrence Textile Strike
about: In January 1912, mill owners in Lawrence cut pay after a state law shortened the working week for women and children. Thousands of workers walked out. They were mostly immigrants from many countries speaking many languages. Through a cold winter they picketed, held meetings and sent some of their children to stay with families in other cities.
artistBio: After about two months, the workers won pay raises, and mills across New England raised wages too. The strike is often called the Bread and Roses strike, after a slogan about wanting both fair pay and a decent life, though historians debate how much the phrase was used at the time. It is remembered as a turning point for textile workers.

title: Orchil (Lichen Purple)
about: Orchil is a purple to red dye made from certain lichens, such as those growing on coastal rocks. The lichen is soaked for weeks in an ammonia liquid, which in the past was usually stale urine. The mix slowly turns deep purple. Wool and silk dyed with it are bright, but the color fades in light.
artistBio: Orchil was used in the ancient Mediterranean, sometimes as a cheaper purple than shellfish dye. In medieval Florence, the Rucellai family were said to have made their fortune from it. In 18th-century Scotland a version called cudbear was patented and made in Glasgow. Synthetic dyes replaced it in the late 1800s.

title: Safflower
about: Safflower is a thistle-like plant with orange flowers. The petals hold two dyes. A yellow one washes out in water. A red one, carthamin, is drawn out with an alkali, then fixed with acid. It gives pinks and scarlets on silk and cotton. The red is lovely but fades easily in sunlight.
artistBio: Safflower has been grown for thousands of years in Egypt, India and Asia. In Japan it is called benibana and was used for kimono and for cosmetics like lip color. The Yamagata region was known for growing it. Because so many petals were needed, the strongest reds were very costly.

title: The Lucet
about: A lucet is a small two-pronged tool, shaped like a lyre or a fork. The maker wraps yarn around the prongs in a figure eight and lifts the lower loop over the upper one, again and again. A square, springy cord grows down through a hole or below the base. It is simple, fast and needs no other equipment.
artistBio: Lucet cords were used for lacing clothes, drawstrings and ties before buttons and elastic. The tool was common in Europe for centuries and enjoyed a revival in Victorian times. Today historical reenactors, braiders and children learning fiber crafts use lucets, made from wood or bone.

title: The Cotton Gin
about: A cotton gin separates cotton fiber from its seeds. Simple roller gins, in which fiber is pulled between two rollers, were used in India for centuries. In 1793 Eli Whitney built a gin for the sticky-seeded short-staple cotton grown in the American South. Wire teeth on a turning drum pulled the fiber through narrow slots, leaving the seeds behind.
artistBio: Whitney's gin made upland cotton profitable. Cotton growing spread across the South, and with it the enslavement of people forced to plant and pick it. The number of enslaved people in the United States grew greatly in the decades after. The gin is a clear case of a fiber tool that changed history, for the worse as much as the better.

title: The Jesse Cope
about: A cope is a long, half-round cloak worn by priests. This one shows the Tree of Jesse, the family tree of Christ, which grows as a winding vine from the sleeping figure of Jesse. Kings and prophets sit in the loops of the vine, each holding a scroll. The faces and drapery are stitched so finely that they look almost painted. It survives incomplete, but the design is still easy to read.
artistBio: Opus anglicanum, English work, was the most prized embroidery in medieval Europe, and popes and kings ordered it. Professional embroiderers, men and women, worked in London workshops. Their names are almost never recorded. The Jesse Cope is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, alongside other pieces of English medieval embroidery.

title: The Layton Jacket
medium: Linen embroidered with silk and silver-gilt thread, with spangles
about: A woman's jacket of white linen, covered in coiling stems that hold honeysuckle, roses, pansies and other flowers, with birds and butterflies in between. Gold thread and tiny metal spangles catch the light. It is one of the few garments from the period that can be matched to a portrait: a painting shows Margaret Layton wearing this very jacket.
artistBio: Jackets like this were worn by well-off women in early Stuart England, and the embroidery was usually done by professionals. The painting of Margaret Layton is attributed to Marcus Gheeraerts the Younger. Both the jacket and the portrait are in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, where they are often shown together.

title: The Banner of Las Navas de Tolosa
medium: Silk and gilt thread tapestry weave
about: A large banner woven in silk and gold thread. Its center holds an eight-pointed star made of interlacing bands, surrounded by bands of Arabic script with verses from the Qur'an. Tiny repeated patterns fill every gap. The colors, mostly red, green, white and gold, are still strong after eight centuries.
artistBio: It was made for the Almohad rulers who controlled much of Spain and North Africa. Tradition says Christian forces took it at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, though some historians think it reached Castile another way. It is kept at the royal monastery of Las Huelgas in Burgos, Spain, which holds a museum of medieval textiles.
c: Pendón de las Navas de Tolosa Las Huelgas

title: Transylvanian Church Rugs
about: These are Turkish rugs, many with a niche or arch at each end and a lively border of cartouches or stars. They hang from the balconies and pews of Lutheran churches in Transylvania. Because they were rarely walked on, many survive in fine condition, with colors far brighter than rugs of the same age kept in homes.
artistBio: The rugs were woven in western Anatolia for trade. Saxon merchants in Transylvanian towns bought them and gave them to their churches as gifts and memorials. The Black Church in Brașov holds the best-known group. Collectors once called them Transylvanian rugs, a name that stuck even though they were made in Turkey.

title: Holbein Carpets
about: Holbein carpets are a family of Turkish rugs with bold geometric designs. Some have rows of small octagons inside interlaced lines; others have a few large octagons in squares. The borders often hold angular script-like patterns. Reds, blues and yellows dominate. The designs come from a long tradition of Anatolian weaving.
artistBio: They are named after Hans Holbein the Younger, who painted rugs of this kind in his portraits, though they appear in Italian and Flemish paintings well before him. Scholars use these paintings to help date the rugs. Surviving examples are in museums in Istanbul, Berlin and elsewhere, and in churches in Transylvania.

title: Ottoman Çatma Velvet
artist: Velvet weavers of Bursa and Istanbul
about: Çatma is a Turkish silk velvet with a raised pile pattern against a flat ground, often brocaded with gold or silver thread. Large carnations, tulips and pomegranates spread across the cloth in deep red and cream. Many surviving pieces are cushion covers, made as single panels with a row of small arches at each end.
artistBio: Bursa was the center of Ottoman silk weaving, and its velvets were sold across Europe and the Middle East. Many cushion covers ended up in European collections and in the treasuries of neighboring states. Today they are found in museums in Istanbul, London, Washington and beyond, and they still influence furnishing fabrics.

title: Aubusson Tapestry
about: Aubusson weavers work on a horizontal low-warp loom, weaving from the back of the tapestry. They follow a full-size painted guide, the cartoon, often marked with numbers for each color. Each color area is built up in small sections with hand-wound bobbins. A large piece can take several weavers many months.
artistBio: Tapestry weaving in this small town in central France goes back centuries, and it became a royal manufactory under Louis XIV. In the 20th century Jean Lurçat and other artists revived it with bold modern designs. The craft is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage, and the Cité internationale de la tapisserie in Aubusson keeps it going.

title: Guernica Tapestry
artist: Jacqueline de la Baume Dürrbach, after Pablo Picasso
about: A full-size woven copy of Picasso's 1937 painting of the bombing of Guernica. The screaming horse, the bull, the mother with her dead child and the broken soldier are all here, in shades of grey, black and white with soft brown tones. In wool the image looks a little warmer than in paint, but no less painful.
artistBio: Nelson Rockefeller commissioned the tapestry, and it was woven in France in the workshop of Jacqueline de la Baume Dürrbach, with Picasso's approval. It was lent to the United Nations in 1985 and hung outside the Security Council chamber for decades. The Rockefeller family took it back in 2021 and returned it the next year.

title: Idrija Lace
about: Idrija lace is a bobbin lace built from a narrow tape that winds and loops to form flowers, leaves and curling lines. The tape is made in one continuous piece, joined to itself as it goes. Finished pieces range from small doilies to collars and large tablecloths. The open spaces between the tapes give it a light, airy look.
artistBio: Idrija was a mercury-mining town, and lacemaking gave miners' families extra income. A lace school opened there in 1876 and still teaches children and adults. The town holds a lace festival each year. Bobbin lacemaking in Slovenia, with Idrija at its heart, is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

title: Vologda Lace
about: Vologda lace is a bobbin lace with a smooth, dense tape that outlines bold shapes against a fine mesh ground. Snowflakes, stars, flowers and birds are common, often in white on white. The tape keeps an even width as it curves, so the patterns read clearly from across a room.
artistBio: Lacemaking spread among peasant women in the Vologda region of northern Russia, and by the 19th century it was a major cottage industry. The craft was later organized into workshops and taught in schools. Vologda has a lace museum, and the lace remains one of the best-known Russian crafts.

title: Ruskin Lace
artist: Lacemakers of the English Lake District
about: Ruskin lace is made on handwoven linen. Threads are drawn out to leave square holes, and the edges are bound with buttonhole stitch. The squares are then filled with needle-lace designs of wheels, triangles and picots. The finished work has a crisp, geometric look and is used for edgings, collars and church linen.
artistBio: The work grew out of John Ruskin's belief in handwork. In the late 1800s he backed a linen industry in the Lake District, where local women spun and wove linen. The lace style drew on old Italian cutwork. A small number of makers keep it alive today, and the Ruskin Museum in Coniston shows examples.

title: Dorset Buttons
medium: Linen or cotton thread over metal rings or discs
about: Dorset buttons are made of thread alone, wrapped around a small ring or disc. For the best-known kind, the cartwheel, the ring is first covered with blanket stitch, then threads are laid across it like spokes and woven round and round to make a flat wheel. Others are domed or worked over a disc of horn or fabric.
artistBio: For two centuries women and children in Dorset made these buttons at home as piecework. The trade collapsed in the mid-1800s when machines began making cheap buttons, and many button-making families left the county. In recent decades makers have revived the craft, and the buttons now appear on knitwear and as small jewelry.

title: Boutis
