medium: Cotton whole-cloth quilting stuffed with cotton cord
about: Boutis is a whole-cloth quilt made from two layers of fine cotton. The maker stitches the design through both layers with tiny running stitches, making narrow channels and small closed shapes. Cotton cord or wadding is pushed in from the back to raise the pattern. Held up to the light, the design glows through.
artistBio: The work developed in Marseille and southern France and was sold abroad as Marseille work. Boutis pieces marked weddings and births, and a bride's petticoat or a baby's cover could take months. The craft nearly disappeared in the 20th century but is taught again today, and museums in Provence collect older pieces.

title: Assisi Embroidery
medium: Cotton or silk counted-thread embroidery on linen
about: Assisi embroidery turns the usual idea around. The background is filled with cross-stitch, while the birds, beasts and flowers are left as plain linen. Each shape is outlined with a fine line of double running stitch. Red and blue are traditional colors, so the motifs appear as white silhouettes in a field of color.
artistBio: The style draws on older Italian counted work. It was revived in Assisi in the early 1900s, when local women began making it for sale using old designs as models. It became popular across Europe and America in needlework magazines. Today it is still made in Assisi and by stitchers worldwide.

title: Mantón de Manila
artist: Chinese embroiderers for the Spanish market
place: Southern China, traded via Manila to Spain
medium: Silk embroidered with silk thread, with knotted silk fringe
about: A large square silk shawl, folded into a triangle and worn over the shoulders. It is embroidered with flowers, birds and sometimes small figures, and edged with a long knotted fringe that swings as the wearer moves. Many are embroidered the same on both sides. They are worn at fairs and in flamenco dance.
artistBio: The shawls were made in southern China and shipped to Manila, then carried across the Pacific to Mexico and on to Spain on the Manila galleons. That route gave them their name. Over time Spanish workshops also began making them. They became a symbol of Andalusia and are still made, worn and handed down.

title: Rushnyk
about: A rushnyk is a long, narrow ritual cloth of linen, embroidered or woven at the ends. Patterns include the tree of life, birds, flowers and geometric forms, usually in red and black. Rushnyky are draped over icons and family photographs, used to carry bread and salt to guests, and tied around a couple's hands at weddings.
artistBio: Women made rushnyky for every stage of life, from birth to burial, and a young woman prepared many before her wedding. Each region had its own colors and stitches. The tradition continued through hard times and remains a strong part of Ukrainian identity. Rushnyky are kept in homes, churches and museums across Ukraine and abroad.

title: Slutsk Sashes
medium: Silk woven with gold and silver thread
about: These long, wide sashes were wound several times around the waist over a noble's long coat, the kontusz. They are woven in silk and metal thread with flowers at the ends and a patterned middle. Many are double-faced, with a different color scheme on each side, so the wearer could choose the look by how it was folded.
artistBio: Sashes like these were first imported from Persia and Turkey. In the 18th century the Radziwiłł family set up a workshop in Slutsk, led by a master weaver of Armenian descent, Jan Madżarski, to make them locally. Today the sashes are a national symbol in Belarus and are held in museums in Belarus, Poland and Lithuania.

title: Hedebo Embroidery
about: Hedebo is a Danish whitework, white thread on white linen. Early pieces used drawn threadwork and satin stitch to make flowers and leaves. Later styles cut shapes out of the linen and filled them with needle-lace wheels, rings and pyramids worked in buttonhole stitch. It decorated shirts, pillowcases and bed linen.
artistBio: Hedebo is the name of a rural area between Copenhagen and Roskilde. Farm women there made the work for their own households and their daughters' dowries. The style changed over time and became popular across Denmark in the late 1800s. It is still taught by Danish needlework groups, and many pieces are in Danish museums.

title: Indian Cottons from Fustat
artist: Block printers and dyers of Gujarat
place: Made in Gujarat, India; found at Fustat, Egypt
about: These are fragments of everyday cotton cloth printed with wooden blocks and dyed in indigo blue and madder red. Patterns include rosettes, lotus flowers, ducks, rows of geese and simple stripes. The cloth was used for clothing and furnishings. Many pieces are worn and patched, which shows they were used until they fell apart.
artistBio: Fustat was the old city of Cairo, and its dry rubbish mounds kept thousands of textile scraps. Indian cloth was traded across the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea to Egypt. The Ashmolean Museum in Oxford holds a large collection. The fragments help historians trace a trade in printed cotton that is centuries older than European records.
c: Fustat Indian block printed cotton Ashmolean

title: Nanjing Yunjin Brocade
medium: Silk brocade with gold and silver thread
about: Yunjin means cloud brocade, for its rich color and shine. It is woven on a tall draw loom worked by two people. One sits above the loom and lifts the pattern threads by hand following a coded pattern, while the other throws the shuttles below. Dragons, clouds and flowers appear in many colors, often with gold thread.
artistBio: Nanjing's brocade workshops supplied the Ming and Qing courts with imperial robes and furnishings. The craft shrank when demand fell in the 20th century, but it was protected and revived. It is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, and the Nanjing Yunjin Research Institute still weaves on the great looms.

title: Li Textiles of Hainan
medium: Cotton and hemp; warp ikat, weaving and embroidery
about: Li women spin, dye, weave and embroider all of their cloth. They tie and dye warp threads before weaving, weave on backstrap looms, and add designs in supplementary weft and embroidery. Patterns show people, frogs, birds and deer in red, yellow and black on dark grounds. The cloth is made into wrapped skirts, jackets and headcloths.
artistBio: The Li are one of the oldest peoples of Hainan. Skills pass from mother to daughter, and there are no written patterns. As fewer young women learned, the craft became endangered, and in 2009 it was placed on UNESCO's list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding. Schools and workshops on the island now teach it again.

title: Nishijin-ori
medium: Silk brocade, often with gold and silver thread
about: Nishijin-ori is a family of richly patterned silks woven in one district of Kyoto. It is best known for heavy obi sashes and for the brocades used in Noh costumes and temple cloths. Threads are dyed before weaving, and many designs use flat gold or silver strips. Work is divided among specialists in many small workshops.
artistBio: Weavers have worked in this part of Kyoto for over a thousand years. The name means Western Camp, from the army camp that stood there during the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477; weavers returned to the area after the war. Nishijin weavers later adopted the Jacquard loom. The district still has looms and a textile center.

title: Yūki-tsumugi
medium: Hand-spun silk, kasuri dyed, ground-loom woven
about: Yūki-tsumugi is a soft, warm silk for kimono. The thread is pulled by hand from silk floss made of stretched cocoons, without twisting, so it keeps air and stays light. Patterns are made by binding bundles of thread before dyeing. The cloth is woven on a ground loom, with the weaver's body holding the warp tension.
artistBio: The cloth is named after the town of Yūki, and it has been made in the region for centuries. One kimono length can take months of work, mostly spinning. The full traditional process is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. Older wearers say the cloth gets softer with each year of use.

title: Ojiya-chijimi and Echigo-jōfu
about: These are fine ramie cloths for summer kimono. Ramie fibre is split by hand into thin strands and joined end to end, then woven on a ground loom. Chijimi has a crinkled texture from hard-twisted weft. In late winter the finished cloth is spread on the snow in the sun, which bleaches it gently.
artistBio: The region of Echigo, now Niigata, has some of Japan's deepest snow, and the long winters gave families time to spin and weave. The cloth was once paid as tax and sold to the cities. The making of Ojiya-chijimi and Echigo-jōfu is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. Few people can now do every step.

title: Hansan Mosi
about: Mosi is a fine, crisp cloth made from ramie. Weavers split the fibers with their teeth into very thin strands, join them by rolling them on the knee, then size and weave them. The best mosi is almost see-through and feels cool against the skin. It was made into summer clothing for both men and women.
artistBio: The Hansan area is known as the home of the finest Korean mosi, and women there have passed the skills down for generations. It is slow work that wears down the weavers' teeth. The weaving of mosi in the Hansan region is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, and a mosi museum and festival keep it known.

title: Tais
medium: Cotton, backstrap loom, often warp ikat
about: Tais is the hand-woven cloth of Timor. Women weave it on backstrap looms in long panels, using warp ikat, supplementary weft and other methods. Designs differ by district and family, with crocodiles, birds, people and geometric forms. Tais is worn at ceremonies, given at births, marriages and funerals, and exchanged between families.
artistBio: Weaving tais has been part of Timorese life for generations, and patterns carry the identity of each community. After independence, tais became a national symbol of Timor-Leste. In 2021 it was placed on UNESCO's list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding. Weaving groups now sell tais to keep the skills alive.

title: Banarasi Sari
about: A Banarasi sari is a silk sari woven with patterns in gold and silver zari. The end piece, the pallu, carries the richest work, often a row of kalga (paisley shapes) or flowering plants. Small floral buttis are scattered across the body. Many brides in north India wear a Banarasi sari for their wedding.
artistBio: Varanasi has been a weaving center for a very long time, and its brocades grew in fame under Mughal patronage. Many weavers are from Muslim Ansari families who have worked the looms for generations. The sari has a Geographical Indication tag. Power looms and cheap copies are a serious challenge for handloom weavers today.

title: Kasuti
about: Kasuti is counted-thread embroidery worked by counting threads, with no drawing on the cloth. Four main stitches are used: a double running stitch, a zigzag running stitch, a darning stitch and a cross stitch. Motifs include temple towers, chariots, elephants, lotus flowers and lamps. It is traditionally stitched on Ilkal saris.
artistBio: Kasuti comes from the Dharwad region of North Karnataka, where women stitched it on saris and blouses for weddings and festivals. The double running stitch is worked so the back looks the same as the front. Kasuti has a Geographical Indication tag, and women's cooperatives now make it for sale.

title: Zardozi
medium: Gold and silver thread, wire and sequins on silk or velvet
about: Zardozi is heavy embroidery in metal thread. The cloth is stretched on a large wooden frame, and several workers sit around it. They couch down metal threads and stitch on coiled wire, spangles and beads to make raised, shining patterns. It decorates bridal clothes, shoes, cushions and ceremonial hangings.
artistBio: The word comes from Persian, meaning gold sewing. The craft flourished at the Mughal court. It declined later but revived in the 20th century, and Lucknow, Agra and other cities have large zardozi trades. Most workers are men, often working in small workshops for long hours. Today some use copper or plastic thread.

title: Korhogo Cloth
medium: Hand-woven cotton painted with mud and plant dyes
about: Korhogo cloth is made from narrow strips of hand-woven cotton sewn together. Artists paint designs onto it with a dark dye made from plants and fermented mud, using knives or brushes. They show animals, masked dancers, birds and hunters in bold black outlines. Each cloth is painted by hand, so no two are the same.
artistBio: The cloth comes from Senufo communities around the town of Korhogo in northern Côte d'Ivoire. Painted cloths were once worn by hunters and used in ceremonies. In the 20th century artists began making them for a wider market. Painters in villages near Korhogo still make them, and they are sold throughout West Africa and abroad.

title: Ndop Cloth
medium: Cotton strip cloth, stitch-resist dyed with indigo
about: Ndop is a large indigo cloth with white patterns. Strips of cotton are sewn together, and the design is drawn and then stitched tightly with raffia thread so the dye cannot reach those parts. After dyeing, the stitches are cut out and the white shapes appear: circles, lizards, spiders, moons and lines in a dense, lively grid.
artistBio: In the kingdoms of the Cameroon Grassfields, ndop belonged to kings and title holders. It was hung behind rulers, worn at ceremonies and used to mark sacred spaces. The dyeing was often done by specialists in other regions and traded in. Ndop is still used at royal festivals, and fine old examples are held by museums in Europe and Africa.

title: Boucherouite Rugs
medium: Recycled cloth strips knotted on a cotton or wool warp
about: Boucherouite rugs are made from strips of old clothing, sheets and even plastic bags, knotted into a warp like pile yarn. The result is bright and shaggy, with free shapes, bands and diamonds in unexpected color mixes: pink beside orange, lime beside purple. No two are alike, and each one records the cloth a household had to spare.
artistBio: The name comes from a Moroccan Arabic phrase about torn, reused cloth. Women began making them as wool became costly and second-hand clothing more common in rural Morocco. They were first made for home use. Since the 1990s collectors and designers abroad have taken an interest, and they are now sold widely.

title: Huaca Prieta Textiles
about: Huaca Prieta is an ancient mound on the north coast of Peru. Its dry layers held thousands of textile fragments, mostly twined by hand without a loom. Some show faint designs of condors, crabs and snakes made by shifting colored threads. The colors have faded, but patient study has brought many of the images back to light.
artistBio: The archaeologist Junius Bird excavated the site in the 1940s. In 2016 researchers reported that some cotton fragments from Huaca Prieta were dyed with indigo about 6,000 years ago, the oldest known use of indigo anywhere. The finds show that people in the Andes were skilled with fiber long before pottery or large cities.

title: Otavalo Weaving
medium: Wool and cotton, hand and treadle looms
about: The Kichwa Otavalo people weave ponchos, blankets, belts, tapestries and scarves. Traditional dress includes white cotton blouses embroidered with flowers for women and dark blue ponchos for men. Weavers use backstrap looms for belts and treadle looms for larger cloth. Many designs mix old Andean patterns with new ones made for buyers.
artistBio: Under Spanish rule, Otavalo people were forced to weave in colonial workshops. Later they turned that skill into an independent trade. The Saturday market in Otavalo's Plaza de Ponchos is famous, and Otavalo traders travel worldwide. Their success has made the Otavalo one of the best-known Indigenous communities in South America.

title: Tarabuco Weaving
medium: Wool or synthetic yarn, warp-faced weaving
about: Tarabuco weavings are warp-faced cloths with neat bands of small, detailed figures: people, horses, birds, condors, plants and scenes from daily life. They appear in rows, often in red, white and black. Women wear them as shawls and bags; men wear ponchos. The designs are tight and orderly, unlike the wild creatures of nearby Jalq'a weaving.
artistBio: The Yampara people live around the town of Tarabuco near Sucre. Weaving is learned at home, often starting in childhood. The town's Pujllay festival in March brings out the best weavings, worn by dancers and musicians. Weavings are sold at the Sunday market, and a textile museum in Sucre shows both Tarabuco and Jalq'a work.

title: Lakota Star Quilts
place: The Dakotas and the northern Plains, USA
about: A star quilt shows one large eight-pointed star made of many small diamond pieces in rings of color. The star radiates out from the center and fills most of the quilt. It is often called the Morning Star. Star quilts are given to honor people at graduations, naming ceremonies, weddings and funerals, and wrapped around a person's shoulders.
artistBio: Lakota and Dakota women learned quilting from missionaries and teachers in the late 1800s. The star design echoes older star images painted on buffalo robes, and the quilts took on many of the robes' roles in giving. Star quilts are central to giveaways on reservations today. Many families keep quilts that honor relatives across generations.

title: American Jacquard Coverlets
about: These bed covers are woven in two colors, often indigo blue or red wool with white cotton. A center field of large flowers or stars is framed by borders of eagles, buildings, trees or birds. In one corner a block often shows the customer's name, the date and the weaver's name, so many coverlets can be traced to a maker and a family.
artistBio: Many of the weavers were immigrants from Germany, Scotland and Ireland who brought their skills to America. They used the Jacquard attachment to weave complex pictures. Families often supplied their own homespun wool. The trade faded as factory blankets took over. Thousands of coverlets survive in museums, historical societies and family homes.

title: Ceinture Fléchée
artist: French Canadian and Métis finger weavers
about: The ceinture fléchée, or arrow sash, is a long wool belt with a pattern of arrowheads and lightning-like zigzags in red, blue, green and yellow. It is made by hand, without a loom, by braiding and interlacing hundreds of threads. The long fringes at each end are often braided. It was tied around the waist over a coat.
artistBio: Voyageurs of the fur trade wore these sashes to hold their coats and support their backs while carrying heavy loads. Women in the area of L'Assomption, Quebec, made many of the finest. The sash became a symbol of the Métis Nation and of Quebec, and it is worn at the Quebec Winter Carnival.

title: Pangnirtung Tapestries
about: Pangnirtung tapestries are woven wall hangings based on drawings by Inuit artists. They show hunters on the ice, families in camp, sea creatures, birds and stories from the North. Weavers interpret the drawings in wool, choosing colors and blending yarns to suggest snow, water and light. A finished tapestry is a shared work of artist and weaver.
artistBio: A weaving studio opened in Pangnirtung on Baffin Island in 1970, to give local people paid work in the arts. It is now part of the Uqqurmiut Centre for Arts and Crafts. The tapestries are shown in galleries across Canada and abroad. The centre also produces prints by local artists.

title: Oomingmak Qiviut Lace
artist: Knitters of the Oomingmak Musk Ox Producers' Co-operative
about: Qiviut is the soft underwool of the musk ox, combed out as the animals shed. It is warmer than sheep's wool and very light. Knitters turn it into lacy scarves, smoke rings and caps. Each village's knitters use their own pattern, often taken from a local design such as a parka trim or a basket.
artistBio: The Oomingmak co-operative, based in Anchorage, was set up in 1969 to give Alaska Native women in remote villages a source of income. Hundreds of knitters, mostly Yup'ik and Iñupiaq, have taken part. Each item comes from a known village. The co-operative's work brought qiviut to knitters worldwide.
c: qiviut musk ox lace knitting Oomingmak

title: Tāniko
about: Tāniko is a Māori finger-twining technique for making bold geometric bands. Weavers twist pairs of colored fiber around passive threads, making sharp triangles, zigzags and diamonds. Traditional colors are black, red-brown and white, from natural dyes. Tāniko forms the borders of cloaks and is used in headbands and belts.
artistBio: The fiber comes from harakeke, prepared by scraping and softening the leaves. Patterns can carry meanings and connect to ancestors and places. Tāniko is central to the cloaks worn on important occasions. Today Māori weavers teach it in workshops and schools, and it also appears in contemporary art and fashion.

title: Siapo
medium: Bark cloth from paper mulberry, natural dyes
about: Siapo is Samoan bark cloth. Inner bark from the paper mulberry tree is scraped and beaten into a thin sheet. Patterns are made in two ways: by rubbing dye over the cloth laid on a carved board, or by painting freehand. Designs include leaves, starfish and geometric shapes in rich brown and black on a cream ground.
artistBio: Siapo was used for clothing, bedding and gifts at weddings, funerals and title ceremonies. Its brown dye comes from the bark of the 'o'a tree. The craft declined with imported cloth but is now taught again in Samoa and Samoan communities abroad. Older siapo is held in museums in the Pacific, Europe and America.

title: Lei Hulu (Feather Lei)
medium: Bird feathers tied or sewn to a cord or backing
about: A lei hulu is a lei made from feathers, worn on the head or around the neck. Feathers are bound tightly in small bunches along a cord, so they stand out in a dense round tube, or stitched flat in rows. Some lei have a single color; others have bands or spirals. A single lei can take many hours.
artistBio: In old Hawaiʻi, feather lei were made from the feathers of native forest birds and were worn by chiefs. Many of those birds are now extinct. Today makers use feathers from pheasants, geese and other birds. Families and teachers have kept the craft alive, and feather lei are worn at important events.

title: Mappa
about: Each Mappa is an embroidered map of the world. Every country is filled with the pattern of its national flag, so the map changes as borders and governments change. The oceans are filled with one color, sometimes chosen by the embroiderers. Words in Italian and Persian run around the borders. Over the years the maps became a record of political change.
artistBio: The Italian artist Alighiero Boetti traveled to Afghanistan and set up a collaboration with women embroiderers in Kabul. After the Soviet invasion in 1979, the work continued with Afghan refugees in Pakistan. Boetti designed the maps; the women stitched them. The Mappe are now in collections worldwide, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

title: More Love Hours Than Can Ever Be Repaid
medium: Found handmade stuffed animals and afghans sewn to canvas
about: Dozens of handmade stuffed animals and crocheted afghans, bought at thrift stores, are sewn together into a large wall hanging. The toys are worn and faded. The title points to the hours of care that went into making them, and to the gifts that come with a debt. The piece is both cheerful and sad.
artistBio: Mike Kelley (1954–2012) was an American artist from Detroit who worked in Los Angeles. He used toys, crafts and everyday objects to explore childhood, family and class. This work was shown with a smaller piece, The Wages of Sin. It is in the collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York.
c: Mike Kelley More Love Hours Than Can Ever Be Repaid

title: Madonna of the Yarnwinder
about: The Virgin Mary sits in a rocky landscape with the Christ Child on her lap. The child has taken her yarnwinder, a simple stick tool for winding spun thread, and gazes at it. Its crossbar makes the shape of a cross, a hint of his future death. Mary reaches out as if to stop him, then holds back.
artistBio: Leonardo da Vinci worked on this composition in the early 1500s, and two versions survive, both thought to be painted partly by Leonardo and partly by his assistants. The Buccleuch version was stolen from Drumlanrig Castle in Scotland in 2003 and recovered in 2007; it has been lent to the Scottish National Gallery. The other, the Lansdowne version, is privately owned.

title: Shearing the Rams
about: Inside a timber woolshed, men bend over sheep and shear them with hand blade shears. Light comes through the gaps in the walls and falls on the wool. Boys carry fleeces, and a young girl working as the tar-boy smiles out at the viewer. The painting shows the hard, skilled work behind Australia's wool industry.
artistBio: Tom Roberts (1856–1931) was born in England and grew up in Melbourne. He was a leader of the Heidelberg School of Australian painters. He made sketches for this painting at Brocklesby sheep station in New South Wales. It is in the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne and is one of the best-loved pictures in Australia.

title: Interior with an Egyptian Curtain
about: A window opens onto a palm tree that bursts with green and yellow light. Beside it hangs a bold Egyptian appliqué curtain in red, black and white, with a pattern of large leaves and shapes. On a table below sits a bowl of fruit. The curtain and the tree compete for attention, and both seem full of movement.
artistBio: Henri Matisse (1869–1954) loved textiles all his life; he came from a weaving town in northern France and collected cloth from many places. He owned this curtain, a piece of Cairo tentmakers' appliqué, and painted it here at his home in Vence. The painting is in the Phillips Collection in Washington, D.C.
c: Matisse Interior with Egyptian Curtain Phillips

title: Self-Portrait as a Tehuana
about: Frida Kahlo paints herself wearing the festive headdress of the women of Tehuantepec, a ring of stiff white lace that frames her face. Fine lines like roots or threads spread from the lace. A small portrait of Diego Rivera is painted on her forehead. The lace and embroidery are painted with great care.
artistBio: Frida Kahlo (1907–1954) often wore Tehuana dress: embroidered huipils, long skirts and lace. For her it was a way to claim Mexican Indigenous culture and a strong female identity. This painting is also known as Diego on My Mind. It belongs to the Gelman collection of Mexican art.
c: Frida Kahlo Self-Portrait as a Tehuana

title: Crochet
medium: Yarn or thread worked with a single hook
about: Crochet uses one hook to pull loops of yarn through other loops. Work starts with a chain. Each stitch is finished before the next begins, so only one loop stays on the hook. Stitches differ by how many times the yarn is wrapped before pulling through: single, double, treble and so on. Crochet can be worked in rows or in rounds, flat or in three dimensions.
artistBio: Similar looped work is very old, but crochet as we know it was first described in print in Europe in the early 1800s. It spread quickly because it needs only a hook and thread. Irish crochet lace helped families survive the famine years. Today crochet is used for blankets, garments, toys, coral reef models and large art installations.

title: Coiled Basketry
medium: Grasses, rushes, pine needles or other fibers
about: In coiled basketry, a bundle of grass or other fiber is wound in a spiral and stitched to the coil below it. The stitching material, often a thin strip of leaf or bark, wraps the new coil and passes through the old one. The basket grows round by round from the center. Shape comes from where each coil is placed.
artistBio: Coiled baskets are made across the world, from Africa and Asia to the Americas and Australia. Gullah sweetgrass baskets, Pomo feathered baskets and Tohono O'odham baskets all use coiling. The method can make baskets tight enough to hold water. Some of the oldest known baskets are coiled.

title: Appliqué
medium: Fabric pieces stitched to a fabric ground
about: In appliqué, shapes cut from one fabric are stitched onto another. The edges may be turned under and sewn with tiny stitches so they almost vanish, or left raw and held with decorative stitching. In reverse appliqué, layers are stacked and cut away to show the colors beneath. Appliqué makes bold pictures and patterns quickly.
artistBio: Appliqué is found in many cultures. The Fon of Benin, the tentmakers of Cairo and the quilters of Hawaiʻi and Baltimore are all known for it. Guna molas use reverse appliqué. Appliqué made banners, flags, quilts and clothing, and it is still a favorite with quilters and textile artists today.

title: Woodblock Printing on Cloth
medium: Carved wooden blocks, dye or mordant pastes, cotton or silk
about: A design is carved into a wooden block so the pattern stands up. The block is pressed into dye or a mordant paste and then stamped firmly onto cloth. The printer moves the block along, lining it up with the last print. Different blocks add each color in turn. Small marks at the edges help match the blocks.
artistBio: Block printing on cloth was done in China, India and Egypt long ago. Indian printed cottons were traded across Asia and to Europe, where they sparked a craze. Block printers in Rajasthan, Gujarat and elsewhere still work by hand, and the method remains popular with artists and small studios.

title: Drawn Thread Work
medium: Linen or cotton fabric with embroidery thread
about: In drawn thread work, some threads are pulled out of the fabric, leaving bands of loose threads in one direction. The embroiderer then groups and ties these threads with stitches to make ladders, zigzags and lacy patterns. In some styles both warp and weft are removed to make an open grid, which is filled with needle-lace.
artistBio: It is one of the oldest forms of whitework and was used on church linen, shirts and household linen in Europe. Danish Hedebo, Norwegian Hardanger, Mexican deshilado and Ruskin lace all use drawn threads. Simple hemstitching is the most common form, still used to edge napkins and handkerchiefs.

title: Mordanting
medium: Alum, iron, tannin and other mordants
about: Many natural dyes will not stay in fiber on their own. A mordant is a substance, usually a metal salt such as alum, that binds the dye to the fiber. Wool is simmered in a mordant bath before dyeing, or the mordant is added to the dye bath. Different mordants change the color: madder with alum gives red, with iron a dark purple-brown.
artistBio: Mordants were used by ancient dyers in Egypt, India and China. Alum was traded across the Mediterranean and was valuable enough to be a major business in medieval Europe. Printing different mordants on cotton, then dyeing in one bath, gave Indian chintz its many colors. Natural dyers today still mordant their wool before dyeing.

title: May Morris
about: May Morris was the younger daughter of William Morris. She learned embroidery from her mother, Jane, and her aunt, Bessie Burden. At 23 she took charge of the embroidery department of Morris & Co. She taught, lectured in Britain and America, and wrote a book on decorative needlework. She also edited her father's collected works.
artistBio: May Morris designed and stitched wall hangings, bed hangings, cushions and portières, and designed the Honeysuckle wallpaper. She helped found the Women's Guild of Arts in 1907, as women were then shut out of the Art Workers' Guild. Her own reputation was overshadowed by her father's for a long time, but exhibitions have since brought her work back into view.

title: Bernat Klein
place: Born in Yugoslavia; worked in Scotland
about: Bernat Klein was born in Senta, then in Yugoslavia, and studied in Jerusalem and at Leeds before settling in Galashiels in the Scottish Borders. There he started his own textile company. He was a painter as well as a designer, and he based his fabric colors on his own paintings, many full of soft, layered color.
artistBio: Klein became famous in the 1960s for tweeds mixed with mohair, velvet ribbon and loops, in bright, blended colors. Leading Paris fashion houses used his fabrics. He later worked as a color consultant and wrote a book on color. His home, High Sunderland, built by the architect Peter Womersley, is now a protected building.

title: Kaffe Fassett
place: Born in San Francisco; based in London
about: Kaffe Fassett grew up in California and trained as a painter. He moved to London in the 1960s. On a visit to a Scottish wool mill he bought yarn and learned to knit, and he soon found that knitting let him paint with color. He went on to design knitwear, needlepoint, quilts and fabrics.
artistBio: His work is known for large numbers of colors in one piece, often with simple shapes repeated many times. He designed knitting patterns for Rowan yarns and printed fabrics for quilters. His book Glorious Knitting came out in 1985. He has taught workshops around the world and encouraged many people to be bolder with color.

title: Varvara Stepanova
medium: Textile design, painting, graphic and costume design
about: Varvara Stepanova was a Russian Constructivist artist. She and her partner, Alexander Rodchenko, believed art should serve everyday life. In 1923 she and Lyubov Popova went to work at the First State Textile Printing Factory in Moscow, where they designed fabrics for ordinary people. She also designed sportswear and theater costumes.
artistBio: Her fabric designs used circles, stripes, triangles and grids in one or two colors, made with a ruler and compass. Many were printed and sold. They looked very different from the floral prints of the time. Stepanova also made paintings, book designs and posters. Her textile designs are now in museums and still inspire designers.

title: Fukumi Shimura
medium: Tsumugi silk weaving with plant dyes
about: Fukumi Shimura was born in Ōmihachiman in Shiga Prefecture. She learned weaving from her mother and began weaving seriously in her thirties. She worked with tsumugi, a hand-spun silk, and dyed it with plants she gathered: indigo, madder, gromwell and many others. She was named a Living National Treasure of Japan in 1990.
artistBio: Her kimono are woven in bands and blocks of soft color, inspired by nature, poetry and the seasons. She wrote books on color and plants that are widely read in Japan. With her daughter, Yōko Shimura, she founded a school in Kyoto to teach dyeing and weaving. Her work is in major Japanese museums.

title: The Field of the Cloth of Gold
medium: Cloth of gold, silk, tents and pageantry
about: In June 1520, Henry VIII of England and Francis I of France met for about two weeks in a field near Calais. Both kings tried to outshine the other. They brought thousands of followers and built tents and a temporary palace hung with cloth of gold, a fabric woven with real gold thread. There were feasts, jousts and wrestling.
artistBio: The meeting was meant to build friendship between two old enemies, but within a few years they were at war again. It shows how valuable fine cloth was: rich textiles were the main way rulers displayed power. A large painting of the event is in the Royal Collection at Hampton Court.
w: Field of the Cloth of Gold
c: Field of the Cloth of Gold painting

title: Feed Sack Dresses
medium: Printed cotton flour and feed sacks
about: Flour, sugar and animal feed were sold in cotton sacks. Farm and working families washed the sacks and sewed them into dresses, aprons, shirts, quilts and curtains. By the late 1930s manufacturers began printing the sacks with flowers, checks and children's prints, and labels were made to wash out. A woman might choose feed by the pattern she needed.
artistBio: During the Great Depression and the Second World War, when money and cloth were scarce, feed sack cloth clothed many families. It shows how thrift and taste went together. Paper sacks replaced cotton in the 1950s. Today feed sack fabric is collected, and its prints appear in many quilts from the era.

title: Lac
medium: Red dye from the resin of lac insects
about: Lac is a red dye from tiny scale insects that live on certain trees in India and Southeast Asia. The insects cover the branches with a resin crust, called sticklac. Soaking the crushed crust in water releases a red dye. With different mordants it gives crimson, scarlet and purplish reds on silk and wool.
artistBio: Lac was used for centuries in India, Persia and China, and was traded to Europe. It colored silks and rug wool. After the arrival of cochineal from the Americas, lac lost ground in Europe. The resin left after removing the dye became shellac, used for varnish. Natural dyers still use lac today.

title: Blade Shears
about: Blade shears are a single piece of steel bent into a loop at the back, with two blades that spring apart. The shearer squeezes them to cut and lets go to open them again. They cut wool close to the sheep's skin without power. A skilled shearer moves the sheep in set positions so the fleece comes off in one piece.
artistBio: Before shears, wool was often plucked by hand as sheep shed. Iron shears of this simple shape go back over two thousand years. Machine shears arrived in the late 1800s and now do most shearing. Blade shears are still used in some cold areas because they leave more wool on the sheep, and by small flock keepers.

title: The Distaff
about: A distaff is a stick or frame that holds unspun fiber, such as flax or wool, so the spinner's hands stay free. Fiber is wrapped or tied onto it and drawn off a little at a time. It can be held under the arm, tucked into a belt, set in a stand or fixed to a spinning wheel. Flax especially needs one, as its long fibers tangle easily.
artistBio: For thousands of years the distaff was a sign of women's work, shown in art from ancient Greece to medieval Europe. The phrase the distaff side still means the female side of a family. In parts of Europe, 7 January was St. Distaff's Day, when spinning resumed after Christmas. Spinners still use distaffs today.

title: Spinning Wheel Scroll
medium: Ink and color on silk, handscroll
about: A plain country scene. A young mother sits on the ground nursing her baby while she turns a spinning wheel. A little way off, an old woman in patched clothes holds the long threads that run back to the wheel. The figures are drawn with simple lines, and the painting shows the steady work of spinning in a farm household.
artistBio: Wang Juzheng was a painter of the Northern Song dynasty, known for figures and scenes of ordinary life. Little else is known about him. The scroll is one of the earliest known Chinese paintings to show a spinning wheel in use. It is held by the Palace Museum in Beijing.

title: Five Stars Rising in the East Armguard
about: A small rectangle of silk brocade, once worn as an armguard, woven in blue, green, red, yellow and white. Clouds curl across it, with birds, tigers and other creatures among them. Woven into the pattern are Chinese characters that read, roughly, "Five stars rising in the east, good for China." It refers to an old belief about the planets lining up as a lucky sign for the empire.
artistBio: It was woven in a Han dynasty silk workshop and carried far west along the trade routes. Archaeologists found it in 1995 in a tomb at Niya, an oasis site on the southern edge of the Taklamakan Desert. The dry sand kept the colors bright. It is held by the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region Museum in Ürümqi and is counted among China's most protected relics.
c: Five stars rising in the east brocade Niya

title: Textiles from the Cave of Letters
medium: Wool and linen, dyed wool yarn
about: Families hiding in a desert cave during the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome left behind their clothes and household goods. Among them were wool mantles with woven notched-band and gamma-shaped corner marks, tunics with colored stripes, and linen. There was even a bundle of dyed wool skeins in many colors, kept ready for weaving. They show what ordinary people wore in Judea nearly two thousand years ago.
artistBio: The textiles were made at home or by local weavers and dyers. Yigael Yadin's team excavated the cave in 1960 and 1961, along with letters from the revolt's leader that gave the cave its name. The desert air kept the wool and colors in good condition. The finds are held by the Israel Museum and Israeli antiquities collections.
c: Cave of Letters textiles Bar Kokhba

title: The Linen Wrappings of Wah
artist: Linen weavers of Middle Kingdom Egypt
about: Wah was a storeroom manager for an important official. When he died he was wrapped in a great quantity of fine linen sheets and pads, layer upon layer, until his mummy was much larger than his body. Some sheets carry small ink marks. X-rays later showed jewelry hidden inside, including a broad collar and a silver scarab, placed there by the people who wrapped him.
artistBio: The linen was woven from flax, probably in households and estate workshops, and saved over years for burial. Linen was valuable in Egypt, so wrapping a body in so much of it was a mark of care and status. Wah's tomb was found intact by Metropolitan Museum archaeologists in 1920. His mummy, still wrapped, is in the Met in New York.
c: Mummy of Wah Metropolitan Museum linen

title: The Chelsea Carpet
about: A large, very finely knotted carpet with a deep red ground. Two big star-shaped medallions sit in the middle, and the field around them is full of flowering trees, birds, lions, deer, dragons and phoenixes. The design is laid out in mirror image, so each half reflects the other. It feels like a garden full of life, packed with detail.
artistBio: It was knotted in Iran, probably in a court workshop, though the exact city is not known. The name is much later: the Victoria and Albert Museum bought it in the 1890s from a dealer on the King's Road in Chelsea, London. It is still in the V&A and is one of the best-known early Safavid carpets.
c: Chelsea carpet Victoria and Albert Museum

title: The Kiswah
artist: Weavers and embroiderers of the Kiswah workshop
medium: Black silk, gold- and silver-covered thread
about: The Kiswah is the black cloth that covers the Kaaba, the holiest site in Islam. It is made of panels of black silk woven with faint verses and prayers. Around the upper part runs a wide band of Quranic text, embroidered in gold- and silver-covered thread. A new Kiswah replaces the old one every year, and pieces of the old cloth are given as honored gifts.
artistBio: For centuries the cloth was made in Egypt and carried to Mecca in a grand procession, a custom that lasted until the 1960s. Today it is made in a dedicated workshop in Mecca, where weavers and embroiderers work on it through the year. The embroidery is done by hand with great care. It is one of the most honored textiles in the world.

title: Ottoman Imperial Tents
medium: Cotton, silk and wool appliqué on canvas
about: Ottoman sultans and generals went to war with whole tent palaces. The outside was plain, to shed rain. Inside, the walls were covered with appliqué: rows of arches, flowering vases, tulips and carnations cut from colored cloth and sewn down in red, blue and gold. Standing inside one felt like being in a garden pavilion rather than a camp.
artistBio: They were made by skilled tentmakers working for the state. Many tents came to Europe as war trophies, especially after the Ottoman defeat at Vienna in 1683, and others by trade and as gifts. Fine examples survive at Wawel Royal Castle in Kraków and in the Turkish Chamber in Dresden, among other collections.

title: Q'eswachaka Rope Bridge
date: Inca period to today, rebuilt every year
about: A footbridge of woven grass hangs over the Apurímac River gorge, about 30 meters long. Every year families from nearby Quechua communities gather grass, twist it into thin cords, then braid the cords into thick cables. Over a few days they stretch new cables across the river, weave on side rails and floor, and let the old bridge fall into the water. It is a fiber craft on a huge scale.
artistBio: The bridge is the last of its kind still kept up from the Inca road network, which used many grass bridges. Its rebuilding is a festival with offerings to Pachamama and shared meals. UNESCO listed the knowledge and rituals of its renewal in 2013. When the rebuilding was missed during the pandemic, the old bridge collapsed, and the communities rebuilt it in 2022.

title: Cowichan Sweater
artist: Coast Salish knitters of the Cowichan Valley
about: A heavy, warm sweater knitted from thick hand-spun wool in the sheep's own colors: cream, gray, brown and near black. Bands of geometric patterns, birds, deer or whales run around the body. The wool is spun only lightly, and often keeps some of its natural lanolin, so it sheds rain well. Many have a shawl collar and a zip front.
artistBio: Coast Salish women had a long tradition of spinning and weaving before settlers brought needle knitting in the 1800s. They joined the two skills and made something new. The sweaters became prized across Canada, and knitting kept many families going. In recent decades knitters have spoken out about cheap copies and stressed that a true Cowichan is made by Coast Salish hands.

title: Octopus Bags
artist: Métis, Cree, Dene and Ojibwe women
place: Northern Plains and Subarctic, North America
medium: Velvet or wool cloth, glass beads, silk thread
about: These bags get their name from the eight tabs that hang from the bottom in four pairs. They are usually made of black or dark blue velvet or wool cloth, covered in flowing floral designs in glass beads or silk embroidery. Men wore them at the belt or over the shoulder to carry pipes, tobacco and fire-making kits, which is why they are also called fire bags.
artistBio: They were made by women in Métis, Cree, Dene, Ojibwe and neighboring communities, especially in the fur trade country of the Red River and the north. The floral style was so strong among the Métis that the Dakota and Cree called them the flower beadwork people. Old bags are now in many museums, and beadworkers today still make them.

title: Two Grey Hills Rugs
artist: Diné (Navajo) weavers of Two Grey Hills and Toadlena
about: These rugs use only the natural colors of sheep: white, gray, tan, brown and black, with grays made by carding light and dark wool together. No dyes are used. A dark border frames a busy center of stepped diamonds and hooked shapes. The best are spun and woven so finely that they are often compared to tapestry. They look calm from a distance and complex up close.
artistBio: The style grew up in the early 1900s among Diné weavers near the Two Grey Hills and Toadlena trading posts, in the Chuska Mountains area. Families still raise sheep and spin their own yarn there. Daughters learn from mothers and grandmothers. Two Grey Hills weaving is among the most respected regional styles of Diné rugs.

title: Edo Firefighters' Coats (Hikeshi Banten)
medium: Layered cotton, sashiko quilting, resist dyeing
about: Edo's town firefighters wore thick coats made of several layers of cotton quilted together with close rows of stitching. Before going into a fire they soaked the coat in water to protect themselves from heat and sparks. The outside was usually plain indigo. The inside could hold a bold picture of a hero, a dragon or a tiger, shown off when the coat was turned out after a fire.
artistBio: Edo was a crowded wooden city where fires were common, and firefighting brigades were proud, close-knit groups. Their coats were made by local quilters and dyers. Few survive because they were worn hard. Fine examples are now in museums in Japan and abroad, and they are admired for both their sturdy stitching and their hidden art.

title: Kurume Kasuri
artist: Inoue Den and the weavers of Kurume
about: Kurume kasuri is cotton cloth with blurry white patterns in deep indigo. Before dyeing, bundles of yarn are tightly bound in places so the dye cannot reach them. When woven, the white spots line up into crosses, flowers, birds or simple pictures. The soft edges come from the tiny shifts of the yarn on the loom. It was everyday clothing cloth, strong and handsome.
artistBio: Local tradition credits Inoue Den, a girl in Kurume around 1800, who noticed white specks in a faded indigo garment and worked out how to make them on purpose. Her method spread through the region. Kurume kasuri became one of Japan's best-known cotton cloths. Today a small number of workshops still dye with natural indigo and weave by hand.

title: Amami Ōshima Tsumugi
artist: Weavers and mud dyers of Amami Ōshima
medium: Silk, dyed with sharinbai bark and iron-rich mud
about: This silk cloth has a deep, soft black-brown color and very fine patterns. The color comes from mud dyeing. Silk threads are dyed many times in a brown liquid made from the bark of the sharinbai tree, then rubbed in the iron-rich mud of the island's rice paddies. The tannin and iron react to make the dark shade. The pattern threads are bound and dyed before weaving.
artistBio: The cloth comes from Amami Ōshima, an island south of Kyushu, where weaving goes back centuries. In the Edo period it was sent as tribute to the Satsuma domain. The work is slow and passes through many hands, from binding the threads to weaving. It is prized for kimono today, and the island's makers work to keep the craft going.

title: Noren (Shop Curtains)
about: Noren are short fabric curtains hung across doorways, split into panels so people can pass through. Shops dye them with their name or crest, often in white on indigo. Hanging out the noren in the morning means the shop is open, and taking it in means closed. They also block wind, dust and sun, and keep a little privacy.
artistBio: Cloth door hangings appear in Japanese picture scrolls from the Heian period. By the Edo period every kind of shop used them. The word noren also came to mean a business's good name and reputation. Dyers still make them by hand with stencils and paste resist, and you see them in front of sushi bars, bathhouses and homes across Japan.

title: Hwarot (Korean Ceremonial Robe)
medium: Silk, embroidered with silk and gold thread
about: A long red silk robe with wide sleeves banded in blue, yellow, and other colors, ending in white cuffs that hide the hands. The robe is covered in embroidery: peonies, lotus flowers, phoenixes, water, rocks and characters for long life and many children. Each picture is a wish for the person wearing it. The robe is heavy, bright and full of meaning.
artistBio: The hwarot began as formal dress for royal women in the Joseon court. Later, ordinary brides were allowed to wear one on their wedding day, a single day of royal dress. Embroiderers at court and in homes made them. Many survive, and fine examples are in the National Palace Museum of Korea and other collections.

title: Bai Tie-Dye of Zhoucheng
about: White patterns of flowers, butterflies, fish and stars float on a blue background. To make them, women draw a design on white cotton, then stitch along the lines and pull the thread tight, or bind small bunches of cloth. The cloth goes into indigo vats many times. When the stitches are cut, the hidden parts show white, with soft, feathery edges.
artistBio: The Bai people of the Dali area have a long tie-dye tradition, and the village of Zhoucheng is its best-known center. The cloth was used for headscarves, clothes, and household cloths. Many families still stitch at home and bring work to local dyeing workshops. The craft is recognized as part of China's national intangible heritage.

title: Rogan Art
about: Rogan is painting with a thick, sticky paste made by boiling castor oil for days and mixing it with color. The artist lifts a thread of paste on a metal stylus and lets it fall onto the cloth in fine lines, without the stylus touching the fabric. Often half a design is drawn, then the cloth is folded to print a mirror image on the other half. The usual motif is a tree of life.
artistBio: Rogan was once used to decorate clothes and bedding in Kutch. As cheaper printed cloth arrived, it nearly died out. One Khatri family in the village of Nirona kept it going and now teaches others. Rogan became widely known in 2014, when India's prime minister gave a Rogan tree of life to the US president.

title: Swat Valley Embroidery
about: Dense geometric patterns in bright pink and magenta silk cover dark cotton cloth. Most of the stitching is surface darning worked from the back, counting the threads of the cloth to make stars, triangles and stepped diamonds. Small touches of yellow, white or green break up the pink. It was used for women's shawls, wedding shawls, dresses and bedding.
artistBio: The embroidery was made by women in the villages of the Swat Valley in northern Pakistan. It is related to the phulkari of Punjab but has its own bold style. Older pieces were collected widely in the 20th century and are now in museums and private collections. Embroiderers in the region still work in the same stitches.

title: Qalamkar of Isfahan
about: Qalamkar cloths are cotton printed by hand with carved wooden blocks. The printer dips a block in dye and stamps it onto the cloth, again and again, matching edges to build borders, medallions, birds, flowers and sometimes figures. Colors are mostly reds, browns, blacks and soft blues. The finished pieces become tablecloths, wall hangings and bed covers.
artistBio: The name means work of the pen, from an older practice of drawing designs on cloth by hand. Block printing became the main method, and Isfahan its center. The craft has been passed down in workshops in the city's bazaars, where printers still work at long tables. Many blocks in use are family heirlooms.

title: Assiut Shawl (Tulle bi Telli)
artist: Embroiderers of Assiut and Upper Egypt
medium: Cotton net with flat metal strips
about: These shawls are made of fine cotton net worked with tiny flat strips of silver, copper or brass. The embroiderer threads a strip through a wide needle, passes it through the net, then folds and presses it flat. Thousands of small metal stitches make diamonds, birds, camels and people. The shawl is soft and drapes well, and it shimmers as it moves.
artistBio: The craft grew in Upper Egypt, especially around the city of Assiut. In the 1920s these shawls became a fashion in Europe and America and were worn as dresses and wraps in the Art Deco years. Egyptian women still make them, and the old ones are sought after by collectors and dancers.

title: Akhnif Cloak
about: The akhnif is a hooded wool cape worn by men in the mountains of southern Morocco. It is dark, often black or deep blue, with a large almond-shaped panel in orange or red across the back, woven with small patterns inside. Many people see an eye in the shape. The cape is woven all in one piece, including the shaping for the hood.
artistBio: The capes were woven by Amazigh women on upright looms in their homes, and they took weeks of work. They were worn for warmth and on important occasions. Fewer are made now, though some weavers still keep the skill. Old capes are in museums of Moroccan art and in private collections.

title: African Wax Print
artist: Dutch and African mills; West African traders and designers
place: Netherlands, West Africa and Central Africa
about: Wax prints are bright cotton cloths printed on both sides with bold patterns, often with fine crackle lines where dye seeped through the resist. Patterns range from flowers and birds to everyday objects, and many get popular names from traders and wearers. In much of West and Central Africa they are used for dresses, wrappers and outfits for weddings and celebrations.
artistBio: In the 1800s Dutch factories made machine copies of Javanese batik for sale in Indonesia, but the copies did not sell well there. They found a much bigger market in West Africa, where buyers liked the crackle and color. Vlisco, founded in 1846 in Helmond, is the best-known maker. Today many wax prints are made in Africa, and African designers lead the style.

title: Dida Raffia Cloth
about: Dida raffia cloths are woven as tubes, squares and long scarves from raffia palm fiber. After weaving, the cloth is tied in many small bunches and dyed, so patterns of circles, dots and lines appear in yellow, red, brown and black. The result is soft-edged and lively. The cloths were worn as skirts and wraps on special occasions.
artistBio: They were made by the Dida people of southern Côte d'Ivoire. Raffia weaving is an old craft across Central and West Africa, but the Dida tube-woven cloths are especially distinct. They became valued by collectors in the 20th century and are now in museum collections in Africa, Europe and North America.

title: Santa Cruz Feather Money (Tevau)
artist: Makers of the Santa Cruz Islands
date: Probably centuries old; made into the 20th century
about: Tevau is a long coil made of thousands of tiny plaques, each covered with the bright red feathers of a small forest bird, the scarlet honeyeater. The plaques overlap like scales along a fiber backing, and a finished coil can be many meters long. It was rolled up and kept safe in the house. Its main use was in marriage payments.
artistBio: Making tevau took the work of several specialists: bird catchers, people who made the plaques, and the one who bound the coil. The skill was held in the Santa Cruz Islands of the southeastern Solomons. Coils are kept by families and are also held in museum collections around the world.

title: Yolŋu Pandanus Weaving
about: Yolŋu weavers strip young pandanus leaves, dry them and dye them with roots, bark and other plants. A yellow root gives yellow, and mixed with ash it turns red. The strips are coiled or twined into mats, baskets, string bags and dilly bags called bathi. Some are plain and practical, others are bold with stripes and color.
artistBio: Weaving has long been part of Yolŋu life and ceremony, with knowledge passed down by women. Some sacred forms are for ceremony only. Today weavers work through community art centers in places such as Galiwin'ku and Ramingining, and their work is shown in major Australian galleries alongside bark painting.

title: Jaki-ed (Marshallese Clothing Mats)
about: Jaki-ed are finely plaited mats once worn as clothing, wrapped around the waist. They are woven from soft prepared pandanus leaf, with borders of geometric patterns in dark hibiscus fiber. The finest are thin and supple like cloth. Wearing them marked rank and belonging, and they were also given as valued gifts.
artistBio: Women of the Marshall Islands made them for centuries. After missionaries brought cotton clothing in the 1800s, the mats were no longer worn and the skill faded. Only a few elders kept it alive. In recent years Marshallese weavers and cultural programs have worked to revive jaki-ed and teach it to younger women.

title: The Sheldon Tapestry Maps
about: These are large wall hangings that show maps of English counties, woven in tapestry. Rivers wind in blue, towns appear as tiny churches and houses, and hills, parks and woods are all marked. Borders are full of flowers, fruit and figures. They are among the earliest maps of English counties made at this scale, and they were meant to impress visitors.
artistBio: Ralph Sheldon, a Warwickshire landowner, commissioned them for his house. They were probably woven in a workshop at Barcheston connected to his family. The set covered Worcestershire, Warwickshire, Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire. Surviving pieces are held in Warwick, at the Market Hall Museum, and in Oxford, among other places.

title: The Mortlake Acts of the Apostles
about: These tapestries show scenes from the lives of Peter and Paul, such as the miraculous catch of fishes and Paul preaching at Athens. The designs come from Raphael's full-size cartoons, first made for the Sistine Chapel a century earlier. The Mortlake weavers added new wide borders. The figures are large and solid, and the scenes read clearly from across a room.
artistBio: The Mortlake works was set up in 1619 under James I, with weavers brought from Flanders. In 1623 Prince Charles, later Charles I, bought seven of Raphael's cartoons so Mortlake could weave from them. Several sets were made, and some survive in English country houses and European collections. The cartoons themselves are on loan to the V&A from the Royal Collection.
c: Mortlake tapestry Acts of the Apostles

title: Perugia Towels
medium: Linen with blue cotton pattern bands
about: Long white linen cloths with bands of blue pattern woven across the ends. The bands hold rows of griffins, lions, birds, dragons, castles and fountains, often facing each other in pairs. They were used as towels, table runners and covers in churches and homes. You can spot them on the tables of Italian paintings of the Last Supper from the period.
artistBio: They take their name from Perugia, though they were woven in many towns in Umbria and nearby. Weavers made them on simple pattern looms, and the blue came from woad or indigo-dyed cotton. Many survive because churches kept them. Examples are in museums such as the Met, the V&A and Italian collections, and modern weavers in Umbria still make them.

title: Roba de Llengües (Mallorcan Ikat)
about: Roba de llengües means cloth of tongues. It is an ikat: the threads are tied and dyed before weaving, so the pattern has soft, flickering edges, like little flames or tongues. Colors are usually blue, red, green or ochre on a light ground. It is used for curtains, bedspreads and upholstery, and is part of the look of old Mallorcan houses.
artistBio: Ikat probably came to Mallorca through Mediterranean trade, and the island made it its own. Once many workshops wove it. Today a few family workshops still produce it, some with old shuttle looms. It is one of the very few European ikat traditions still alive.

title: Lenços dos Namorados (Sweetheart Handkerchiefs)
artist: Young women of the Minho region
about: A square handkerchief embroidered with hearts, keys, birds, flowers and short love verses. The verses are often written as spoken, with spelling mistakes that are now part of the charm. A young woman made one for the man she liked and gave it to him. If he wore it in public, it meant he accepted her. If he gave it back, the answer was no.
artistBio: The tradition comes from the villages of the Minho, around Viana do Castelo and Vila Verde. Girls learned embroidery at home, and the handkerchief was a way to speak about love without words being said out loud. Today local women make them both to keep the custom and for sale, and the region protects them as a certified craft.

title: Szűr (Hungarian Herdsman's Cloak)
medium: Fulled wool cloth, appliqué and embroidery
about: The szűr is a long, heavy cloak of thick white fulled wool, worn by shepherds and herdsmen of the Great Hungarian Plain. It was worn draped over the shoulders with the sleeves hanging empty. The sleeves were often sewn shut at the end and used as pockets. The collar and edges carry bright appliqué and embroidery of roses and tulips in red, blue and green.
artistBio: Szűr were made by guild tailors, the szűrszabók, from cloth fulled by local mills. Richer decoration showed a young man's pride. A well-known custom gave rise to a saying: a suitor left his cloak at a girl's house, and if it was put outside the door, he was rejected. Hungarians still say someone's szűr was put out when they are sent away.

title: Koniaków Lace
about: Koniaków lace is crocheted with very fine thread into doilies, tablecloths, collars and curtains. Designs are full of flowers, leaves and star shapes, worked in openwork so they look almost like bobbin lace. Each maker has her own patterns, often worked out in her head rather than written down. The lace is usually white or cream, crisp and delicate.
artistBio: The craft grew in this mountain village in southern Poland in the early 1900s and spread through families, mostly women. It became a source of income in a poor farming area. In the 2000s the crocheters made headlines by also making lace underwear, which brought new interest. Koniaków now has a lace museum and holds lace fairs.

title: Kihnu Striped Skirts (Kört)
about: On the small island of Kihnu, women still wear long wool skirts woven at home with vertical stripes. Red is the main color, mixed with orange, black, green and blue stripes. The skirts are worn every day, not only on festival days. The shades of the stripes can change with a woman's age and life, and darker skirts are worn in times of mourning.
artistBio: Kihnu kept its old ways partly because it is isolated in the Gulf of Riga. Women weave, knit mittens and stockings, and pass on songs and dances. In 2008 UNESCO added the Kihnu cultural space to its intangible heritage list. The striped skirt is the island's best-known sign of that living culture.

title: Lielvārde Belt
about: A long, narrow belt woven in red and white, with a dense run of small geometric shapes along its length. It is woven with many fine warp threads, and the pattern appears as the weaver picks up threads by hand. Many people read the shapes as old Latvian signs. The belt is wrapped several times around the waist with folk dress.
artistBio: It takes its name from the town of Lielvārde, on the Daugava River, where it was part of local dress. In the 20th century it became a national symbol, worn at song festivals and used in designs and logos. Weavers still make them by hand, and a single belt can take weeks.

title: Welsh Tapestry Blankets
about: Welsh tapestry blankets are not tapestry at all, but double cloth: two layers of wool woven at once and swapped back and forth to make the pattern. The result is thick, warm and reversible, with colors swapped on the back. Classic designs are bold geometric shapes, and in the 1960s and 70s mills made them in strong oranges, browns and purples.
artistBio: Wales had many small woollen mills powered by streams. Double-cloth blankets became their best-known product. Most mills closed in the 20th century, but a few still work, and old blankets have become popular again with collectors. A Welsh blanket was once a common wedding gift, called a carthen.

title: Sanquhar Gloves
about: Sanquhar gloves are knitted in two colors, usually black and white, in small all-over check patterns. Each pattern has a name, such as the Duke, the Shepherd's Plaid or Midge and Fly. The wearer's initials are often knitted into the cuff. They are knitted fine and tight, so they fit closely and keep the wind out. Each finger is patterned too.
artistBio: The small town of Sanquhar in southwest Scotland had a long knitting tradition, making stockings and gloves from local wool. The patterns were passed from knitter to knitter. The craft almost faded in the 20th century, but local knitters and patterns published by others kept it alive. Sanquhar gloves are now known to knitters around the world.

title: Valenciennes Lace
about: Valenciennes lace is a flat, fine bobbin lace. The pattern and the mesh ground are made together from the same thread, with no heavier outline thread around the flowers. That makes it smooth and even, and strong enough to wash. It was used to trim collars, cuffs, handkerchiefs and baby clothes. The finest pieces took a very long time to make.
artistBio: It began in the town of Valenciennes, then part of Flanders and later of France. The lace was famous in the 1700s. Later the main centers moved to Belgian towns such as Ypres, where lacemakers worked into the 1900s. Machine-made versions became common, but handmade Valenciennes is still admired as one of the most refined bobbin laces.

title: Gion Matsuri Float Hangings
artist: Kyoto float neighborhoods; weavers from many lands
about: Each July, huge wooden floats roll through Kyoto for the Gion Festival. Their sides are hung with textiles: Japanese embroidery and brocade, Chinese silks, Persian and Indian carpets, and even Flemish tapestries showing scenes from European stories. Because of these hangings, the floats are often called moving museums. Some pieces are hundreds of years old.
artistBio: The festival began over a thousand years ago as a ritual against plague. Merchant neighborhoods in Kyoto, each owning a float, bought rare imported textiles through trade to decorate them. Many originals are now preserved and replaced with careful new copies woven in Kyoto. The festival is listed by UNESCO as intangible heritage.

title: Fabric Sculptures
about: Sonia Gomes makes sculptures by twisting, knotting, wrapping and stitching cloth. Many pieces hang from the ceiling like vines or swollen knots. She uses old fabrics, lace, and clothing, often given to her by people who want their old things to live on. The works carry traces of the lives and bodies those fabrics touched.
artistBio: Sonia Gomes is a Brazilian artist from Minas Gerais. She began showing her work later in life, and gained wide attention when she was included in the Venice Biennale in 2015. She speaks of her work as connected to her Afro-Brazilian heritage and to handwork learned in childhood. Her sculptures are in major museum collections.

title: Santa Cruz River
about: A long carpet that shows a stretch of the Santa Cruz River in Patagonia from above, with blue water, green banks and gray rocks. It is tufted by hand from wool, with thick and thin piles to suggest the land's shape. The work records a landscape at risk from dam building. You can walk beside it and see the river like a map.
artistBio: Alexandra Kehayoglou is an Argentine artist who grew up around her family's carpet factory in Buenos Aires. She uses leftover wool from the factory to make carpets of grasslands, glaciers and rivers. She also made a runway carpet of a meadow for a Dries Van Noten fashion show. Her work joins textile craft with concern for the land.

title: Coral Reef Textiles
medium: Wool and cotton yarns, latch hook, crochet, felting
about: Big wall pieces that look like coral reefs seen from above. Some areas are bright with color, others are bleached white to show reefs that are dying. The surfaces are built from many techniques: latch-hook rug making, crochet, knitting and felting. Bumps, loops and tufts make them look alive. The yarn is mostly leftover from the textile industry.
artistBio: Vanessa Barragão is a Portuguese textile artist from the Algarve coast. She works with deadstock and waste yarns from factories to cut waste in her own practice. Her pieces speak about ocean life and climate change. She makes them by hand in her studio.

title: Hereke Carpets
artist: Weavers of the Hereke Imperial Factory
about: Hereke carpets are known for their very fine knotting, especially the silk ones, which can have more than a hundred knots in each square centimeter. Designs often follow classical Ottoman and Persian patterns: medallions, flowering vines, prayer arches and garden scenes. The silk catches the light, so colors seem to change as you walk around the carpet.
artistBio: The Ottoman state founded a factory at Hereke, near İzmit, in 1843 to supply the palaces, including the new Dolmabahçe Palace. It wove silks and carpets for the court and as diplomatic gifts. After the empire ended, the factory continued under the Turkish state. Today the name Hereke stands for top-quality Turkish carpets.

title: Pochampally Ikat
about: Pochampally ikat saris have crisp geometric patterns in diamonds, zigzags and checks. Before weaving, the threads are tied and dyed in planned sections, sometimes both warp and weft, so the pattern forms on the loom. The colors are strong and the edges slightly blurred, which gives ikat its look. Cotton is used for everyday saris and silk for special ones.
artistBio: Pochampally is a village in Telangana that gave its name to the style; many nearby villages also weave it. The village is called Bhoodan Pochampally because in 1951 it saw the first land gift of Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan movement. The weaving has a protected geographical indication. Many families work on handlooms at home.

title: Inabel
about: Inabel is a strong, soft cotton cloth woven on handlooms in the north of the Philippines. It is used for blankets, towels and clothing. The best-known pattern is binakol, a dizzying design of lines that seem to spin and bend. People say the pattern confuses and keeps away bad spirits, which is why binakol blankets are used on beds.
artistBio: Weaving in Ilocos goes back centuries, and the region traded its cloth widely. The craft declined in the 20th century as factory cloth took over. Weavers in towns such as Paoay and Vigan keep it alive, and recent revival efforts have brought inabel into fashion and home design.

title: Funeral Banner of Lady Dai
about: A T-shaped painting on silk that lay over the coffin of Lady Dai. It shows three worlds. At the top is heaven, with the sun holding a crow and the moon holding a toad. In the middle, the elderly Lady Dai leans on a cane with her attendants. At the bottom is the underworld, held up by a giant figure. It is a map of the soul's journey.
artistBio: It was painted by unknown court artists of the Western Han dynasty. It was found in 1972 in Tomb 1 at Mawangdui, along with Lady Dai's remarkably preserved body and fine silk clothing. It is one of the earliest major Chinese paintings on silk, and is held by the Hunan Museum in Changsha.

title: Portrait of Eleonora of Toledo with Her Son
about: Eleonora of Toledo, wife of Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, sits beside her young son Giovanni. Most of the painting is her dress: white satin covered in a bold black and gold pattern of arabesques and pomegranate-like shapes, cut in velvet and woven with metal thread. Bronzino paints each loop of thread and the pearls at her neck with cool precision.
artistBio: Agnolo Bronzino was the Medici court painter in Florence. The dress shows off the silk weaving that made Florence rich. A long-told story said Eleonora was buried in this dress, but her grave held a different one. The painting is in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

title: March: The Triumph of Minerva
about: This fresco is part of a great hall painted with the months of the year. In the top band for March, Minerva, goddess of wisdom and crafts, rides in a chariot drawn by unicorns. On one side gather scholars and lawyers. On the other sit women busy with cloth work at looms and embroidery frames. It honors weaving and needlework as arts under Minerva's care.
artistBio: Francesco del Cossa was a painter from Ferrara who worked for Duke Borso d'Este. The Hall of the Months was painted by him and other Ferrarese artists. Some of the frescoes have been lost, but March is among the best preserved. It remains in place at Palazzo Schifanoia in Ferrara.
c: Francesco del Cossa March Triumph of Minerva Schifanoia

title: Suzanne Sewing
about: A woman sits on the edge of a bed, unclothed, mending a piece of white cloth in her lap. Behind her hangs a mandolin and a piece of patterned fabric. The light is plain and the body is painted without flattery. It is a quiet, ordinary moment of sewing, shown with an honesty that surprised viewers at the time.
artistBio: Paul Gauguin painted it early in his career, when he was still a stockbroker and Sunday painter. It was shown at the Impressionist exhibition of 1881, where the critic J.-K. Huysmans praised it. It is now in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek in Copenhagen.

title: The Girlhood of Mary Virgin
about: The young Mary sits at an embroidery frame, stitching a lily onto red cloth. Her mother, Saint Anne, sits beside her and watches. An angel tends a lily plant, and her father Joachim prunes a vine outside. Everything is full of symbols: the lily for purity, the books for virtues. The embroidery shows Mary at work on a woman's household craft.
artistBio: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. This was his first finished oil painting, and one of the first works signed with the letters PRB. His sister Christina posed for Mary, and his mother for Saint Anne. The painting is at Tate Britain in London.

title: Trapunto
about: Trapunto is stuffed quilting. Two layers of cloth are stitched together along the outlines of a design. Then, from the back, the maker opens a small gap in the lower layer and pushes in wadding or cord to fill each shape. The design rises up like low relief. Seen in raking light, a plain white trapunto piece looks carved.
artistBio: The name is Italian, and one of the oldest known examples is the Tristan Quilt, made in Sicily in the late 1300s. Whitework quilts with stuffed and corded designs were popular in Europe and America in the 1700s and 1800s. Quilters today use the same idea by hand and by machine, often adding extra wadding only under chosen motifs.

title: Maedeup (Korean Knotting)
about: Maedeup is the Korean art of decorative knotting. A single silk cord, often folded in two, is tied into tight, symmetrical knots with names taken from flowers, insects and everyday things, like the butterfly knot or the chrysanthemum knot. Knots are combined with tassels to make ornaments. The front and back look the same, and the knots are pulled firm so they hold their shape.
artistBio: Knotted cords and tassels decorated clothing, fans, instruments and palace furnishings in Korea for centuries, and the craft flourished in the Joseon period. The best-known use is the norigae, an ornament hung from a woman's hanbok. Korea recognizes master knotters as holders of intangible cultural heritage, and they still dye the cords and make the tassels by hand.

title: Nuno Felting
about: In nuno felting, loose wool fibers are laid thinly on a sheer fabric such as silk gauze or chiffon. The maker wets them with warm soapy water and rubs and rolls the layers. The wool fibers work their way through the open weave and lock into it, then shrink. The fabric puckers into ripples and texture, making a light, drapey felt.
artistBio: The method was developed in the early 1990s by the Australian feltmaker Polly Stirling, working with Sachiko Kotaka. The name comes from nuno, the Japanese word for cloth. It spread quickly through feltmaking groups worldwide. It is now popular for scarves, garments and art pieces, and is a good use for fine wools.

title: English Paper Piecing
about: Fabric is folded and basted over small paper shapes, most often hexagons. Two covered shapes are held face to face and their edges whipped together with tiny stitches, then more are added one by one. When all the sides are joined, the basting and papers come out. It makes sharp points and angles, and it can be done by hand anywhere, a few pieces at a time.
artistBio: The method was common in Britain by the 1700s, and quilters took it to America and Australia. The hexagon pattern Grandmother's Flower Garden is its best-known design. In some old quilts the papers were left inside, and historians use the letters, bills and school copybooks cut for templates to help date the quilts.

title: Clamp-Resist Dyeing
about: A pair of wooden boards is carved with the same design in mirror image. Folded cloth is clamped tightly between them. When dye is poured in, it flows through channels in the boards and reaches only the uncovered parts, while the pressed parts stay pale. Unfolded, the cloth shows a repeating pattern, often mirrored, with soft edges.
artistBio: The method, called jiaxie in Chinese, was used in Tang China, and fine examples survive in the Shōsōin treasure house in Nara. In Japan a related method is called itajime.
