In southern Zhejiang, dyers made blue and white clamp-resist quilt covers with story scenes into the 20th century, and a few workshops still make them.

title: Fulling and Waulking
about: Fulling finishes woven wool cloth. The cloth is soaked and pounded, trampled or rubbed, so the wool fibers tangle and shrink a little. It becomes thicker, softer, warmer and better at keeping out wind and rain. In the Scottish Hebrides this was called waulking: women sat around a long board and beat the wet tweed in rhythm, singing Gaelic waulking songs to keep time.
artistBio: Fulling is very old; the Romans had fulling workshops. Water-powered fulling mills spread across medieval Europe. The work left its mark on English surnames: Fuller, Tucker and Walker all once meant someone who fulled cloth. Waulking by hand went on in the Hebrides into the 20th century, and its songs are still sung today.

title: Shen Shou
about: Shen Shou was born in Suzhou and learned embroidery as a small child from her mother. In 1904 she embroidered pieces for the Empress Dowager Cixi's seventieth birthday, and Cixi gave her the name Shou, meaning long life. She went to Japan to study art and craft, then ran embroidery schools in China. Late in life, as she grew ill, she dictated her methods to the scholar Zhang Jian.
artistBio: She developed a style called simulation embroidery, using many shades of silk and changing stitch directions to show light and shadow as in Western painting. Her embroidered portrait of Queen Elena of Italy was sent to Italy in 1911, and her portrait of Jesus won a top prize at the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition. Her manual, published in 1919, is still studied.

title: Keisuke Serizawa
about: Keisuke Serizawa grew up in Shizuoka and trained in design. In the late 1920s he read the ideas of Yanagi Sōetsu about the beauty of everyday crafts and saw Okinawan bingata cloth. Both changed his life. He went to Okinawa to learn and became a stencil dyer, cutting his own paper stencils and dyeing cloth with rice-paste resist.
artistBio: His work includes kimono, folding screens, banners, calendars and book designs, with clear, cheerful shapes, letters and scenes. He was a leading figure in the mingei folk craft movement. In 1956 he was named a Living National Treasure for katazome. A museum devoted to his work and his collections stands in Shizuoka.

title: Mary Meigs Atwater
about: Mary Meigs Atwater was born in Illinois and studied art. She moved with her husband, a mining engineer, to mining towns in the American West. In the 1910s she took up handweaving and became fascinated with old American coverlet patterns. She studied, collected and decoded them, at a time when few people in the United States still wove by hand.
artistBio: In the 1920s she founded the Shuttle-Craft Guild, which sent weaving patterns and lessons by mail to weavers around the country. Her Shuttle-Craft Book of American Hand-Weaving appeared in 1928. She is often called the dean of American handweaving, and she helped spark the 20th-century weaving revival.

title: Theo Moorman
about: Theo Moorman was an English weaver who studied at the Central School of Arts and Crafts in London. She worked as a designer in the textile industry. In her own studio she wove wall hangings and church textiles. She wanted weaving to be taken seriously as an art, not only as a way to make cloth.
artistBio: She invented a weave now called the Moorman technique: a fine, nearly invisible second warp ties down thick yarns and fabric strips laid on top of a base cloth. It lets weavers build pictures freely on the loom. Her book Weaving as an Art Form, from 1975, spread the technique worldwide, and weavers still use it.

title: Marie Webster
about: Marie Webster was a quilter from Indiana who began making her own quilt designs in middle age. In 1911 the Ladies' Home Journal printed her quilts in color, and readers wanted patterns. Her designs were mostly appliqué flowers in soft pinks, greens and blues, with clean, open layouts. They looked fresh and modern next to older busy quilts.
artistBio: In 1915 she published Quilts: Their Story and How to Make Them, the first book on the history of American quilts. She later ran a mail-order pattern business with friends from her home in Marion. Her house is now home to the Quilters Hall of Fame, and her quilts are in museum collections.

title: The Bauhaus Weaving Workshop
about: The Bauhaus art school opened in 1919 and promised equal places for women. In practice many women were steered into the weaving workshop. They made it one of the school's most successful parts. At first they wove bold pictorial hangings. Later, under Gunta Stölzl, who became the school's first woman master in 1927, they designed fabrics for factories and sold the designs.
artistBio: Students such as Anni Albers, Otti Berger and Benita Koch-Otte tested new fibers, structures and uses for cloth, from wall coverings to sound-absorbing fabric. The school closed in 1933 under Nazi pressure, and many weavers left Germany. Their ideas shaped modern textile design and the teaching of weaving in Europe and America.

title: The Terrible Knitters of Dent
about: In the Yorkshire Dales, whole families knitted stockings, gloves and caps for sale. Men, women and children knitted while walking, herding or talking, using a knitting stick tucked in the belt to hold one needle and speed things up. In winter, neighbors gathered in one house in the evening to knit together by the fire and share light and warmth.
artistBio: The poet Robert Southey wrote about the terrible knitters of Dent in the 1830s, terrible meaning remarkably fast. Their knitting brought cash to poor hill farms, with goods sold through Kendal. The trade faded with machine knitting, but carved knitting sticks and Dales gloves survive, and the story is a reminder of how much daily life once rested on wool.

title: Snail Purple of Oaxaca
medium: Cotton dyed with sea snail secretion
about: This purple comes from a sea snail, Plicopurpura pansa, that lives on rocks along Mexico's Pacific coast. Dyers find the snails at low tide, blow or press on them gently so they release a few drops of liquid, and dab it onto skeins of cotton thread. Then they put the snail back on the rock, alive. In the sun the color turns from pale green to purple.
artistBio: Mixtec dyers from towns such as Pinotepa de Don Luis have done this for centuries, walking the coast for weeks. The purple thread was woven into posahuanco wrap skirts with indigo and red stripes. Overharvesting in the 20th century harmed the snail, and it is now protected. Unlike Tyrian purple, this dye did not require killing the snails.

title: The Stocking Frame
about: The stocking frame was the first knitting machine. It has a row of fine hooked needles, one for each stitch. The operator uses foot treadles and hand levers to lay yarn across all the needles and pull a whole row of loops through at once. It made flat knitted fabric, which was then sewn into stockings, much faster than knitting by hand.
artistBio: William Lee, a clergyman from Calverton, invented it in 1589. Elizabeth I refused him a patent, and he took his machine to France, where he died. His frame still spread and founded the framework knitting trade of the English Midlands. Frame breaking by the Luddites was aimed at these machines. Modern knitting machines still use the same basic idea.

title: Wool Combs
about: Wool combs have one or more rows of long, sharp steel teeth set in a wooden head with a handle. Wool is loaded onto one comb, and the other is drawn through it again and again. This pulls long fibers straight and parallel and leaves the short ones behind. The long, combed fiber spins into smooth, strong worsted yarn. Combs were often warmed on a stove to help them work.
artistBio: Combing for worsted was skilled, hot work. In England woolcombers had their own trade societies and claimed Bishop Blaise as their patron saint. In the 1800s combing machines in Bradford and elsewhere replaced handcombers. Today hand combs are back in use among spinners who want silky, smooth yarns from long-wool breeds.
